# PEG-LEG GREG — BOOK III — ACT II: THE PRICE OF ATTENTION

**Manuscript-only NotebookLM source. Chapters 220–280.**

---

# CHAPTER 220

## THE LANDLORD

I bought bread on the way to the theatre.

This should not have required a decision.

It did.

The baker named the price. I paid it. He gave me bread. Nobody congratulated me for preserving my ability to remain alive while owing Antonius Vale money.

Progress.

I also bought a small cake of soap because ours had become a translucent insult beside the basin. That hurt more.

Bread was food. Food was defensible.

Soap felt optional right up until I remembered Lyssa leaning away from my shirt the previous evening and saying, "You work in a theatre full of people."

She had not actually said I smelled.

She had created a structure in which I could reach the intended conclusion.

Theatre was corrupting everyone.

I put the soap in my coat, hung the bread from one crutch in a cloth bag, and continued west.

No Hessa note had been under the cup that morning. No magic. No symptoms. Nothing new in my right arm, hand, shoulder, residual limb, or phantom foot. Thirty draws. Twenty-six deliberate shaping attempts. Thirty-four supervised external attempts. One far response observed once and not established as anything more useful than that.

The numbers stayed where they were.

Good.

The theatre did not.

A boy was waiting outside when I arrived.

Not one of ours.

Olin's delivery boy.

He recognized me first.

"You're the oil man."

I stopped.

"I carried one tin."

"Oil man."

"I have done other things."

He shrugged.

I looked at the open front door.

"Why are you outside?"

"Woman's busy."

That could describe Rinna at every hour I had known her.

Inside, someone was dragging a bench across the floor. Jori was on a ladder adjusting a lamp bracket. Nessa had a green coat spread over two chairs and was arguing with Pell about whether a tear had existed yesterday. Marek stood onstage holding a wooden cane and looking deeply pleased with himself.

Normal.

Good.

The boy said, "Master Olin sent me."

That changed the morning.

I looked at him again.

"The man came back?"

"Yes."

"Brown coat?"

"Yes."

"Thin face?"

"Yes."

"Dark hair?"

"Yes."

"Quiet?"

The boy thought.

"Not loud."

Better answer.

"Did Olin tell you to tell me?"

"He said tell the woman."

"Excellent."

I moved aside and pointed through the door.

"Let's find the woman."

Rinna was in the rear passage counting folded handbills while Davin tried to convince her that twelve and fourteen were different numbers for a reason.

"They are both enough," she said.

"For different streets."

"People can walk."

"That is not how handbills work."

"Then make more."

Davin looked at me.

"Help."

"No."

"Coward."

"Olin sent word."

Rinna stopped counting.

The boy appeared behind me.

She put the handbills down.

"What happened?"

The boy told it badly.

That was not criticism. He was thirteen and had apparently been sent across Carrow because an adult merchant did not want to leave his shop. He started with the man coming in, skipped to Olin getting angry, returned to a question about oil, forgot whether the man had touched the counter, remembered he had not, and then explained that Master Olin had said not to answer anything.

Rinna did not interrupt until he finished.

Then she asked, "What did he ask? Exact if you can."

The boy looked at the ceiling.

"If you bought the oil."

"How?"

"He said, 'She bought it anyway?'"

Rinna nodded once.

"Then?"

"Master Olin said he doesn't talk about customers."

"Good."

The boy looked surprised by the praise.

"Then he asked if you paid cash."

"Exact?"

"I think, 'She paid cash for it?'"

"What did Olin say?"

"Same thing. Customers."

Rinna glanced at me.

I said nothing.

The boy continued.

"Then he asked if you were still doing shows. Master Olin said if he wanted a handbill he could get one somewhere else."

Davin made a small sound that might have been a laugh.

Rinna did not.

"Anything else?"

The boy hesitated.

"He asked where you keep it."

Rinna's face changed.

Not fear.

Attention.

"Keep what?"

"Money."

"Exact words."

The boy squeezed his eyes shut.

"Does the woman keep the money at the hall?"

Nobody spoke for a moment.

From the stage, Marek shouted, "I am not limping. The character is limping."

Nessa shouted back, "The character is doing it badly."

The boy looked toward the noise.

Rinna said, "What did Olin answer?"

"He told him to buy oil or leave."

"Did he buy oil?"

"No."

"Did he leave?"

"Yes."

"Did he threaten Olin?"

"No."

"Did he say Bren?"

"No."

"Did he say theatre money was spoken for again?"

"No."

"Did he ask about carts?"

"No."

"Did he ask about Greg?"

The boy looked at me.

"Oil man?"

I closed my eyes.

"Greg," Rinna said.

"No."

Good.

Rinna took a scrap of paper from the shelf and wrote while the boy watched.

MAN RETURNED TO OLIN.

ASKED:
SHE BOUGHT IT ANYWAY?
SHE PAID CASH FOR IT?
STILL DOING SHOWS?
DOES THE WOMAN KEEP THE MONEY AT THE HALL?

OLIN GAVE NO ANSWERS.

She looked at the boy.

"Anything wrong?"

He read slowly.

"He said 'she bought it anyway,' not 'did she.'"

Rinna scratched out the first line and rewrote it.

I liked him.

"Anything else?" she asked.

"No."

"Good. Tell Olin thank you."

The boy did not leave.

Rinna waited.

He shifted his feet.

"I saw him later."

There it was.

I felt the old part of my mind stand up too quickly.

Rinna said, "Where?"

"I had the glass order for the woman near South Steps. He was ahead of me after I came off Narrow Street."

"Doing what?"

"Walking."

"With anyone?"

"No."

"Following anyone?"

"Don't know."

"Which way?"

"Toward Mason's Cut."

My hands tightened on the crutch grips.

Mason's Cut.

Grit on Bren's boot.

A detail I had used before I understood whether it mattered.

Now the same place-name appeared again, carried by a boy who sold lamp oil and had no reason to care about my theories.

I wanted to ask how far.

Which entrance.

Whether the man turned.

Whether he met anyone.

Whether he went into a building.

Whether the boy saw the left side of his coat.

Whether there was mud on his boots.

Rinna said, "You saw him walking toward Mason's Cut."

"Yes."

"Did you see him enter Mason's Cut?"

"No. I turned for South Steps."

"Good."

I hated the word good.

It was correct.

Rinna added:

BOY LATER SAW HIM WALKING TOWARD MASON'S CUT. DID NOT SEE HIM ENTER.

Then she folded the paper once.

"Thank Olin for me."

The boy nodded.

I said, "Wait."

Rinna looked at me.

I knew what she thought I was about to do.

Possibly because I was thinking about doing it.

"I'm not following him."

"Excellent."

"I was going to give the boy bread."

The boy looked interested.

Rinna looked at my bag.

"Your bread?"

I reconsidered the entire moral structure of generosity.

I tore off a piece.

The boy accepted it.

"Thank you, oil man."

"Leave."

He did.

Rinna picked up her handbills again.

I stared at her.

"That's it?"

"No."

"Good."

"You're Landlord today."

I stared harder.

"That is not what I meant."

"I know."

She handed me three pages.

LANDLORD.

Nine lines.

I looked toward the stage where Marek was still practicing the bad limp.

"Which play?"

"The Cousin."

"I haven't done Landlord."

"You have watched it."

"That is not the same thing."

"Correct. Teren wants you in ten minutes."

"What are we doing about the man?"

"Talking to two more people we actually do business with. I am doing that. You are being a landlord."

"He asked where you keep the money."

"Yes."

"That is more specific."

"Yes."

"Mason's Cut."

"He walked toward it."

I exhaled.

"You enjoy this."

"No. I enjoy you not making my paper worse."

Fair.

The Cousin was a stupid play.

This was not criticism either. It knew.

A man pretended to be his own wealthy cousin to avoid paying three separate people. The lie became difficult because the cousin had supposedly rented a room from my character, the Landlord, who had never seen him. Marek played the liar. Hara played his sister. Pell played a creditor with an alarming hat.

My job was mostly to want rent.

I had experience.

Teren put me beside the stage door and ran the scene once.

I entered too early.

"Again," he said.

"I thought the knock was mine."

"It was the creditor."

"There are two knocks."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Doors."

Terrible explanation.

Again.

This time I waited for the second knock and entered correctly.

Marek turned toward me with the broad, desperate smile of a man whose entire life had become paperwork.

"My dear landlord."

"Rent."

Teren said, "No."

I stopped.

"That is my line."

"You're waiting for it to be funny."

I looked at him.

"It is one word."

"Exactly."

"How do I not wait with one word?"

"Want the rent."

I hated theatre.

Again.

Marek smiled.

"My dear landlord."

"Rent."

Better.

Not because I changed the word.

Because I interrupted the smile.

Marek reacted faster.

"Of course. My cousin has it."

"Then I want your cousin."

"He is away."

"Then I want the rent."

Teren pointed at me.

"Keep that."

"It is written."

"I know."

Excellent profession.

We worked for another twenty minutes.

I missed a chair on the first turn and clipped it with one crutch. Nessa moved it half a foot and told me not to pretend the chair had attacked.

"It was in my route."

"Your route was wrong."

"Hostile furniture."

"Wrong route."

She won.

By midday Rinna had returned from somewhere with dust on her hem and two fewer handbills.

She did not announce a breakthrough.

She told Jori that the lamp-glass woman would send word if anyone asked about theatre purchases. She told Davin that the cart repair man had been told the same thing. Then she put the remaining handbills back on the shelf and asked whether the front hinge was still sticking.

It was.

We worked on the hinge.

That was the strange part.

The man had asked where the money was kept.

The hinge still needed oil.

Both facts occupied the same building.

By afternoon the house began filling.

The Cousin was paired with a shorter piece I had seen but never performed in. I only had Landlord. Good.

My nine lines did not deserve panic.

I panicked modestly anyway.

The first scenes went cleanly.

Hara got the first real laugh by entering with a basket, taking one look at Marek's fake mustache, and saying nothing for so long that he finally touched it to check whether it had fallen off.

It had not.

The audience understood her entire opinion before she spoke.

When she finally said, "Cousin," the room broke.

Marek almost lost his next line.

Almost.

He recovered by bowing too deeply, which made the mustache lift at one corner.

Hara watched it happen.

Then looked at the audience.

Bigger laugh.

Nothing I did came close.

Good.

My entrance came after the creditor's second knock.

I heard the first.

Waited.

Heard the second.

Entered.

Marek smiled.

"My dear landlord."

"Rent."

The audience laughed.

Not much.

Enough.

I continued.

Competent.

Ordinary.

Then I made the mistake.

Marek said his cousin had gone to visit an aunt.

My line was, "Then your aunt may pay me."

I said, "Then your cousin may pay me."

Which was the entire problem.

Marek stared at me.

I stared back.

The audience waited.

He said, "He would, if he were not visiting my aunt."

Right.

I could have tried to repair it cleverly.

I did not.

"Then your aunt may pay me."

A small laugh.

The scene continued.

Backstage, Teren caught my sleeve as I passed.

"You repeated him."

"I know."

"Listen."

"I was listening."

"To yourself."

Annoying.

Accurate.

Then he let go because another scene was happening and my personal development was not the theatre's emergency.

Excellent.

The final Landlord scene went better.

No invention.

No rescue.

I entered on the correct knock, wanted rent, did not collide with furniture, and left when the scene ended.

After curtain, the audience became coats and voices and feet moving toward the street.

The company became work again.

Benches shifted.

Props returned to boxes.

Marek peeled off the mustache and stuck it to Pell's sleeve.

Pell did not notice for almost a minute.

Hara did.

She told no one.

I respected her enormously.

Rinna paid me the normal copper.

I put it away.

I did not immediately imagine it crossing Antonius Vale's counter.

Not because the debt had stopped existing.

Because bread existed too.

Soap existed.

Oil existed.

Crutch tips wore down.

Clothes tore.

People who planned to repay debts still had to remain people long enough to do it.

This was obvious.

I had apparently needed several adults to explain it.

Rinna was at the rear table with the folded paper from that morning.

I stopped beside her.

"Any more word?"

"No."

"Did anyone else get asked?"

"Not that I know."

"You're going to keep talking to suppliers?"

"People we actually use."

"Not everyone."

"I don't have time to create a citywide society for people annoyed by strangers."

"Could charge dues."

"Go home."

I looked at the paper.

"The money question matters."

"Yes."

"More than the oil question."

"Maybe."

I smiled.

She saw it.

"Don't."

"You said maybe."

"About importance, not identity."

"The paper survives us being stupid."

"I regret teaching you anything."

"You didn't teach me."

"Worse."

I went home.

Lyssa was not there.

That was becoming normal enough that I did not sit around inventing explanations.

I washed.

The new soap worked offensively well.

I ate some bread.

I considered the copper from the show.

Then put it with the rest of my money.

Not Vale money.

Not food money.

Money.

I could decide what it became when I needed to.

Lyssa arrived near dusk carrying a narrow wrapped bundle under one arm and a small packet in the other.

She put both on the table.

"You bought soap."

"I have been financially reckless."

She looked at me.

"Use more next time."

Cruel.

She unwrapped the smaller packet. Dried fruit.

I forgave her.

"Your day?" she asked.

I told her.

Olin's man returned.

Olin gave him nothing.

The questions.

Oil.

Cash.

Shows.

Where Rinna kept the money.

The boy later saw him walking toward Mason's Cut.

Did not see him enter.

No Bren name.

No threat.

No direct connection proven.

Lyssa ate one piece of fruit.

"And you didn't follow him."

"No."

She looked suspicious.

"I considered it professionally."

"What profession?"

"Landlord."

"What?"

I explained the play.

She laughed at the wrong part, which was apparently me saying the cousin should pay when the entire scene already depended on the cousin not being there.

"It was one line."

"It was the important line."

"There were nine."

"Eight, then."

I took dried fruit before she could become worse.

After a moment she said, "You heard about him before he cost you something this time."

I stopped chewing.

That was true.

Not victory.

Not safety.

Olin had simply done what Rinna asked.

A merchant had refused to answer questions about a customer. A boy had carried a message. Rinna had written down the words. Two more businesses knew how to reach her.

Small things.

Ordinary things.

Useful things.

"Yes," I said.

Lyssa nodded and went back to opening her larger bundle.

Inside was a dark sleeve with three chalk marks near the cuff.

Her work continued too.

No Hessa note came that night.

No one knocked.

Somewhere in Carrow, a thin-faced man in a brown coat had asked where the theatre kept its money.

I did not know where he slept.

I did not know who paid him, if anyone did.

I did not know whether Mason's Cut meant anything beyond the direction he had walked.

But for the first time, he had come looking for information and left without getting it.

We had gotten his questions instead.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 221

## THE PARTICIPANT

The note was under the cup.

Lyssa found it before I did because she had moved the cup to get at the last heel of bread.

"Your physician has learned table manners," she said.

"She isn't my physician."

"Your terrifying woman from the Guild has learned table manners."

"Better."

Lyssa handed me the folded paper and took the bread.

It contained six words.

AFTER MIDDAY. SAME ROOM. EAT FIRST.

Under that, smaller:

NO PRACTICE.

I turned the note over.

Nothing.

"Romantic," Lyssa said.

"She knows what I like."

"Restrictions?"

"Food."

"Cruel."

She was already dressed to go out, a wrapped bundle of finished work tied under one arm and another smaller packet on the table. I had learned not to ask whether the second packet was coming or going unless I wanted an explanation involving three customers, two sets of measurements, a woman who changed her mind about cuffs, and a button seller who apparently lied as a profession.

I ate.

That was easier.

Thirty successful supervised minimal draws. Twenty-six deliberate shaping attempts. Thirty-four supervised external-effect attempts. Intermediate response repeated. Far response observed once. Far response not established. No range. No independent anything.

The numbers had been sitting still long enough that I had stopped carrying them in the front of my head.

Hessa had not.

Lyssa tied her hair back, checked the bundle, then looked at me.

"Theatre first?"

"Until midday."

"Then Guild?"

"After midday."

"That is what I asked."

"Then yes."

She took the smaller packet too.

"I'm late because of you."

"I have done nothing."

"You spoke."

"Unreasonable standard."

She kissed my cheek on the way past.

"Eat again before you go."

"Hessa wrote that."

"Then two women agree. Be afraid."

The door shut behind her.

I was.

Not about the experiment.

Mostly.

The theatre had no messages waiting when I arrived.

I checked without pretending I had not checked.

Rinna was at the front table with a stack of tickets, a chipped cup, and the folded paper from Olin's boy tucked beneath a ledger. Nobody from the lamp-glass woman. Nobody from the cart repair man. Nobody from Olin.

No new warning.

No brown coat.

No Bren.

The building had survived the night despite my absence from Mason's Cut.

I tried not to take that personally.

Rinna looked up.

"You're here."

"Usually."

"Until?"

"Midday. Hessa wants me after."

"Magic?"

"Probably."

"Useful magic?"

"Absolutely not."

"Good."

She pointed toward the stage.

"Jori needs hands."

I lifted both crutches.

"I have made a terrible scheduling error."

"He knows which ones."

Jori needed me to sit at the edge of the stage and hold the lower end of a painted wall flat while he replaced two leather ties along the back. This was excellent work because it required almost no walking and allowed me to criticize him continuously.

"That knot is ugly."

"You're holding canvas."

"I can see."

"Then look somewhere else."

"It remains ugly when I do that."

He pulled the tie tight.

The wall was part of a room that had been a rich man's parlor, a magistrate's office, a widow's dining room, and once, through desperation, the interior of a ship.

The painted window had survived all of them.

The ship had been difficult.

"Higher," Jori said.

I lifted my end.

"Not you. The canvas."

"We are currently connected."

"Less."

I lowered it.

"There."

For the next hour I was a clamp with opinions.

It was restful.

Marek crossed behind us carrying three hats and wearing none of them. Nessa chased him down because one had a pin still in it. Hara sat in the first row going through pages with Teren. Someone in the rear passage dropped a box and swore with enough conviction that I briefly considered applauding.

Theatre.

Rinna passed once.

I said, "Anything?"

She knew what I meant.

"No."

Then she kept walking.

That was all the threat received that morning.

Good.

At midday Jori released me from service after deciding the wall could once again survive being furniture.

Rinna gave me half a heel of cheese from a paper wrapping and pointed at Hessa's note when I tried to refuse.

"How do you know what that says?"

"You told me she said eat first."

"I regret sharing information."

"Learn from Olin."

I ate the cheese.

Then I went to the Guild.

The same room was waiting.

Hessa had meant that literally.

Same narrow table. Same board. Same chair. Same glass shield. Same paper-fin assembly. Same control beside it. The far position had been marked on the floor with two short chalk lines that I remembered from the last session.

I stopped in the doorway.

"You preserved it."

Hessa looked up from her notes.

"Yes."

"Nobody needed the room?"

"They did."

"And?"

"They used another room."

I considered the institutional power required to make that sentence happen.

"I want to become you."

"Sit down."

Apparently training had begun.

I put my crutches where she indicated, not where I remembered putting them. She checked the chair position against a mark on the floor, then checked my right foot, the angle of my knee, the position of my hips, and the distance from my right forearm to the table edge.

"Same shirt?" I asked.

She looked at me.

"No."

"Then the experiment is ruined."

"If your shirt moves the paper through glass, I will revise several things."

Fair.

She checked my right hand.

"Anything since last session?"

"No."

"Thumb?"

"Normal."

"Wrist?"

"Normal."

"Forearm?"

"Normal."

"Shoulder?"

"Normal."

"Residual limb?"

"Fine."

"Phantom?"

I waited a moment before answering because it was there once I looked for it, the ordinary absent foot occupying its impossible position without pain.

"Present. Quiet."

She wrote that down.

"Sleep?"

"Enough."

"Food?"

"Bread. Cheese."

"Water?"

"Yes."

She slid a cup toward me anyway.

I drank.

"Question?" she asked.

"Can far repeat."

"Under what conditions?"

I looked at the apparatus.

"These. Away only. Same position."

"Good."

I waited.

"That's all?"

"That is the question."

"No intermediate first?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Because I am not asking whether intermediate still works today."

I looked at the far chalk marks.

"No closer control?"

"The control is there."

She pointed to the second paper assembly beside the target.

"You mean distance control."

"Yes."

"No."

I liked experiments more when I was allowed to add things to them.

That was probably why Hessa ran them.

The minimal draw came first.

Same as always now, which was a dangerous phrase to think about anything involving mana.

Hessa gave the instruction. I settled, found the familiar internal route, and drew the smallest amount I could manage under supervision.

The sensation arrived cleanly enough to recognize and small enough not to become interesting.

Hessa watched my hand, then my face.

"Return."

I returned it.

No lingering thumb sensation. No unexpected spread. No catch in the wrist.

Thirty-one successful supervised minimal draws.

She waited.

I waited.

Nothing developed.

Then deliberate shaping.

Not a new shape. Not a new direction. Not an attempt to make anything stronger.

She gave me the same narrow setup we had been using before external work, and I followed it as carefully as I could.

The problem with doing something twenty-seven times was that familiarity started pretending to be precision.

Hessa stopped me halfway through.

"Again."

I let the shaping collapse under instruction.

"What?"

"Your shoulder moved."

"My shoulder is attached."

"It lifted before the change."

I thought back.

She was right.

I had braced without noticing.

"Does that count?"

"No."

"Then I'm still at twenty-six."

"Yes."

That annoyed me more than it should have.

She knew.

"Do you want a larger number or a usable record?"

"Both."

"Choose."

"Usable record."

"Again."

The second shaping sequence was cleaner. Right hand quiet. Wrist quiet. Forearm working but not straining. Shoulder down. Hessa watched the whole thing, then had me return.

"Count it," she said.

Twenty-seven supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Then the glass went between me and the paper.

Far position.

Away only.

The paper fin looked ridiculous from there.

That was not scientifically relevant.

It was still true.

Hessa checked the target, then the control. She closed the door. Waited for footsteps in the corridor to pass. Checked the glass edge. Checked the paper again.

"Attempt thirty-five," she said. "Far. Away only. Begin when ready."

I settled.

The first difficulty was not mana.

It was wanting the paper to move.

That sounded stupid because moving the paper was the point.

But wanting it to move made me watch for movement, and watching for movement made every tiny shift in shadow feel important. I had learned enough to distrust enthusiasm.

I looked where Hessa had told me to look.

I drew under supervision.

Shaped.

Held the requested direction.

Away.

Nothing.

The target did not move.

The control did not move.

My right forearm tightened near the end, but not enough for Hessa to stop me before the interval finished.

"Return."

I returned.

She checked both fins.

"No observed response," she said.

I nodded.

Attempt thirty-five.

Far.

No observed response.

Control unchanged.

She gave me a longer rest than I wanted.

I did not complain because complaining sometimes made rests longer.

I flexed my right fingers once when she told me to. Rolled the shoulder once. Drank water.

"Forearm?"

"Worked. Fine now."

"Shoulder?"

"Fine."

"Residual limb?"

"Fine."

"Phantom?"

I checked.

"Same."

She wrote.

The second external attempt began with less hope.

This was probably useful.

Attempt thirty-six.

Far.

Away only.

I drew.

Shaped.

Held.

For several seconds nothing happened.

Then the target fin turned.

Not much.

A small rotation, the leading edge shifting away from me while the rear edge followed less cleanly. It was not the straight little displacement I wanted. It was not dramatic. I almost doubted it had happened until Hessa said, "Return."

I returned immediately.

The control had not moved.

Hessa came around the table without speaking. She crouched beside the board, looked through the glass from one side, then the other, checked the paper's position against the marks, and wrote for a long time.

I kept my mouth shut for almost all of it.

"Observed?" I asked.

"Yes."

That was enough to make my chest tighten.

"Away?"

"Net away. With rotation."

"Like thirty-three?"

She looked at the earlier page.

"Similar category. Not identical movement."

I wanted to ask whether that meant far worked.

I had known Hessa too long.

Instead I asked, "What does it establish?"

"Nothing yet that the third attempt cannot make less simple."

There she was.

Attempt thirty-six.

Far.

Small rotational response with net displacement away.

Control unchanged.

Far response observed again.

Across more than one session now.

I could feel the sentence trying to grow teeth.

Hessa did not feed it.

She made me rest.

This time my forearm stayed faintly warm after I opened my hand. Not pain. Not tingling. Work.

She pressed along the muscle and asked whether anything changed.

"No."

"Shoulder?"

"Fine."

"Hand?"

"Fine."

"Thumb?"

"Fine."

She waited another minute anyway.

"Third?" I asked.

"If the forearm returns to baseline."

I sat there and attempted to make my forearm less interesting through moral character.

It did not work.

Time did.

The warmth faded.

Hessa checked again.

"Third. Then stop."

"Even if nothing happens?"

"Yes."

"Even if something happens?"

"Yes."

"You remove all incentive."

"Good."

Attempt thirty-seven.

Far.

Away only.

The room had become too familiar by then. Glass. Paper. Chalk. Board. My hand on the same part of the table. Hessa standing at the same angle. A cart rattling somewhere outside the Guild building and fading down the street.

I drew.

Shaped.

Away.

Nothing.

I held until Hessa's interval ended.

Nothing.

The control remained still.

The target remained still.

My shoulder started to rise near the end.

I noticed it this time and lowered it.

Hessa noticed me noticing.

That did not make the paper move either.

"Return."

I returned.

She checked the apparatus.

"No observed response."

"One of three."

"Today."

"Two far responses total."

"Observed in separate sessions under the current apparatus."

"That sounds longer."

"It is more accurate."

I leaned back carefully.

"So far works."

"No."

Worth trying.

"Far has repeated."

She considered that.

"A far response has now been observed in more than one session under the current apparatus."

"That is what I said with fewer words."

"No. You removed response, observed, session, and apparatus."

"They were implied."

"That is where bad records breed."

I looked at the paper fin.

It had moved once today.

Once out of three far attempts today. Once before. Failures around both.

Intermediate had behaved better when we tested it.

The far position had not become a range. It had become a place where something had happened twice.

Annoyingly, those were different statements.

Hessa wrote the session summary while I drank the rest of the water.

I could read part of it upside down.

FAR RESPONSE OBSERVED ACROSS MORE THAN ONE SESSION UNDER CURRENT APPARATUS.

FAR RELIABILITY NOT ESTABLISHED.

INTERMEDIATE REMAINS MORE RELIABLE ON CURRENT EVIDENCE.

NO RANGE ESTABLISHED.

NOT GENERALIZED.

I pointed.

"You could have written 'Greg is magnificent.'"

"Unsupported."

"Cruel."

"Also irrelevant."

She checked my hand again before letting me stand.

The session ended at thirty-one successful supervised minimal draws, twenty-seven supervised deliberate shaping attempts, and thirty-seven supervised external-effect attempts.

Restrictions did not change.

I asked because apparently humiliation was part of the apparatus.

"Independent draw?"

"No."

"Paper?"

"No."

"Coins?"

"No."

"Thread?"

"No."

"Larger object?"

"No."

"Practice?"

"No."

"One tiny celebration?"

"You may eat."

"Again?"

"Frequently, if possible."

I took my crutches.

"Next question?"

"Not today."

"You have one."

"Yes."

"What is it?"

"Not today."

There were times I suspected Hessa had entered medicine only because interrogation was not respectable enough.

Outside, Carrow had continued without waiting for my evidence.

A wagon blocked half the street. Two apprentices were arguing over a coil of rope. A woman with a basket shouted at a man who had apparently stepped in front of her and then committed the greater crime of defending himself.

I went back toward the theatre because I still had part of the day.

Rinna was at the same front table.

The paper from Olin's boy was gone from beneath the ledger.

I noticed.

She noticed me noticing.

"Put away," she said.

"Anything new?"

"No."

Good.

She looked at me.

"Useful magic?"

I considered Hessa's page.

"One piece of paper moved a little."

"Can you do it again?"

"Sometimes. Under glass. In one room. With Hessa watching. At a marked distance. After being fed."

Rinna nodded.

"So no."

"I dislike how quickly everyone understands this."

"Can you carry pages?"

"Yes."

"Useful."

She handed me a stack.

I carried pages.

Not many. From front table to Teren, then from Teren to Hara because he had given me the wrong stack, then back to Teren because Hara already had hers and wanted to know why he was creating paper migration as a profession.

I had no role that evening.

I stayed through the first half of rehearsal anyway, sitting near the side while Teren worked a scene between Marek and Hara. My right forearm felt normal. My shoulder felt normal. The phantom foot remained quietly where it could not be.

Nobody asked me to move anything with my mind.

Excellent workplace.

By the time I left, the lamps were being lit for the evening show.

I was not in it.

That was fine too.

At home Lyssa had beaten me back by enough time to occupy most of the table with cloth.

I put Hessa's note beside the basin.

She looked up.

"Well?"

"Paper moved."

"Good."

"Once."

"Less good?"

"Still good. Just specifically good."

She threaded a needle.

"Did you hurt yourself?"

"No."

"Did she change the rules?"

"No."

"Then specifically good."

I sat across from her.

"It happened at far again."

"Far from what?"

I opened my mouth.

Closed it.

"The paper."

"How far?"

"A marked place in Hessa's room."

Lyssa looked at me.

I pointed at her.

"Exactly. This is why she won't call it a range."

"I didn't ask about a range."

"You accidentally became scientific."

"Terrible."

She went back to the seam.

I watched her make three small stitches.

"The man didn't come back," I said.

"Which man?"

"Brown coat. Nobody sent word."

"Good."

"Rinna said the same thing."

"She's learning."

I smiled.

Lyssa worked. I sat. The room smelled faintly of the soap I had bought and the onions she had started before I came in.

Two far responses existed now.

Not a range.

Not reliability.

Not a weapon.

Not a solution to anything happening at the theatre.

A paper fin had moved a little, twice, on different days, under glass, while Hessa watched and wrote down everything I wanted to shorten.

That was more than once.

For tonight, more than once was enough.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 222

## THE PROPERTY MAN

Lyssa was gone before I finished tying my boot.

This was not unusual anymore. It still produced a brief, stupid moment in which I looked at the room as if it had misplaced her.

On the table she had left half an onion, two pins stuck through a folded scrap of blue cloth, and a note that said:

BUY THREAD IF YOU PASS MAREN'S.

No color.

No amount.

No indication of whether Maren was a person, a shop, or a threat.

I turned the note over.

Nothing.

Apparently Hessa had started a school.

I ate the rest of yesterday's bread, checked the crutch tips because the left one had begun to feel slightly softer on wet stone, and left the thread problem for Future Greg. The morning was clear enough that the street had already collected carts, apprentices, dogs, two women arguing over cabbages, and a man carrying a door by himself for reasons I could not improve by knowing.

At the theatre, nobody was interested in my magical accomplishments.

This was comforting because neither was I.

The front door stood open. Rinna's table had moved a little farther back from it than usual, enough that someone passing on the street could see her but not the ledger beside her. The cash box was not there.

I noticed.

"Cash box moved."

"Yes."

I looked toward the stage instead.

Three people were looking for the same umbrella.

It was not an umbrella anyone sane would use outdoors. The handle curved like a bird's neck. The canopy was striped yellow and green, one rib had been repaired with wire, and somebody had painted tiny red flowers along the edge. I had seen it in at least four plays, none of which required the same kind of weather.

Nessa stood beside an open property chest with both hands on her hips. Marek was holding a sword, a basket, and a hat that did not belong to him. Hara had one shoe on.

"The umbrella was here," Nessa said.

Marek said, "It remains a compelling theory."

"You used it yesterday."

"In rehearsal."

"That was yesterday."

"Time does work that way."

Hara, from the floor, said, "If he has hidden it in the sword chest again, stab him with whatever you find first."

I stopped just inside the aisle.

Nobody told me where to stand.

I did not need them to.

The left side of the stage was clogged with a bench, two rolled backdrops, and Jori's ladder. I went right, passed behind the front row, and set my crutches against the property table where they would not catch anyone moving from the rear passage.

Nessa looked at me.

"Did you see the umbrella?"

"Not today."

"Yesterday."

"Stage left after The Letter Box. Davin carried it toward the rear because the handle caught his sleeve."

Davin shouted from somewhere behind the flats, "It attacked me."

Nessa pointed.

"Find him."

"I am not an umbrella dog."

"You remembered where it went."

That was how employment happened in theatre.

Davin had not hidden the umbrella. He had put it on a hook beside the costume racks because the curved handle fit there and because nobody had told him that the hook belonged to belts.

Nessa found me standing beneath it.

"You passed it twice," I said.

"I was looking for an umbrella."

"It remains one."

"It was with belts."

"Disguise."

She took it down and shoved it into my free hand.

"Property table. Do not give it to Marek."

Marek appeared in the rear passage.

"I heard my name."

"No umbrella," Nessa said.

"I have no interest in umbrellas."

Hara called, "Liar."

Marek looked offended.

"Not in this play."

That distinction apparently mattered.

By the time the company stopped misplacing things, I had acquired a job.

Not a role.

A job.

The afternoon pairing was The Widow's Guest and The Honest Clerk. I had a small speaking part in the second piece, a delivery man with four lines and a parcel. Before that, Nessa wanted me at the property table because Davin had to help Jori with a wall brace and the usual property runner had not come in.

"What does the property runner do?" I asked.

Nessa stared at me.

"Runs properties."

"I regret asking."

"You know most of the pieces."

"I know enough to know Marek steals hats."

"I borrow hats."

Marek had returned.

Nessa did not look at him.

"You also know where people enter now," she continued. "Keep the table clear. Put things back where they belong. If someone asks for a prop, give them the one for their scene, not the one that looks funniest."

"That feels targeted."

"It is."

She walked away.

Marek reached for the striped umbrella.

I moved it behind me.

He smiled.

I did not.

He left.

I had become authority.

Limited authority. Umbrella authority.

Still.

The property table was a long scarred board on two trestles just behind the right wing. Everything needed for the first piece had been arranged in rough scene order: a letter, a small purse with nothing in it, the ugly umbrella, a wooden cup, a shawl pin, two folded handkerchiefs, and a silver-painted key that opened nothing.

The key was familiar. I had carried it as a servant weeks ago and dropped it once behind a chair.

It still had the nick along one edge from landing on the stage.

I picked it up, then put it back before nostalgia became another form of theft.

Hara came through fastening the second shoe.

"Key after the letter," she said.

"I know."

"Good."

She took three steps, stopped, came back, and moved the key two inches farther from the purse.

"Why?"

"Marek sweeps with his sleeve."

"I have never swept anything in my life," Marek said from the other side of the flat.

Hara raised her voice.

"Exactly."

She left.

I looked at the table.

Then at Marek's sleeve when he came through five minutes later.

Wide cuff.

Loose stitching.

He reached for the purse during the run.

The cuff brushed the place where the key had been.

Hara had been right.

I disliked evidence that benefited other people.

The morning run was not really a rehearsal. Everyone already knew The Widow's Guest. Teren stopped only when something physical had changed enough to matter.

The bench was six inches farther downstage because one leg had begun to wobble and Jori wanted it on a flatter board. The moved bench changed Hara's first cross. She adjusted once. Marek forgot, nearly met her shoulder to shoulder, and corrected without anyone saying anything.

I watched from the property table while sorting the handkerchiefs.

One had a red stitched border.

One did not.

The red one belonged to the second scene because the widow recognized it later.

I knew that.

Nobody had told me today.

A month ago I would have been pleased enough with that fact to repeat it to myself.

Today I put the red one where it belonged and kept watching.

Teren pointed at me.

"Parcel."

I looked at the table.

My parcel was not there.

That was because I had not put it there.

I had been so busy becoming master of other people's objects that I had forgotten the one I actually needed.

"Excellent," I said.

"What?" Nessa asked.

"My role is improving."

She followed my eyes to the empty place.

Then she laughed once and went to find the parcel.

It was under the front table, wrapped in brown cloth and tied with twine. Rinna had used it to flatten a stack of handbills.

"Why is my parcel doing office work?"

Rinna looked down.

"Because it was heavy."

"It contains wool."

"Heavy wool."

"It is fake wool."

"Still worked."

I carried it back.

Nessa marked a square on the property table with chalk.

"Parcel lives here."

"I can remember."

"Apparently not."

Fair.

We ran my scene once before midday.

I entered through the right wing after the clerk's second line, crossed to the desk, put down the parcel, said four lines, took a receipt, and left.

The first time, I reached for the receipt too early.

Not dramatically.

My hand simply moved toward it while Pell, playing the clerk, was still asking whether the parcel had come from North Street.

Teren stopped us.

"Greg."

"I know the street."

"Your hand."

I looked at it. It was already halfway to the receipt.

"What about it?"

"You know you're getting the receipt. The delivery man doesn't yet."

I put my hand back.

"Again."

That was all he gave me. We reset.

Pell asked, "North Street?"

"South."

"You were told North."

"I was told wrong."

He frowned at the parcel.

"Then I cannot take it."

"Then I will carry it back."

Only after he sighed, took the parcel, and pushed the little wooden receipt across the desk did I reach for it.

Better.

The difference was tiny.

It was also visible.

Theatre had an irritating amount of work hidden inside things that looked like nothing.

At midday, Davin brought meat pies from the corner stall and nearly caused a riot by failing to buy enough.

There were eight pies and more than eight people.

Rinna said, "Half."

Marek said, "Some of us are larger."

Hara said, "Some of us are louder."

Nessa cut the pies.

Marek received half.

Justice returned to Carrow.

I ate sitting on the edge of the stage with my crutches laid beside me. Jori had already shifted one of the narrow stools out of the path behind the wing without asking. He had been doing that for several days now, not always the same stool, just whatever object would catch a crutch or force me into somebody else's lane.

The first time, people had discussed where I could pass.

Now they moved things and argued about umbrellas instead.

Better use of human attention.

Rinna came through carrying a bundle of tickets.

"Any word?" I asked.

"No."

That was the entire conversation.

She kept walking.

I finished my half pie.

The FAR result from yesterday crossed my mind once when a scrap of paper near the open door lifted in a draft and skittered beneath a bench.

I watched it go.

Then Davin made me crawl under the bench for it because apparently I was closest.

Magic remained useless.

After midday the theatre changed from rehearsal mess to performance mess.

Different mess.

Costumes came off hooks. Hair was pinned. Props moved from storage to tables. Jori checked the brace behind the widow's room wall. Rinna counted tickets at the front. Teren stopped answering questions that had answers written on pages.

I stayed at the property table through The Widow's Guest.

That turned out to be harder than my own four-line role.

People arrived from the dark and expected objects.

Hara's letter.

Pell's key.

Marek's cup.

Hara's handkerchief.

Nessa's pin.

The striped umbrella went out and came back wet because Marek had dipped one edge into a stage bucket for no reason I could determine.

Nessa saw it.

"Marek."

"It was raining."

"There is no rain."

"There is emotionally."

She took the umbrella from him and handed it to me.

"Dry it."

"How?"

"With a cloth."

I found a cloth.

This was apparently stagecraft.

The strongest moment of the piece had nothing to do with any of us getting the right objects.

Marek entered in the second scene supposed to be a nervous guest hiding a letter from the widow. The audience already knew he had put it in his coat.

Hara, as the widow, asked whether he was warm.

He said no.

She looked at the coat.

Then at the fireplace.

Then at the audience.

Marek took one careful step away from the fire.

Hara took one careful step toward him.

The audience started laughing before either of them said another word.

He moved again.

She followed.

By the third step they were circling the room without acknowledging it, Hara calm and Marek increasingly desperate, until he finally said, "It is a very comfortable coat."

The room broke.

I nearly missed the cup handoff because I was watching.

Nearly.

Pell came offstage with his hand already out.

I saw him in time and put the cup into it without looking down.

He went back on.

Nobody died.

Progress.

Between pieces, the property table changed.

Objects from The Widow's Guest went left into return baskets. The Honest Clerk pieces came forward.

Parcel in the chalk square.

Receipt at the desk.

A quill.

Two folded invoices.

A sealing block.

A hat for Pell that Marek was forbidden to touch.

He touched it.

Nessa slapped his hand.

"Hostile workplace," he said.

"Document it."

"I need a clerk."

"You are surrounded by actors."

"None literate enough."

Pell, already wearing the hat, said, "I can write your complaint."

Marek considered him.

"Conflict of interest."

Then the curtain call from the first piece ended and nobody had time to continue.

My four lines were coming.

I did not rehearse them under my breath.

That surprised me only after I noticed I was not doing it.

The words were there.

More importantly, I knew where the parcel was, where Pell would stand, which side of the desk kept my crutch clear, and when the previous actor would leave the lane.

Teren passed behind me.

"Wait for him to finish the question."

"I know."

He looked at my hand.

I held both palms up.

"No receipt."

"Good."

He left.

My cue came while Nessa was still tying back the first play's shawl beside me.

I heard it.

Picked up the parcel.

Went.

The entrance was ordinary.

That might have been the best part.

Pell looked up from the desk.

"North Street?"

"South."

"You were told North."

"I was told wrong."

A laugh, small and immediate.

Not because I had done anything special. Pell had spent the previous scene establishing that the clerk believed every written label more than any living person.

He looked at the parcel.

"Then I cannot take it."

"Then I will carry it back."

"That would be inefficient."

"I have carried worse."

Another small laugh.

Pell took the parcel.

He pushed the receipt toward me.

I waited until it moved.

Then reached.

Correct.

My third line was, "Sign it properly."

I said it.

My fourth was, "I have been blamed for better handwriting."

That got a better laugh than it had in rehearsal, mostly because Pell looked genuinely offended.

I left on time.

Backstage, Nessa handed me the striped umbrella.

I stared at her.

"Wrong play."

"I know. Hold it."

"Why?"

"Marek is looking for it."

I held it behind the flat.

Marek came through thirty seconds later.

"Have you seen the umbrella?"

"No."

Nessa looked at me.

I looked at Nessa.

Marek narrowed his eyes.

"You are both terrible actors."

"Go," Teren said.

Marek went.

The rest of the show did not need me onstage.

It needed me at the table.

A quill disappeared and was found behind the desk.

The sealing block came back in Pell's pocket.

One invoice tore because Hara stepped on it during an exit.

Davin tried to replace it with a handbill folded to the same size.

I stopped him.

"Wrong paper."

"It looks right."

"It says tomorrow's show on the back."

"Nobody sees the back."

"Until Marek unfolds it."

Davin considered the possibility.

"Fine."

We found another invoice.

I was getting disturbingly good at preventing theatre from becoming visibly stupid.

Privately stupid remained beyond repair.

After the final curtain, the company dissolved into labor.

The audience moved out. Benches scraped. Costumes came off. The property table became three piles: return, repair, and somehow wet.

Rinna came behind the front table only after the doors were nearly shut. She brought the cash box with her from somewhere else in the building.

I noticed that too.

This time I did not say anything.

She set it beside the ledger, counted with Davin standing on the other side of the table, then closed it again before the front doors reopened for anyone carrying benches.

No announcement.

No guards.

No dramatic secrecy.

A slightly different routine.

That was enough.

Rinna paid me one copper for the day's work and performance.

I put it away.

Nessa came past with the repaired umbrella.

"Property man tomorrow?"

"Was I property man today?"

"You kept Marek from taking the hat."

"Heroic."

"You also almost gave Pell the cup late."

"I did not."

"Almost counts backstage."

"That is not how Hessa counts."

"I don't know who that is."

"Better life."

She left.

Jori called from the stage, "Greg."

"What?"

"Your lane."

I looked.

Someone had shoved the narrow stool back behind the wing during cleanup.

Right where I would pass.

Before I moved, Davin hooked it with his foot and dragged it aside without interrupting whatever he was saying to Pell.

Nobody looked at me.

Good.

I collected my crutches and went home.

Maren turned out to be a shop.

I learned this because I passed it.

The sign had a spool painted on it, which seemed unfairly helpful.

I stood outside, took Lyssa's note from my pocket, and read it again.

BUY THREAD IF YOU PASS MAREN'S.

No color.

I went inside.

The woman behind the counter asked, "What kind?"

"My partner left me a note designed to test the strength of our relationship."

She did not smile.

Professional.

I showed her the scrap of blue cloth with the pins still through it.

She looked at the cloth.

"Matching?"

"I would like to survive."

She found a spool close enough that I could not see the difference.

I bought it.

At home, Lyssa had not returned yet.

I put the spool beside her cloth, washed, ate the last piece of onion with cheese, and occupied the only clear corner of the table with absolutely nothing.

She arrived after dusk carrying no bundle at all.

That was unusual enough that I looked at her hands.

"Finished?"

"Delivered."

"Paid?"

She looked at me.

"Do you ask Rinna that?"

"Frequently."

"Then stop."

She saw the thread.

Picked it up.

Held it beside the cloth.

"Good."

I felt an unreasonable amount of pride.

"Maren helped."

"Maren usually does."

"So the note was actually for Maren."

"The note was for you."

"Debatable."

She sat, leaned back, and closed her eyes for a moment.

I did not give her the theatre report.

She did not ask for it.

After a while she opened one eye.

"Did the paper move today?"

"No paper."

"Did the dangerous man appear?"

"No dangerous man."

"Did you work?"

"Extensively."

"Doing what?"

I considered the day.

"Protecting an umbrella."

She closed her eye again.

"Important."

"Finally, someone understands."

I put the copper from the theatre with the rest of my money.

Lyssa nudged the spool of thread toward her side of the table, then reached across and took my hand.

We sat there without solving anything.

Tomorrow the umbrella would probably disappear again.

That seemed like enough trouble to prepare for.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 223

## THE MAINTENANCE MAN

The left crutch tip had become worse overnight.

Not dramatically. It had not split, fallen off, or transformed into a weapon against me. It simply compressed farther than the right one when I put weight through it, which made the crutch feel a little soft on stone and a little too friendly with smooth floorboards.

I noticed because I had become the sort of person who noticed crutch tips before breakfast.

There were worse developments.

Lyssa was at the table with the blue cloth from yesterday spread in front of her. The thread I had bought sat beside it, already threaded through a needle. She had used perhaps four inches of it.

I looked at the spool.

"Excellent purchase."

She did not look up. "Maren chose it."

"I transported it."

"Heroic."

I put the left crutch beside the table and pressed the tip with my thumb.

Lyssa glanced over. "That the one you said felt soft?"

"Yes."

"Replace it."

"I was going to assess it."

"Replace it after assessing it."

"Very controlling."

She bit the thread, tied it, and finally looked at me. "You fall on that floor at the theatre and somebody will make a speech."

That was convincing.

I ate bread and cheese while she finished the seam. She had another customer after midday, which I learned because she wrapped the blue piece, wrapped two other pieces I had not seen before, then realized one of them still had a pin in it and unwrapped the entire bundle again.

I watched this with the respect due to another profession's disasters.

"Do you have work tonight?" she asked.

"Probably."

"Role?"

"Unknown."

"Umbrella?"

"Threat level unresolved."

She smiled without looking up.

I left before she did.

The crutch repairer was not far out of my way. I had used the shop before for grips and ferrules, and the man behind the counter remembered me well enough to point at the left crutch before I finished explaining.

"That one's wearing faster."

"That is what I came to tell you."

"Good. Saves time."

He turned the crutch in his hands, pressed the rubber, checked the edge, then compared it to the right one. He did not ask how I had injured my leg, whether I had always used crutches, or whether I had considered a more inspirational relationship with adversity.

He said, "You load the left harder when you turn."

I frowned. "Do I?"

"Look."

He set both crutches upright. The left tip had worn slightly more along one side.

"Could be streets. Could be you. Could be both."

That was a much less satisfying explanation than discovering a conspiracy in my walking.

"Can you replace just one?"

"I can replace seventeen if you pay me."

"One seems sufficient."

He fitted a new tip, trimmed the edge, made me test it on the shop floor, then adjusted it once because the first fit caught slightly when I rolled the crutch forward.

I paid him.

The copper left my hand without producing a moral crisis.

Very mature.

Outside, the new tip felt almost annoyingly firm.

I reached the theatre to find Jori underneath the cart.

Not near it.

Under it.

His boots stuck out beside one wheel while Davin stood over him holding a mallet and offering advice with the confidence of a man not trapped beneath timber.

"The axle doesn't care what you think," Jori said.

Davin looked at me. "Tell him leverage matters."

"Leverage matters."

"Thank you."

Jori's voice came from under the cart. "Not to the cracked brace."

I stopped beside them.

The theatre cart sat in the narrow side yard with one rear wheel blocked. A short diagonal brace beneath the bed had split near an old bolt hole. It was not the axle. The cart was not collapsing. It was also clearly not going anywhere useful until somebody replaced the brace.

"Did this happen today?" I asked.

"Found it today," Davin said.

"Different statement."

Jori slid out far enough to look at me.

"Don't encourage him."

"I was encouraging evidence."

"Go inside."

I went inside.

Nessa immediately handed me a wooden tray with six fake pastries on it.

Apparently I remained employed.

"Property table?" I asked.

"Half hour. Then Teren wants you."

"Role?"

"Neighbor."

I stared at her.

"Again?"

"Different neighbor."

"I have already represented the concept."

"You'll survive."

The property table had kept yesterday's chalk square for the parcel. Someone had written UMBRELLA beside another empty space.

I looked at Nessa.

She looked away.

"Where is it?"

"With Marek."

"Why?"

"He is using it."

"In a play?"

She considered.

"No."

I closed my eyes.

This was theatre continuity.

The morning piece was The Doctor's Supper, which involved a physician, a patient pretending not to be ill, two relatives, a servant, and enough food props to make Nessa hate everyone. My four-line Neighbor appeared only to return a borrowed pot and accidentally reveal that the supposedly bedridden patient had been seen dancing the previous night.

I had no emotional relationship with the pot.

This helped.

Teren ran the scene once. I entered at the right cue, put the pot on the table, and waited through Hara's line.

Then I made a different mistake.

Marek, playing the patient's brother, crossed behind me before my second line. I saw him coming and shifted early to give him space.

Teren stopped us.

"Greg."

"I was in his way."

"You weren't yet."

I looked at Marek.

He had stopped two steps behind me.

Teren pointed to the mark near my foot.

"Stay until he makes you move."

"He's going behind me."

"Then let him go behind you."

"I have crutches."

"I know."

Marek said, "We have met."

Teren ignored him.

"If you move before he reaches you, the audience sees you making room for an actor. The neighbor doesn't know his route."

That was irritatingly similar to yesterday's receipt without being the same problem.

I was becoming talented at knowing too much.

We reset.

This time Marek crossed. I stayed. He adjusted behind me, took the wider line, and my next line landed where it was supposed to.

Teren nodded.

That was the correction.

Work continued.

Near midday, a man came through the front door and asked for Rinna.

He was broad through the shoulders, gray at the temples, and had black grease worked permanently into the lines of his hands. I recognized him after a moment as the cart repair man Rinna had spoken to two days earlier, though I had only seen him once from across the yard.

Rinna came from the rear passage carrying a folded costume.

"You came."

"Had reason."

That changed the room without making it stop.

Nessa was still sorting pastries. Teren was still arguing with Pell about a line. Somebody behind the stage dropped something wooden.

Rinna set the costume down.

"What happened?"

The repair man glanced toward the open front door.

Rinna stepped farther inside.

He followed.

I did not move closer.

I was already close enough.

"A man came by yesterday," he said. "Asked after your cart."

Rinna's face did not change much.

"Which cart?"

"He described this one. Small theatre cart. Painted side scraped near the rear."

Davin looked toward the side yard.

The description was accurate.

Rinna asked, "What did he ask?"

The repair man rubbed his thumb across one knuckle.

"First if I still worked on it."

"What did you say?"

"Told him I work on carts."

"Then?"

"He asked when you usually bring it in. I said when it breaks."

Davin smiled.

Rinna did not.

"What else?"

The man thought.

"He asked if it usually goes out after the late show."

There it was.

Rinna said, "Exact?"

"Near enough. 'They take it out after the late show?'"

"Anything else?"

"Asked if the same fellow drives it."

Rinna waited.

The repair man added, "Might've said 'same man.' I don't remember fellow."

"Good."

He looked at her.

"Good?"

"Good that you don't remember."

That confused him for half a second.

I understood.

Rinna took a scrap of paper from beneath the ledger.

"Did you answer either question?"

"No. Told him I fix wheels. Don't keep theatre hours."

"Anything about money?"

"No."

"Anything about a box?"

"No."

"Did he ask who owns the cart?"

"No."

"Did he ask about me?"

"Not by name."

"Greg?"

The repair man glanced at me.

"No."

Rinna nodded.

"Describe him."

This was the part where bad certainty became tempting.

The repair man looked toward the ceiling as if the man might still be written there.

"Brown coat. Dark hair."

"Age?"

"Not old."

"Face?"

He touched his own cheek.

"Thin, maybe. Narrow."

"Voice?"

"Quiet enough."

My stomach tightened.

Not proof.

Still.

Rinna wrote:

MAN ASKED CART REPAIRER:
THEY TAKE IT OUT AFTER THE LATE SHOW?
SAME MAN DRIVES IT? [WORDING UNCERTAIN]

REPAIRER GAVE NO THEATRE HOURS / ROUTINE.

DESCRIPTION:
BROWN COAT.
DARK HAIR.
NOT OLD.
NARROW/THIN FACE.
QUIET VOICE.

CONSISTENT WITH OLIN DESCRIPTION.

She stopped there.

I read it upside down.

"Consistent."

"Yes."

"Not same man."

"Correct."

The repair man looked between us.

"You already had someone asking?"

Rinna folded the paper once.

"Questions at another business."

"Same sort?"

"Different questions."

He nodded slowly.

"Anything you want me to do?"

"If somebody asks again, don't answer theatre routines. Send word."

"That's what I did."

"Then keep doing it."

He seemed almost disappointed that there was no second part involving heroics.

Good.

He left.

Davin waited until the door shut.

"Late show."

Rinna looked at him.

He pointed toward the yard.

"They're asking when the cart leaves."

"Someone is."

"The brown-coat man."

"Description is consistent."

Davin exhaled through his nose.

I said, "First where the money sits. Now how things move."

Rinna looked at me.

"Yes."

That was the first time she agreed without trimming the sentence.

I felt worse, not better.

"It fits."

"It fits a concern," she said. "It does not tell us what he plans."

"If he plans anything."

"Correct."

Marek had come close enough to hear the last part. He was still holding the striped umbrella.

I looked at it.

He looked at me.

"Not now," I said.

He slowly lowered the umbrella.

Progress everywhere.

Rinna called Jori in from the yard.

He arrived wiping grease from one forearm.

She gave him the narrow version.

Someone asked when the cart went out after the late show and whether the same man drove it.

Description was consistent with the Olin visitor.

No useful answers given.

No plan established.

Jori listened, then said, "Cart isn't going anywhere tonight."

Davin pointed toward the yard.

"Brace."

"Yes."

Rinna looked at him.

"How long?"

"Tomorrow if I get the piece cut."

"Then leave it."

That was one decision.

She looked at Davin.

"After shows, nobody tells strangers when anything leaves. If someone asks, send them to me."

"Already doing that."

"Good."

Then she took the cash box, which had not been visible anyway, and moved it from beneath the rear shelf to somewhere I did not see.

I watched her go.

Nessa put a fake pastry into my hand.

"Table."

Apparently the threat had used its allotted time.

The afternoon performance still needed six pastries, one pot, two letters, a physician's bag, a shawl, a wooden spoon, and a striped umbrella that was not supposed to be in the play.

I returned it to the property chest.

Marek saw.

"You wound me."

"I am learning maintenance."

"Of joy?"

"Of inventory."

The house filled.

The Doctor's Supper was not one of the company's better plays. It had one excellent scene and several scenes required to reach it.

Hara played the physician.

Pell played the patient who insisted he was dying until any actual treatment was proposed.

Marek played the brother.

My Neighbor had four lines and a pot.

The strongest moment came in the second scene when Hara asked Pell to describe his symptoms.

He said, "Weakness. Chills. Sudden heat. Dizziness."

Hara put two fingers to his wrist.

"Anything else?"

Pell looked toward the supper table.

"Hunger."

Hara released his wrist.

"Tragic."

The audience laughed.

Pell said, "Is it serious?"

Hara looked at the pastries.

"Possibly fatal if dinner is delayed."

The room broke.

My entrance came later.

I heard the cue while helping Nessa untangle a shawl pin.

I picked up the pot and went.

Marek crossed behind me.

This time I did not move early.

He adjusted.

My crutch stayed inside the mark.

Nobody noticed.

That was the point.

I put down the pot.

"Your brother left this at my house."

Marek said, "Impossible."

"I watched him carry it in."

Pell, from the bed, said, "I was ill."

"You were dancing."

A modest laugh.

"Fever."

"You climbed a table."

"Delirium."

I looked at Hara.

"Then his delirium owes me a new pot."

Bigger laugh than rehearsal.

Not enormous.

Enough.

I left.

Backstage, Nessa handed me the physician's bag because Hara was coming off the other side and would need it in twelve seconds.

I took it without asking why.

Hara appeared.

I gave it to her.

She went back onstage.

No discussion.

I liked that more than the laugh.

After the show, the cart remained in the yard.

Usually something would have gone with it. A folded wall, a chest, spare benches, whatever the next day's arrangement required.

Tonight Jori stacked two pieces just inside the rear door instead.

"Morning," he said.

Nobody argued.

Rinna waited until the front doors were shut before bringing the cash box out. Davin counted with her. When Pell asked whether the cart needed loading, she said, "No. Tomorrow."

That was all.

No guard.

No escort.

No one stood at the door pretending not to stand at the door.

The theatre had simply stopped making tonight look exactly like every other night.

Rinna paid me one copper.

I put it away.

Then I remembered the crutch tip.

Not because it failed.

Because it did not.

I had spent money that morning so the problem would remain boring.

Possibly the finest use of money available.

On the walk home, the new tip gripped wet stone cleanly when I turned.

I noticed once.

Then stopped noticing.

Lyssa was home before me, sitting at the table with the blue cloth spread across her lap and the matching thread running through it in small dark stitches.

"You used it."

She looked at the spool.

"That is what thread is for."

"I thought it might be ceremonial."

She held out her hand.

I gave her my coat.

This was not what she had meant, but she took it anyway and put it over the back of the chair.

"Crutch?" she asked.

"New tip."

"Good."

"Very expensive emotional journey."

"Did you fall?"

"No."

"Then boring."

"Exactly."

She went back to the seam.

I washed, found something to eat, and sat across from her.

For a while neither of us spoke.

Then she said, "Dangerous man?"

"No appearance."

"Paper?"

"No paper."

"Umbrella?"

"Contained."

She nodded.

I considered leaving it there.

Almost did.

"Someone asked about the theatre cart."

Her needle stopped for only a moment.

"Who?"

"Cart repair man doesn't know. Description sounds like the other one. Brown coat, dark hair, narrow face. Quiet. Could be same. Not proven."

"What did he ask?"

"When it goes out after the late show. Whether the same man drives."

Lyssa resumed stitching.

"Did the repair man tell him?"

"No."

"Then your people heard again before it became anything."

"Yes."

That was true.

I looked at her thread moving through the cloth.

"They asked where the money sits. Now they're asking how things move."

She tied off one stitch.

"You know what they're asking."

"Not why."

"Right."

I hated how familiar that word had become.

She did not tell me to investigate.

She did not tell me not to.

She shifted the cloth, checked the seam against the edge, and held out one hand without looking.

I put my hand in it.

The theatre cart sat in the yard with a cracked brace.

The cash box was somewhere Rinna had not shown me.

A man who might be the same man had asked when things left.

None of that told me what happened next.

For once, we knew a little more before paying for the lesson.

That would have to be enough.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 224

## THE CHECKER

Lyssa had taken the table again.

Not permanently. She did not own the table, despite growing evidence to the contrary. But when I woke, half of it was covered by blue cloth, the other half by a darker piece she had not shown me before, and the narrow remaining strip held my breakfast with the confidence of a refugee camp.

I sat sideways.

"You know there are other surfaces," I said.

"There are other breakfasts."

I looked at the bread.

"Threatening."

She had three pins between her lips and did not answer.

The new left crutch tip felt normal enough that I had forgotten about it until I stood. It gripped the floor cleanly, neither too soft nor too eager to catch. The repairer's work had succeeded so thoroughly that I resented having spent money on something I could no longer complain about.

That was probably the point.

Lyssa took the pins from her mouth.

"Are you at theatre all day?"

"I don't know yet."

"Useful."

"I try."

She folded the blue cloth over itself and checked the seam. "If you pass the west market, get onions."

"Color?"

She stared at me.

"I learned from the thread."

"Onion-colored."

"Excellent. I know exactly what to do."

A knock came before she could improve the instructions.

It was not ominous.

I knew this because the boy outside looked bored.

He wore a plain brown vest over a shirt that had once been white and held a folded slip between two fingers as though it had personally inconvenienced him.

"Greg?"

"Unfortunately."

"Vale office."

Lyssa looked up.

The boy handed me the slip.

ROOM WORK AVAILABLE. TODAY. AFTER FIRST BELL IF YOU WANT CREDIT.

Below that, in a different hand:

SIT DOWN WORK.

No signature.

I turned it over.

Nothing.

Hessa's school continued to spread.

"Do I answer?" I asked.

The boy shrugged. "They said come or don't."

"Very warm institution."

He had already turned away.

Lyssa said, "You were wondering."

"About onions?"

"Vale."

I looked at the slip again.

She knew because I had mentioned, once, several days ago, that Antonius had not had suitable work waiting every time I checked. That was all. She did not maintain my debt schedule. She maintained three customers, a changing collection of cloth, and apparently control of the table.

"I can do both," I said. "Vale first. Theatre after."

"If they still need you after Vale."

"Theatre always needs someone to hold something nobody else wants to hold."

"Then your future is secure."

I ate the bread.

By the time I left, Lyssa was tying the darker cloth into a bundle and muttering about a cuff.

Outside, Carrow had turned gray. Not rain exactly. The sky simply looked undecided, and every stone in the street seemed prepared to become slippery if given encouragement.

The repaired crutch tip behaved.

I stopped thinking about it before I reached the next corner.

The Vale office was already working when I arrived.

That should not have surprised me. Money rarely waited for people to become emotionally prepared.

Two men stood near the front counter arguing about a delivery date. A woman in a dark scarf sat at the side table with three open account books and a piece of bread balanced on the edge of one page. Somebody in the rear room was moving boxes. A clerk I recognized from earlier visits had ink on two fingers and a strip of paper stuck to his sleeve.

He looked at my note.

"You're here."

"Strong start."

"Sit."

He pointed me toward a table against the wall.

Four stacks waited there.

I looked at him.

"Are these all mine?"

"Only if you're slow."

I sat.

He put a ruled ledger beside the stacks.

"Copies came back from the south accounts. Antonius wants the invoice totals checked against the delivery tallies before we enter them. Mark anything that doesn't agree. Don't correct it yourself."

"Because I am untrustworthy?"

"Because then I have to find what you changed."

"Less flattering."

"More useful."

He showed me the system.

Each invoice had a name, date, goods, and total. Each delivery tally had the same account name and the quantities actually received. Some had short marks in the margin that changed how a line should be read. Returns. Damaged goods. Partial delivery. Deferred item.

The first ten were boring.

This was reassuring.

The eleventh was also boring.

The twelfth almost became exciting because the invoice showed seven lengths of timber and the tally showed six.

I marked it.

The clerk came past twenty minutes later, saw the mark, and glanced at the papers.

"Return mark."

"What?"

He tapped a tiny hooked line beside the sixth entry.

"One rejected at delivery. Invoice stays seven until credit note attaches."

I stared at the hook.

"It looks like someone dropped a hair."

"It means rejected."

"Of course it does."

"You've seen it before."

"Apparently not successfully."

He pushed the papers back.

"Don't remove the mark."

"I wasn't planning to destroy the evidence of my education."

He had already moved on.

I looked at the hook again.

That was one discrepancy solved by me being wrong.

The next stack went faster because now the tiny hooks had acquired meaning.

The work was not difficult in the dramatic sense. Nobody swung a sword. Nobody demanded that I move paper through glass with my mind. Nobody wore a fake mustache, as far as I knew.

It was difficult because the lines were small and repetitive and every fourth page tried to persuade my eyes that I had already checked it.

I developed a method.

Invoice.

Name.

Date.

Quantities.

Tally.

Marks.

Total.

Then back once.

Not because I had become a financial professional.

Because skipping around made me lose my place.

The woman with the bread finished eating it and replaced the account book without brushing away the crumbs. The clerk removed one crumb with a wet fingertip while continuing a conversation about warehouse storage. A runner came in, left a packet, collected another, and went out again. Twice, Antonius crossed the rear doorway without acknowledging me.

The office existed very comfortably without my participation.

I preferred that.

Near the bottom of the second stack, I found a total that was actually wrong.

At least I thought it was.

The invoice listed four crates at one figure each and two smaller bundles beneath them. The written total did not match the lines.

I added it again.

Same result.

Then I checked the delivery tally.

Same quantities.

No return mark.

No damage mark.

No note.

I marked the page.

This time I did not summon the clerk with my face.

I kept working.

He came eventually.

"Two marks?"

"One was ignorance. This one might be arithmetic."

He looked.

His finger moved down the lines once.

Then again.

He reached for the small scrap pad tucked inside the ledger and added the figures himself.

"Copied wrong."

"Mine?"

"Invoice copy."

He put a short circle around the total.

I felt a small, stupid satisfaction.

The clerk ruined it.

"Don't become proud. You missed the first one."

"I was hoping we had agreed never to discuss that again."

"We did not."

He took the invoice and laid it on a separate pile.

"What happens?"

"Original gets checked. If original is right, copy is corrected. If original is wrong, account gets corrected."

"And if both are wrong?"

"Then someone had a bad morning."

Commercial systems were more honest than magic.

Antonius appeared at my table before midday.

He did not announce himself. He simply stopped beside the chair and looked at the remaining stacks.

"How many?"

I told him.

"Errors?"

"One copy total. One false alarm."

The clerk, from three tables away, said, "Return mark."

Antonius looked at me.

"I know what it means now."

"Expensive knowledge?"

"Only to my dignity."

"Then cheap."

He picked up the incorrect copy.

"Anything else?"

"No."

His eyes moved to my crutches.

"New tip."

I looked down.

"Yes."

"You replaced one?"

"Yes."

"Good."

I waited.

He did not praise fiscal responsibility.

Of course not.

He said, "A bad crutch is an expensive way to make yourself less useful."

There he was.

"I paid for it."

"I assumed the repairer had not become charitable."

"I thought you might object to the spending."

Antonius looked genuinely puzzled.

"Why?"

"The debt."

"Are you planning to repay it while concussed?"

"I wasn't planning to fall."

"Then maintain the equipment that keeps you from doing it."

Not kindness.

Arithmetic with bones in it.

He put the invoice back down.

"Finish the stack."

"Credit?"

"If the work is usable."

"Encouraging."

"Accuracy first. Encouragement is not billable."

He turned away.

I watched him stop at the front counter, listen to half of the delivery argument, ask one question, and make both men begin again from the date.

He was good at being Antonius.

I returned to the pages.

The third stack contained nothing wrong.

This annoyed me.

I had become accustomed to the possibility that careful observation would eventually reward me with a discovery. Instead I checked page after page and proved only that the pages agreed.

That was still work.

The fourth stack gave me another mark.

A delivery tally showed twelve sacks received. The invoice showed ten.

I checked the account name.

Correct.

Date.

Correct.

No hook.

No note.

I marked it.

The clerk came over.

He frowned.

"That one should have an attached continuation."

"Should?"

He checked beneath the invoice, then under the next page.

Nothing.

He went to the rear room and returned with a second bundle.

Five minutes later he found the continuation sheet clipped to the wrong account.

The extra two sacks belonged on it.

"Still an error?" I asked.

"Filing error."

"Do I get partial credit for discovering paper in the wrong place?"

"You get the credit you're already getting for doing the job."

Cruel profession.

He moved the continuation sheet to the correct packet and made a notation.

I looked at the false discrepancy.

Not false, exactly.

The numbers had disagreed because part of the record was somewhere it should not have been.

That mattered enough to fix.

Not enough to become a conspiracy.

I was learning restraint against my will.

At midday the woman in the dark scarf left. Another clerk took her chair without asking whether it was available. Someone brought in a pot of soup and four bowls. I expected to be excluded from this arrangement because debt labor had its dignity.

The ink-fingered clerk put a bowl beside my ledger.

"Don't spill."

"Warm hospitality."

"Don't spill."

The soup had beans and something green in it.

I ate while checking the last six invoices because apparently this office had solved the problem of lunch by refusing to stop working.

Antonius came through once with his own bowl, saw mine balanced too close to the ledger, and moved it three inches farther away without breaking stride.

No one explained the symbolism.

There was none.

I finished the final stack shortly after.

The clerk reviewed my marks.

One copied total.

One misplaced continuation.

One return mark that had embarrassed me.

Everything else agreed.

He carried the marked items to Antonius's room.

I stayed at the table because nobody had told me to leave and because the chair was comfortable.

A few minutes later Antonius called, "Greg."

I went in.

His room had not improved.

Desk. Ledgers. Chair. Shelves. Papers that looked expensive because they were organized.

He had the two actual discrepancies open in front of him.

"Both confirmed," he said.

I sat when he pointed.

"The copy total was wrong. The continuation was filed wrong."

"I feel dangerously competent."

"You found two errors in several stacks of ordinary work."

"Let me have this."

"No."

He wrote something in his ledger.

I watched the pen.

"Credit recorded," he said.

No number.

I did not ask for the total balance.

I knew what I owed because the office knew what I owed, and the number did not need to be narrated to make the debt exist.

"How much credit?"

Antonius looked at me.

"For the work."

He pointed to the line recording the work credit.

I absorbed the figure, then looked at the ledger without trying to calculate my entire life out loud.

The debt moved.

It remained a debt.

That was enough.

Antonius closed the book.

"Theatre today?"
