During the performance, Hara came off holding the blue shawl before the actor onstage had finished his line.

She stopped herself at the wing.

Waited.

The line ended.

She handed me the shawl.

"Nearly."

"Almost counts backstage."

She looked at me.

"Whose terrible rule is that?"

"Nessa."

"Of course."

She went around for her next entrance.

I put the shawl where it lived.

No ceremony.

The name board returned halfway through the early piece.

One side had fresh dark paint.

The other had chalk.

Jori handed it to Nessa.

"Paint is dry enough to hang. Nobody touch the back."

Marek was standing beside her.

Nessa said, "Marek."

"I have done nothing."

"Continue."

The Wrong Funeral setup began as soon as the first audience cleared.

Black bench.

Narrow table.

Candles.

Book.

Door flat.

Name board.

Flowers.

The long spray had been repaired where one cloth lily had started to loosen from its wire. Nessa had wrapped thread around the base and left the old white paint alone.

Readable enough.

The second audience arrived in damp coats and louder voices than the first.

Someone in the front row was already laughing before the play began because his companion had apparently said something better than us.

Unfair.

The opening scene belonged to Hara and Pell.

Hara's widow entered the mourning room first, looked at the name board, and stopped.

Pell asked whether something was wrong.

She said, "Only the spelling."

Pell looked at the board.

"The spelling is correct."

"Then the dead man is wrong."

The audience laughed immediately.

Good start.

The next several minutes built the confusion.

Marek arrived.

Then another actor.

Then a woman who insisted she had never met anyone in the room but had been told there would be food after the service.

Hara kept trying to identify which person had actually known her brother.

Nobody had.

Pell's mourning-house keeper became increasingly committed to pretending this was normal.

Then my cue came.

Nessa gave me the long spray.

"Sideways."

"I know."

Marek, already onstage, heard her through the flat.

His mouth moved.

I knew exactly what he was thinking.

I went before he could say it.

The flowers cleared the door.

Upright.

Cross.

"Flowers for the family."

Pell turned toward me with the expression of a man who had already received too many families.

"Set them with the others."

"I need a name."

"Everyone here has one."

Small laugh.

I held the spray.

"One for the flowers."

Marek raised a hand.

"Use mine."

Hara turned.

"Are you dead?"

"No."

"Then wait."

Bigger laugh.

Marek looked almost offended by the instruction.

I delivered my next line.

"Two more before supper. One of you must belong to somebody."

The audience laughed again.

Not huge.

Enough.

Pell waved at Hara.

"Widow."

Hara said, "Sister."

Pell waved at Marek.

"Nephew."

Marek said, "Unfortunately."

Hara looked at him.

"Mutual."

Better laugh.

Mine was over.

Good.

I asked whether anyone could read the card.

Nobody volunteered.

So I read it.

The dead man's name did not match the board.

The room went still for one beat.

Then Hara looked at Pell.

Not angry.

Tired.

"You have misplaced my funeral."

The audience broke.

That was hers.

Completely.

Pell opened his mouth.

Closed it.

Looked at the name board.

Turned it.

The correct name appeared.

A second laugh rose before he spoke.

Then one of the flowers fell off my spray.

A white cloth lily.

It dropped between my crutches and Hara's shoe.

I saw it.

She saw it.

The audience probably saw it.

For half a second, my body wanted to stop and pick it up.

Bad geometry.

Worse timing.

The scene was moving.

I set the spray beside the bench where we had rehearsed.

The bench had stayed in its two-inch position.

Good.

I left the flower on the floor.

Then I exited.

Backstage, Nessa had already seen it.

"Leave it."

"I did."

"I know."

That was the entire review.

Onstage, Pell had begun explaining the name board.

Hara did not accept the explanation.

Marek tried to leave.

She stopped him.

Then, during the argument, Hara looked down.

She saw the fallen lily.

She bent, picked it up, and held it between two fingers.

Nobody had written this.

I knew because I had six lines and had read everyone else's scene often enough to know when the world went off-book.

Pell stopped talking.

Hara looked at the flower.

Then at the long spray beside the bench.

Then at the corrected name board.

"At least one thing arrived for him."

The audience hit hard.

Not because the line was brilliant by itself.

Because the whole room had spent ten minutes failing to put the right people, name, flowers, and funeral together.

Pell bowed his head as if accepting a judgment.

Marek quietly sat back down.

The scene continued.

Hara kept the lily.

She did not throw it away.

She placed it on the closed book near the end of the scene and never mentioned it again.

Backstage, Nessa exhaled.

"Useful."

I looked at her.

"That word is spreading."

She had no idea what I meant.

Better.

The rest of the play worked.

Not perfectly.

One candle fell over during the second section and was caught by Pell before it rolled off the table.

Davin nearly brought the wrong chair on and caught himself when Jori said his name.

Marek forgot one line, stared at Hara, and she gave him the first two words without making it look like help.

He recovered.

Nobody died except the people the play had arranged in advance.

My second entrance was only to collect the empty flower basket.

No lines.

I had not known I had a second entrance until Nessa pointed at the basket during rehearsal.

Apparently role counts and work counts were different systems.

I went.

The path was clear.

I took the basket.

I left.

The audience did not applaud.

Excellent basket work.

At curtain, Hara received the strongest response.

Marek got a good one too.

Pell bowed like a man who had personally survived administrative death.

I stood where I had been told and did not trip over flowers.

Then the company became labor again.

The long spray went to the property table.

The loose lily came back in Hara's hand.

She gave it to Nessa.

"Greg shed."

"I was carrying it."

"Then it shed you."

Marek looked over.

"Theatre education."

I pointed at him.

"Your face taught us the door."

"At last, respect."

Nessa repaired the lily while we cleared.

Davin carried the name board through the rear passage with the wet side facing away from everything.

He had learned.

Jori watched anyway.

Rinna paid me the normal copper for the day's work.

I put it away.

No debt arithmetic.

No office arithmetic.

A coin earned in a theatre.

I stayed long enough to help return the black bench to the wall.

Jori took one end.

I took the other from a seated position first, then shifted onto my crutches while he took more of the weight.

We had done enough awkward objects together that neither of us explained the sequence.

At the rear door he said, "Tomorrow morning?"

"What?"

"Window trim."

"Again?"

"Still windows."

Apparently civilization had failed to resolve them.

"What time?"

"Morning."

"Specific."

"You know when I get here."

Annoyingly, I did.

That was the invitation.

Or assignment.

At this point the distinction was mostly whether Rinna paid me.

Outside, Carrow had gone dark enough for lamps.

I bought a small paper twist of roasted beans from a street seller because the theatre copper existed and because hunger did not become immoral when Antonius Vale owned part of my future.

I ate half while walking home.

The left crutch tip gripped.

My right hand felt worked from flowers, baskets, props, and crutches.

Not hurt.

Worked.

The room was empty when I arrived.

The dark skirt was gone.

My chair was mine again.

The table held a folded blue-gray piece of cloth I had not seen before, a small bowl with two boiled potatoes, and one of Lyssa's needles stuck through a scrap to keep it from disappearing.

No note.

I ate a potato.

Then the second.

I had nearly finished the beans when Lyssa came in carrying nothing.

That was still unusual enough to notice.

She shut the door with her heel.

"You're home."

"Observant."

She looked at the empty bowl.

"You ate."

"I was unsupervised."

"Risky."

She took off her outer layer and sat where the dark skirt had been that morning.

I looked at the blue-gray cloth.

"New?"

"Old."

I waited.

"New to me."

"Yes."

"Customer?"

She looked at me.

"Cloth."

I nodded.

Important distinction.

She rubbed one wrist with the opposite hand.

"Tired?"

"Yes."

I did not turn that into a diagnosis.

Growth everywhere.

I moved the beans toward her.

She took some.

For a while we ate without reporting our professions.

Then she said, "Flowers?"

I looked at her.

"You remembered."

"You complained about six lines."

"I did not complain."

"You counted them."

Fair.

"The flowers survived."

"Good."

"One escaped."

She ate another bean.

"Bad flower."

"Hara recovered it."

"Good Hara."

That was approximately the entire performance review.

I told her about the name board only because Davin painting the same name on both sides deserved civilian consequences.

Lyssa laughed before I reached the end.

"How?"

"He copied the other side."

"Why?"

"I don't know."

"Did he?"

"No."

"Good."

I smiled.

She leaned her shoulder against mine.

The room was quiet.

No Hessa note.

No Vale packet.

No stranger at the door.

Tomorrow morning Jori expected me for window trim because apparently that had become enough of a sentence.

Lyssa had moved an entire skirt through the room while I was gone and come home with no bundle at all.

The theatre had misplaced a funeral and repaired a flower.

I had six lines.

Hara had the line everyone would remember.

That seemed fair.

Outside, someone upstairs dropped something heavy.

Our hanging cup did not tremble this time.

I did not check.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 229

## THE ROAD ONE

Lyssa was still in bed when I woke.

That had happened before. It had simply become less common than waking to a room she had already rearranged and a note telling me to eat something.

For a moment I stayed still.

Not because I thought she was ill. She was breathing normally, one arm folded beneath the pillow, hair spread toward the wall. She had come home tired. Tired people occasionally slept.

I was becoming dangerously reasonable.

The blue-gray cloth remained folded on the table where I had left it alone the night before. Beside it sat half a loaf, a knife, and two onions I had apparently bought under professional supervision.

I ate bread and one of the roasted beans that had escaped its paper twist onto the shelf.

When I stood, my right hand felt normal again. No tenderness where the flower spray had rested against the palm. Shoulder fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb comfortable. Left crutch tip still boring.

Jori expected me in the morning.

I knew when he got there.

That was irritatingly close to having a schedule.

I was pulling on my coat when Lyssa spoke behind me.

"Blue-gray."

I turned.

Her eyes were still closed.

"Good morning."

"Take it to Marra."

I looked at the table.

Then at her.

"Now?"

"After windows."

That opened one eye.

"You remember?"

"Jori remembers."

"Same thing."

She closed it again.

I picked up the folded cloth. "What am I telling Marra?"

"Nothing."

"Strong assignment."

"Give it to her."

"What is it?"

"Cloth."

"We established that yesterday."

"Then you're ready."

I looked for a note.

There was none.

"Does she know it's coming?"

"Yes."

That was apparently the entire system.

Lyssa had already started falling back asleep.

I folded the cloth once more so it fit inside my coat without dragging against a crutch handle. It made one side of me look as though I had stolen a very flat loaf.

"Anything else?"

"No."

"Food?"

"For you?"

"For either of us."

She opened both eyes now.

"There's bread."

"I noticed."

"Then no."

A pause.

"You're going north?"

"Later."

"Marra?"

"No."

That was useful only because I had asked the wrong question.

I accepted the answer.

At the door she said, "Greg."

I looked back.

"Don't lose it."

"Finally, confidence."

She pulled the blanket higher.

I left.

The theatre was open when I arrived, but only through the side door.

I did not try the front.

That would have been how I used to arrive.

The window trim was already on the low platform near Jori's workbench. Three long painted lengths, two shorter pieces, a pot of glue, and a rag stiff enough to qualify as lumber.

Jori was scraping an old edge with the back of a knife.

He looked up once.

"Long ones."

I put my crutches where they normally went beside the wall and sat.

No explanation.

No demonstration.

I picked up the first long piece and turned the painted face away from my knees.

Jori noticed.

He said nothing.

That was better than being told I had done it right.

For the next half hour I held trim, passed pieces when he asked, and rubbed old glue from one edge with the stiff rag. The work had survived several plays and several repairs. One strip carried cream paint on the front, green along one side, and a line of blue near the back where somebody had apparently once decided the audience could see through wood.

Jori needed the second long piece turned twice because one edge had lifted. The first time I shifted it toward him too quickly and the end bumped the wall.

He looked at the mark.

I looked at the mark.

Cream paint had transferred onto older green paint.

"Historic preservation," I said.

"Hold it still."

That was the correction.

I held it still.

He worked the edge, pressed it flat, then gave me the piece back without checking whether I had understood. I had.

My right palm stayed ordinary. When the long board began pulling awkwardly against my wrist, I put its far end on the platform instead of pretending one good morning had changed leverage. Jori adjusted his side without comment.

Davin came back once, saw us, and said, "Still windows."

"Apparently permanent," I said.

Jori said, "Go find the small nails."

Davin left.

I looked after him.

"Does he know which?"

"Yes."

That was more trust than the instruction sounded like.

"Ship?" I asked.

Jori glanced over.

"Magistrate's room."

"Why blue?"

"Ask the person who painted it."

"Dead?"

"Probably not."

Less interesting.

Davin arrived carrying a short strip of trim and a cup.

He put the cup on Jori's bench.

Jori moved it away from the glue without looking.

Davin held up the strip.

"This one?"

"Too short."

"It reaches."

"Hold it there."

Davin held it against the frame leaning by the wall.

It reached from one corner almost to the other.

Almost.

Davin said, "Paint covers some."

Jori looked at him.

"Paint does not extend wood."

"I know that."

"Good."

Davin lowered the strip.

"What do I do with it?"

"Keep it."

"For what?"

"Something shorter."

Davin considered the entire future of theatre.

"Do we have something shorter?"

"We always do eventually."

That satisfied him.

He leaned the strip beside the workbench, drank from the cup, and disappeared toward the stage.

Nobody asked my opinion.

Excellent morning.

We finished the long pieces before first bell had become meaningfully late. Jori stacked them by size. I knew which side of the rear passage they went on and carried the shortest one myself by pinning it lightly between my right forearm and ribs while using both crutches.

The longer ones stayed with Jori.

Competence did not make my hands multiply.

Nessa passed us in the rear passage carrying a folded black cloth and a basket with no flowers in it.

She looked at me.

"No role."

"I did not ask."

"You were going to."

"I was going to ask about the flowers."

"Repaired."

"Good."

She kept walking.

That ended my relationship with yesterday's funeral.

At the side door Jori said, "Tomorrow maybe."

"Windows?"

"Maybe."

"Specific."

He had already turned back toward the bench.

I took that as dismissal.

Outside, Carrow was clear and bright enough to make every wet patch from yesterday look deliberate. A woman shook a rug from an upstairs window. A porter cursed at a crate whose bottom had failed in the street. Two children were drawing squares in chalk between the stones while a dog systematically ruined the game.

I had a destination.

I did not have to think about the route.

That was the strange part.

From the theatre I went south two streets, crossed near the bread ovens, cut through the lane with the cracked water trough, then west past Sen's red door. I did not check whether I had confused it with the green one.

I had once needed that distinction explained.

Now Marra's green door appeared where it was supposed to while I was thinking about lunch.

Time had done something to the city behind my back.

The door stood open.

Inside, the room was already working.

Not sewing.

Working.

That distinction had become visible to me even when I understood almost none of what the work meant.

Cloth lay across one table. A half-finished garment occupied a chair. Somebody I did not know stood near the wall holding one sleeve out while Marra looked at the shoulder. Jessa was near the rear with a bundle under one arm and two pieces of something pale over the other.

Nobody stopped because I entered.

The room had changed since the first times I had come through it.

Not in any way I could have listed usefully.

The green door was the same. The tables were still crowded. Cloth still migrated between chairs and arms in ways that made ownership difficult from three feet away.

But I knew where not to stand.

A narrow passage along the right wall stayed clear because people used it. The first time I had been here I had occupied it while trying to understand who I was supposed to speak to. Now I moved left without thinking, stopped beside a table nobody was cutting on, and kept both crutch tips out of the path between Marra and the woman by the wall.

Jessa passed me with her bundle and did not slow down.

Months ago somebody would have had to tell me I was in the way.

This time nobody did.

I did not congratulate myself.

I had learned enough theatre to know that a route working was not an applause line.

Marra glanced toward me.

"The road one."

I stopped.

It had been long enough that I almost looked behind myself.

"Still?"

"You came by road."

"There are streets."

She held out one hand without leaving the woman by the wall.

I took the blue-gray cloth from inside my coat.

"Lyssa."

"I know."

Of course she did.

I gave it to her.

Marra put it on the corner of the worktable and returned immediately to the shoulder she had been looking at.

That was my delivery.

No receipt.

No speech.

No explanation of what the cloth would become.

I remained standing for a second because I had apparently expected the city to reward successful transport with information.

Jessa looked over from the back.

"Marked?"

I looked at the folded cloth.

"I was told to give it to Marra."

Jessa crossed the room, lifted one corner of the fold, and found something I had not noticed. Two short chalk strokes sat near the edge.

"Fine."

She let it fall.

I looked at her.

"What does that mean?"

"Marked."

"I gathered."

She had already turned away.

Marra said, "Don't teach him."

"I wasn't."

"Good."

I had missed these people.

Possibly because they treated my confusion as a condition of the room rather than an emergency.

The woman by the wall lowered her arm. Marra adjusted the cloth at the shoulder, said something too quiet for me to hear, and the woman nodded.

Then another customer came through the green door.

She did not look at me.

"Lyssa?"

"North side," Marra said.

"Today?"

"Not back here."

The woman shifted a wrapped parcel from one arm to the other.

"Tell her tomorrow afternoon is fine."

Marra said, "She knows."

The customer nodded.

That was it.

No introduction.

No explanation.

She left.

I looked at Marra.

Marra did not look at me.

Jessa picked up her bundle.

"West?"

Marra said, "Already."

Jessa nodded once and went out through the same door the customer had used.

I watched her leave.

I had no idea what had already gone west.

This seemed healthy.

Months ago I might have followed the sentence until somebody explained it.

Now I had learned that other people's work often survived my ignorance.

Marra finally looked at me.

"Done?"

"Apparently."

"Good."

"Lyssa said you would know."

"I did."

"This is very efficient when nobody tells me anything."

"You carried cloth."

"Successfully."

She looked toward my coat.

"Did you?"

I checked.

The cloth was no longer there.

"Yes."

"Then go eat."

I pointed at her.

"Hessa has spread."

"I don't know Hessa."

"Better life."

Marra had already turned back to the woman with the sleeve.

My part in the room was over.

I left.

Lunch cost money.

This remained rude.

I bought bread from a stall near the west market and a small piece of cheese from a woman who cut it with a wire and weighed it in her hand before naming a price. I paid without thinking about Antonius until after the coin had left me.

Then I thought about him.

The debt still existed.

So did cheese.

Both survived.

I ate sitting on the low wall beside a courtyard where three laundresses were arguing about whose line had been moved. None of them asked me to judge.

Carrow had become generous with these small mercies.

By the time I finished, I had nowhere I was required to be.

The theatre did not expect me back.

Vale had not summoned me.

Hessa had not pinned anything to a door, cup, wall, sleeve, forehead, or other available surface.

Lyssa was somewhere north.

Marra had the blue-gray cloth.

For the first time all day, my labor had failed to produce another labor.

I went home.

The table was empty.

Not completely.

Bread knife.

One onion.

The paper from the roasted beans, flattened now because I had used most of them.

But no cloth.

No pins.

No chalk.

No customer's coat occupying my chair.

I sat in my own chair and discovered that the room looked larger when Lyssa's profession was elsewhere.

Not better.

Larger.

There was an important difference.

I considered repairing my shirt cuff again.

Then I looked at the work I had already done.

The loose thread had become two loose threads.

I chose restraint.

Nobody congratulated me.

I washed, cut the remaining bread, and put the cheese where Lyssa would see it rather than where I would accidentally eat all of it while waiting.

Then I stopped waiting.

I had pages from an older theatre role in my coat. I read them for a while, not because I expected the play, but because I had started carrying pages long enough that old ones appeared in pockets like disease.

The role had five lines.

I remembered four.

That seemed fair.

Late afternoon reached the room without drama.

A cart passed outside.

Somebody argued downstairs.

A child knocked on the wrong door, apologized, then knocked on the next one.

I did not inspect the hanging cup.

Progress maintained.

Lyssa came home before dark.

She carried a loaf under one arm and nothing else.

I looked at the loaf.

She looked at the cheese.

"We both bought food."

"Terrible coordination."

"Could be worse."

"How?"

"We could both have bought onions."

She saw the remaining onion on the table.

"Never mind."

I moved my chair so she could sit across from me.

For a moment neither of us mentioned work.

She cut the new loaf.

I cut the cheese.

We ate the old bread first because civilization had rules.

After several bites she said, "Marra got it."

"I know."

"I know you know."

I looked at her.

"Then why are we doing this?"

"Conversation."

"Unfamiliar structure."

She smiled.

"Jessa found me."

There it was.

I sat back.

"I carried the cloth across Carrow."

"Yes."

"I delivered it successfully."

"Yes."

"And before I could report my triumph, your network closed the loop without me."

Lyssa tore bread.

"I don't have a network."

"Jessa found you."

"Jessa knows where I go."

"Marra knew the cloth was coming."

"Because I told her."

"A customer came in asking for you."

Lyssa looked up.

"What customer?"

"I don't know."

"Useful."

"She said tomorrow afternoon was fine."

Lyssa chewed once.

"Good."

"You already knew."

"Yes."

I pointed at her with the cheese.

"This is exactly what I mean."

"What?"

I tried to find the sentence.

The problem was that every sentence made it sound larger and more organized than the room at Marra's had felt.

Not a system.

Not a business network with arrows and departments.

People.

Routes.

Work.

A woman asking for Lyssa.

Jessa going west for something I did not understand.

Marra knowing why two chalk marks mattered.

My entire contribution fitting inside my coat.

I lowered the cheese.

"Nothing."

Lyssa nodded.

That was probably safer.

She looked at my cuff.

Her expression changed.

I followed her eyes.

"Maintenance."

"You made it worse."

"Temporary repair."

"Temporary damage."

"It held through windows."

"That is not the same thing."

"Jori did not complain."

"Jori works with wood."

"Transferable authority."

"No."

I smiled.

She did not reach for the cuff.

Good.

Instead she ate more cheese.

"Windows?"

"Still windows."

"Important?"

"Apparently permanent."

She nodded as though this matched her understanding of theatre.

I asked, "North side?"

"Work."

That was enough.

We kept eating.

No cloth came out.

No customer knocked.

No one needed the table for fitting, cutting, pinning, writing, sorting, or proving anything.

Halfway through supper I realized we were both using the whole table without negotiating for it.

Lyssa had put her elbows down.

I had the bread near the center instead of guarding one narrow corner from thread.

It felt extravagant.

I did not mention that either.

Tomorrow the table might disappear under cloth again.

Jori might still have windows.

Marra might send something back.

Jessa might already know about it.

Hessa might choose one of her several questions.

Bren might remain absent.

Antonius's ledger would continue being correct whether I looked at it or not.

Tonight Lyssa pushed the cheese toward me.

I pushed the better half back.

She took it.

No argument.

The table held supper.

For once, that was its only job.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 230

## THE REPLICATE

The note was under the door.

Not pinned to it.

Not under the cup.

Not balanced against the bread.

Under the door.

Hessa had apparently discovered mail.

AFTER MIDDAY.

SAME ROOM.

EAT.

LIGHT MORNING.

I read the last line twice.

Lyssa was already gone.

Her side of the bed had cooled. The table held bread, half an onion, my increasingly criminal shirt cuff, and nothing else that belonged to a customer.

No cloth.

No pins.

No chalk.

Yesterday the whole table had belonged to supper.

Today it belonged mostly to my bad sewing.

I touched the cuff.

Two loose threads looked back at me.

"Light morning," I told them.

They did not improve.

The room had no answer for what I was supposed to do with several hours in which nobody wanted labor from me.

Jori had said tomorrow maybe.

Maybe was not a call.

Vale had not sent anyone.

Hessa had specifically told me not to arrive tired, which made volunteering for office work feel like an attempt to lose an argument before it started.

I ate bread.

Then more bread because Hessa would ask.

I considered the onion.

The onion had done nothing wrong.

I left it.

Outside, Carrow had already decided to be busy without me.

A woman on the lower landing was washing a rug with enough water to create a private river down the steps. Two men carried a narrow cabinet through the street sideways and argued about whether sideways counted as progress. A boy walked behind them holding one drawer.

The drawer appeared to be winning.

I went nowhere important.

This was harder than it sounded.

I bought a small meat pie near the west market for later, then spent ten minutes explaining to myself that purchasing food before I was hungry was planning rather than moral collapse.

Antonius Vale did not appear from an alley to disagree.

Good.

I walked slowly enough that my shoulders stayed ordinary.

My right hand felt normal.

Wrist normal.

Forearm normal.

Right leg normal.

Residual limb comfortable.

Phantom foot absent until I checked for it, then present because apparently observation remained intrusive.

I sat on a low wall near a courtyard and read one of the old theatre pages I had found in my coat yesterday.

Five lines.

I still remembered four.

The fifth came back only after I looked.

This proved nothing.

A cart passed.

A dog barked at it.

The dog received no result.

By the time the sun had moved far enough to make after midday a defensible claim, I ate the meat pie and drank water from a public pump.

Then I went to the Guild.

The same room was waiting.

Actually the same.

Same narrow table.

Same board.

Same glass shield.

Same paper-fin target.

Same paper-fin control.

Same chair.

Same intermediate mark.

Same far mark.

Same little scratches in the floor around the chair legs.

Nothing had been improved.

This was becoming reassuring.

Hessa stood beside the board with three pages arranged in a line.

She looked at me.

"Work?"

"No."

That stopped her.

"No theatre?"

"Jori said maybe."

"Vale?"

"No."

"Carrying?"

"A meat pie."

She looked at my hands.

"Anything else?"

"My dignity."

"Sit."

There she was.

I put my crutches where they had gone before and sat.

The chair legs met the floor marks without adjustment.

My right foot went to its mark.

Hips square.

Forearm where she wanted it.

Shoulder down.

Hessa checked anyway.

"Food?"

"Bread. Meat pie."

"Water?"

"Yes."

"Sleep?"

"Normal."

"Right hand?"

"Normal."

"Thumb?"

"Normal."

"Wrist?"

"Normal."

"Forearm?"

"Normal."

"Shoulder?"

"Normal."

"Right leg?"

"Normal."

"Residual limb?"

"Comfortable."

"Phantom?"

"Quiet."

She wrote all of it.

I looked at the target.

"You chose."

"I did."

"One of the several questions."

"Yes."

"Do I get to know which one?"

She turned the top page around.

Four words had been written before I arrived.

INTERMEDIATE

FAR

INTERMEDIATE

FAR

I read them.

Then read them again.

"That's backward."

"From last time."

"Which makes it backward."

"Last time began far."

"I remember. Far, intermediate, far, intermediate."

"Yes."

"Today intermediate, far, intermediate, far."

"Yes."

I waited for more.

Hessa waited for me to stop expecting more.

I lost.

"Why?"

"Last session the apparently easier condition came second and fourth."

"Intermediate."

"Yes."

"Both moved."

"Observed response occurred on both intermediate attempts."

"Hostile sentence."

"Accurate sentence."

"And far did not behave."

"One far attempt produced no observed response with the control unchanged. One produced target and control movement and was contaminated for target-specific interpretation."

"I remember the little bastard."

"The control did its job."

"It moved."

"That was useful."

"To you."

"To the record."

Same thing, apparently.

I tapped the page.

"So now intermediate gets fresh Greg."

"Now intermediate comes first and third."

"And far gets second and fourth."

"Yes."

"Same distances?"

"Same marks."

"Same paper?"

"Same target and control."

"Same direction?"

"Away only."

"Same glass?"

"Yes."

"Same room?"

She looked around.

"I was checking."

"No new object?"

"No."

"No toward?"

"No."

"No farther far?"

"No."

"No secret third distance?"

"No."

"Then the question is whether the difference survives changing order."

"Approximately."

I leaned back.

"That is almost interesting."

She tapped the order page.

"Do not improve it."

"It was written before you arrived. Four external attempts if the apparatus and your body remain usable. No additional attempt because a result is inconvenient. No changing order because one condition responds."

"And if the control moves?"

"We classify the attempt from what happened."

"Repeat?"

"Not automatically."

Still hated that phrase.

Hessa moved the order page away from me.

"First the minimal draw."

"Of course."

"Restrictions have not changed."

"I know."

"Good."

That was not permission to become casual.

Thirty-two successful supervised minimal draws sat behind me.

The next one still required Hessa to watch.

I settled.

Breathed.

Let the room become small.

She gave the instruction.

I drew the smallest amount I could manage.

Clean.

Contained.

No thumb spread.

No wrist catch.

No shoulder movement.

Nothing strange in the residual limb or phantom foot.

"Return."

I returned.

Hessa watched the end of it.

No lingering sensation.

"Count."

Thirty-three successful supervised minimal draws.

She wrote.

I looked at the paper fins.

They remained unimpressed.

The shaping attempt came next.

No new form.

No stronger hold.

No clever variation because boredom had become dangerous.

I drew under supervision and shaped exactly what she asked for.

The sensation held cleanly.

My right shoulder stayed down without needing correction this time.

That felt like progress for almost half a second.

Then I remembered that the goal was not to feel impressed by my own shoulder.

Hessa watched my forearm.

"Return."

I returned.

She checked hand, wrist, forearm, shoulder.

"Any change?"

"No."

"Count."

Twenty-nine supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Then the glass shield came between me and the paper.

The room changed.

Not physically.

Socially.

Hessa stopped being a woman who could be annoyed by my sentences and became a woman waiting for one small object to either move or not move while another object sat nearby for the sole purpose of ruining our confidence.

Attempt forty-two.

Intermediate.

Away.

The target sat at the intermediate mark.

The control sat where it always sat.

Hessa checked both against the board marks.

She checked the glass.

She checked the door.

Somebody crossed the corridor outside.

We waited.

The footsteps faded.

Hessa looked at me.

"Begin when ready."

I settled.

Intermediate first.

That mattered more to me than it should have.

The last two intermediate attempts had both produced clean observed movement.

I knew that.

Hessa knew I knew that.

The paper did not know anything.

Probably.

I drew.

Shaped.

Held away.

Nothing happened.

For long enough that I felt my mind begin trying to help.

Not my body.

My mind.

A little more.

A little harder.

Maybe the last session had been stronger.

Maybe I had been fresher after theatre than I was after a useless morning.

Maybe the angle was wrong.

Maybe.

The target moved.

Small.

Away.

Not much.

Enough that the edge crossed its mark.

The control stayed still.

I did not breathe until Hessa said, "Return."

I returned.

She stepped to the board.

Measured.

Checked the control.

Checked the glass.

Then checked again.

"Observed target response. Small net displacement away. Control unchanged."

I smiled.

Hessa looked at me.

I stopped.

"That was intermediate."

"Yes."

"First attempt."

"Yes."

"Fresh Greg."

She wrote.

"Do not name a condition after yourself."

"Too late."

She finished the line.

"Any body change?"

"No."

"Hand?"

"Normal."

"Wrist?"

"Normal."

"Forearm?"

"Warm."

"Different from ordinary effort?"

I considered.

"No."

"Shoulder?"

"Normal."

"Residual limb?"

"Fine."

"Phantom?"

"Quiet."

She wrote.

I looked at the order page.

Far next.

For one stupid second, the clean intermediate response made the next attempt feel like a test of a thing we already knew.

That was exactly why Hessa had written the order before I arrived.

Attempt forty-three.

Far.

Away.

Same target.

Same control.

Same glass.

Same body position except the target went to the far mark.

Hessa reset everything herself.

I watched.

"You trust me with nothing."

"Correct."

"Efficient relationship."

"Begin when ready."

I settled again.

Far had cleanly responded before.

More than once.

Not last session in a way we could use.

But before.

The paper knew none of that either.

I drew.

Shaped.

Held away.

The target did not move.

The control did not move.

I kept the effort where it belonged.

No leaning.

No shoulder rise.

No tiny attempt to become more persuasive because the paper was ignoring me.

Nothing.

Hessa called the stop.

I returned.

She checked.

"No observed response. Control unchanged."

"Far."

"Yes."

"Second."

"Yes."

"Pattern."

"No."

"Shape."

"No."

"Suggestion."

She looked at me.

I surrendered.

"Recorded event."

"Yes."

She wrote.

We stopped for water.

Not because I was hurt.

Because the plan included a break after two external attempts.

Hessa made me stand.

I used the crutches and walked the short length of the room twice.

My right leg had stiffened a little from sitting.

Normal.

It loosened.

My shoulders felt worked, but less than after theatre.

Hessa checked the residual limb before I sat again.

Comfortable.

No skin issue.

No pain.

No weakness.

No tingling.

No reason to stop.

I sat.

The third word on the order page waited.

INTERMEDIATE.

I liked it now.

That was the problem.

"You expect this one to move," Hessa said.

I looked at her.

"Are you reading my mind now?"

"No."

"Disappointing."

"Do you?"

I looked at the target.

"Yes."

She wrote something.

"That feels unfair."

"It is part of the session."

"What did you write?"

"That you said yes."

"Devastating record."

She reset the target at intermediate.

Attempt forty-four.

Away.

Same apparatus.

Same marks.

Same everything we could reasonably keep the same.

Except it was later.

Except I had seen one intermediate response.

Except I wanted another.

Hessa looked at me.

"Begin when ready."

I settled.

Draw.

Shape.

Away.

Nothing.

I waited.

Nothing.

The urge came quickly this time.

Increase effort.

Not much.

Just enough to make the expected thing happen.

I noticed the urge before I acted on it.

That was useful and irritating.

I kept the effort where it had been.

The target stayed still.

The control stayed still.

I could feel my attention narrowing around the paper as if dislike had mechanical force.

It did not.

Hessa called the stop.

I returned.

Nothing had moved.

She checked anyway.

Target on mark.

Control on mark.

Glass unchanged.

"No observed response. Control unchanged."

I stared at the paper.

"Intermediate."

"Yes."

"It didn't."

"No observed response."

"I saw."

"Good."

That was almost offensive.

I rubbed my thumb once.

Hessa's eyes dropped to it.

"Why?"

"Annoyance."

"Physical."

"No. Mental."

She held out her hand.

I gave her mine.

Thumb normal.

Grip normal.

Wrist normal.

Forearm warm.

Shoulder normal.

"Any discomfort?"

"No."

She let go.

I looked at the target again.

"So intermediate is not the good one."

Hessa sat back.

"It has produced more clean observed responses than far under this apparatus."

"That is not what I said."

"Correct."

"It failed."

"Yes."

"After working first."

"Yes."

"Which is annoying."

"Not evidentiary."

"It is evidence of my character."

"Unfortunately."

I looked at her.

There.

Definitely humor.

She refused to admit it.

One attempt remained.

Far.

Fourth.

The condition that had just failed was the one I had expected to work.

That made far feel less doomed.

Which was also probably useless.

Hessa reset the board.

We waited for a wagon outside to pass.

The room settled.

Attempt forty-five.

Far.

Away.

I began when ready.

Draw.

Shape.

Hold.

Nothing.

The paper remained a paper fin at a distance.

The control remained a second paper fin whose entire career consisted of not helping me feel special.

I maintained the effort.

No extra push.

No shoulder rise.

No change in posture.

Nothing moved.

Hessa called the stop.

I returned.

She checked target.

Control.

Marks.

Glass.

Then me.

"No observed response. Control unchanged."

"Far."

"Yes."

"Again."

"Yes."

That one hurt less than attempt forty-four.

I did not like what that said about expectation.

Hessa wrote the final line.

Forty-two: intermediate, small observed response away, control unchanged.

Forty-three: far, no observed response, control unchanged.

Forty-four: intermediate, no observed response, control unchanged.

Forty-five: far, no observed response, control unchanged.

Four clean attempts.

No control movement.

No apparatus disturbance.

No body change large enough to stop.

I read the list upside down from my chair.

"That is uglier."

"Good."

"You people need a new word."

"No."

"Last session intermediate was two for two."

"Yes."

"Today one for two."

"Yes."

"Far last time was one clean no-response and one contaminated attempt."

"Yes."

"Today two clean no-responses."

"Yes."

"So the difference is still there."

Hessa did not answer immediately.

That meant I had made the sentence too large.

I tried again.

"Intermediate has produced more clean observed responses than far under this setup."

"Yes."

"Across more than one session now."

"Yes."

"Intermediate also failed cleanly today."

"Yes."

"So intermediate response is not reliable."

"Correct."

"Far still has the earlier clean responses from other sessions."

"Correct."

"Today does not erase them."

"No."

"Today also does not strengthen far."

"Correct."

"No range."

"No range."

"Not generalized."

"Not generalized."

I leaned back.

The chair complained.

"Did reversing the order matter?"

"We do not know."

"Excellent."

"We now have one session beginning far and one beginning intermediate under the same four-condition structure."

"With different results."

"Yes."

"Which means?"

"It means we have those results."

I closed my eyes.

"One day I am going to make you say something satisfying."

"That would be poor supervision."

I opened them.

"Restrictions?"

"Unchanged."

"Independent draw?"

"No."

"Independent shaping?"

"No."

"Paper?"

"No."

"Coins?"

"No."

"Thread?"

"No."

"Larger objects?"

"No."

"External testing?"

"No."

"Practice?"

"No."

"Barrier?"

"No."

"Theatre?"

"No."

"Loopholes?"

"No."

"Good."

Hessa stacked the pages.

"That word finally useful?"

"No."

She checked my hand once more.

Then wrist.

Forearm.

Shoulder.

Right leg.

Residual limb.

No concerning change.

Thirty-three successful supervised minimal draws.

Twenty-nine supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Forty-five supervised external-effect attempts.

The numbers had grown.

My permissions had not.

This was becoming the most reliable result in magic.

At the door I stopped.

"Do you still have several questions?"

"Yes."

"More or fewer?"

"Different."

That was somehow worse.

"Next?"

"Not decided."

"Again?"

"Yes."

I looked back at the board.

Intermediate had moved once and failed once.

Far had failed twice.

The control had done absolutely nothing all afternoon and therefore had an excellent day.

I left.

Outside, the sky had clouded without rain.

Carrow was entering the part of afternoon where everybody wanted to finish one thing before dark and therefore blocked each other in the street.

I bought nothing.

This was partly discipline and mostly because I had already bought a meat pie.

At home, Lyssa was not there.

The table had acquired cloth again.

Not much.

A narrow folded piece of brown lay near the wall with three pins stuck through one corner. My chair remained free.

Selective occupation.

I approved.

I put Hessa's note beside the basin and cut bread.

My cuff caught on the knife handle.

I looked at the two loose threads.

They had become three.

Evidence accumulated.

I did not repair it.

That was genuine restraint.

Lyssa came in after dark carrying a small bundle of turnips and no garment.

She saw me.

Then the bread.

Then the note.

"Paper?"

"Once."

She put the turnips down.

"Out of how many?"

"Four external attempts."

She took off her outer layer.

"Same distance?"

"Two intermediate. Two far."

"Which moved?"

"One intermediate."

"The other intermediate?"

"No."

"Far?"

"No."

She nodded.

That was it.

I waited.

She started cutting a turnip.

"You have no larger conclusion?"

"I am hungry."

"Hessa would hate your methods."

"Hessa told you to eat."

I looked at the note by the basin.

"She has spread again."

Lyssa pushed the cut turnip toward me.

"Rules?"

"Same."

"Good."

There was that word.

I ate.

The turnip needed salt.

We had salt.

I added too much.

Lyssa ate one bite, looked at me, and moved the bowl farther from my hand.

No one recorded the result.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 231

## THE MAGISTRATE

The brown cloth was still on the table in the morning.

Three pins through one corner. Narrow fold. No note.

I looked at it long enough to confirm it had not become my business overnight, then ate the last turnip cold because I had ruined the hot version yesterday and consequences deserved continuity.

Lyssa had already gone. My shirt cuff had three loose threads, and I did not touch them. This was restraint of a kind Hessa would never properly appreciate because it involved no apparatus and very poor sewing.

I had no note from her anyway. More importantly, Jori had said tomorrow maybe two days ago, which had become today only through the ordinary cruelty of calendars.

I put on the damaged shirt, took my crutches, and went to see whether maybe had survived.

The side door at the theatre was open.

Inside, the magistrate's room had acquired windows.

Not real windows. That would have been reckless.

The painted wall from two days ago stood onstage with Jori's trim fixed around a broad blue rectangle. From the audience it looked like a respectable office window with pale light beyond it. From the wing I could see cream paint along one edge, green on another, and a narrow stripe of older blue at the back where the same timber had lived several previous lives.

The piece I had bumped against the wall carried a small cream mark near the bottom.

Nobody had repaired it.

The audience would never see it.

I found this deeply offensive.

Davin was kneeling beside a low rail with three short boards across his lap. Jori stood over him holding a longer one.

"That one fits," Davin said.

"It fits because I cut it."

"You cut it because I found the gap."

"You made the gap."

"History is written by carpenters."

Jori saw me.

"You're late."

I looked toward the empty house.

"For what?"

He pointed toward the stage.

"Magistrate."

I waited.

Davin looked up.

"Congratulations."

"On what?"

"Corruption."

That was how I learned I had a role.

Nessa found me before Teren did. She came out of the rear passage carrying a black coat and a bundle of pages.

"No flowers," she said.

"I wasn't worried."

"You should be. Marek knows where they are."

She handed me the coat.

It was shorter than the steward's coat from The Second Toast and heavier through the shoulders. The hem stopped high enough that it would not wrap around a crutch tip when I stood. Nessa checked that before I finished putting it on.

"Good."

"Did you choose this for my dignity?"

"For your legs."

"Less romantic."

"Also the other one smells like Pell."

From the stage Pell shouted, "I can hear you."

Nessa raised her voice.

"Then wash it."

Pell said something I could not make out.

Marek laughed.

The company was already busy enough that nobody explained why.

Teren arrived with a pencil tucked behind one ear and pointed to the pages in my hand.

"The Crooked Fence."

I looked down.

The cast list was short.

WIDOW: HARA

NEIGHBOR: MAREK

CLERK: PELL

MAGISTRATE: GREG

Below that, fifteen lines.

"Fifteen."

"Yes."

"I am advancing."

"You're sitting."

I looked at the stage.

A broad desk had been placed beneath the painted window. Behind it, one chair.

"Ah."

"You stand once."

"Demotion."

Teren ignored that.

"The play opens with you already there. Pell enters, then Hara. Marek comes after. You do not need to make the magistrate important."

"I am the magistrate."

"That's the trap."

He took the pages back long enough to tap one line near the middle.

"Listen to the dispute. Don't play the joke before they give it to you."

"Do I know what the dispute is?"

"You read the title."

"Crooked fence."

"Excellent scholarship."

He gave the pages back.

"Stage."

I had played men who delivered things, carried things, served things, borrowed things, guarded doors, stood in rooms, and once represented the entire concept of being a neighbor.

Magistrate felt suspiciously like employment with furniture.

For once, the job description appealed to me.

The set had more pieces than the painted wall suggested.

Desk. Chair. Clerk's stool. A narrow witness rail Davin and Jori were still arguing about. One rolled map. A wooden seal block that did not seal anything. Three folded petitions. A length of rope. A short painted fence panel that looked as though it had lost an argument with weather.

Nessa put the seal block on the desk.

"Do not hit the desk with it."

I looked at the block.

"Why would I?"

"Because every man who plays this part does."

"Tradition."

"Damage."

She placed a small square of dark leather beside my right hand.

"Hit that."

"How often?"

"Twice."

"Only twice?"

"In the play."

"After?"

"No."

Marek appeared beside us and reached for the block.

Nessa moved it without looking at him.

He stopped.

"I was inspecting justice."

"You can inspect it from there."

He leaned toward me.

"Corrupt."

"Apparently."

He smiled and went to find his fence.

I sat behind the desk.

The chair was solid and slightly too low.

My right foot rested flat. Left knee bent comfortably. I could keep both crutches behind the desk to my right without their tops showing above it if I angled them toward the wall. Standing would require one extra beat to reach them, but the script had enough room before the magistrate crossed to the witness rail.

Jori watched me try it once.

"Rail farther left."

Davin said, "It was farther left."

"It was crooked."

"It's a crooked fence play."

"The fence is crooked."

"Theme."

Jori moved the rail.

Not much. Maybe three inches.

That gave my right crutch a clean plant when I stood.

Teren did not comment.

We began.

Pell entered first as the Clerk carrying the petitions and a face suggesting he had already heard too much from everyone involved.

"Morning docket," he said.

My first line:

"How bad?"

Pell looked at the pages.

"Neighbors."

I looked up.

The company laughed.

Teren said, "Again."

"I did not write it."

"You enjoyed it."

"It is enjoyable."

"Again."

Second time I asked, "How bad?" like a man whose morning could still conceivably be saved.

Pell looked at the pages.

"Neighbors."

Better.

Hara entered before the laugh finished.

Her Widow carried the short fence panel under one arm.

Not a piece of paper.

The fence.

She dropped it in front of the desk.

"Evidence."

I looked at Teren.

He said, "Not you."

Right.

The Magistrate looked at the fence.

"That is a fence."

"It was."

"Has its condition changed?"

"It has moved."

Marek entered through the opposite side.

"It was moved."

Hara turned.

"By you."

"By weather."

"Weather does not own a hammer."

Marek held up both hands.

"Neither do I."

From backstage Davin said, "He does."

Teren turned his head.

Davin disappeared.

We kept going.

The dispute was simple enough to survive fifteen lines and complicated enough to occupy everybody else.

Hara's Widow claimed the fence between their yards had moved two feet into her side.

Marek's Neighbor claimed a storm had shifted the posts.

Hara claimed the posts had moved uphill.

Marek claimed water did strange things.

Pell's Clerk kept producing older descriptions of the property that contradicted both of them because the lane had once been wider, then narrower, then apparently measured by a man who wrote one number differently every time.

The Magistrate wanted one fact that stayed in place.

I understood the role.

At the first run, I did too much with that understanding.

I leaned forward through every ridiculous answer. Watched Hara. Watched Marek. Looked at Pell's papers as though I could force them into coherence through judicial attention.

Teren stopped us after five minutes.

"Greg."

"What?"

"Sit back."

I did.

"You're chasing them."

"I am hearing a case."

"The case comes to you."

I looked at the desk.

"That feels administratively optimistic."

Hara said, "He's right."

Teren pointed at her.

"Do not help him."

"I wasn't helping. The magistrate is desperate."

Marek leaned on the witness rail.

"It is his best quality."

The rail shifted.

Jori said, "Off."

Marek stepped away before Jori reached him, which saved everybody time.

Teren looked back at me.

"You don't need to catch every line. Let them bring the mess."

That was specific enough to use.

We reset.

The second run felt easier once I stopped trying to prove the Magistrate was listening.

Pell gave me the petitions.

I read one.

Hara placed the fence.

Marek blamed weather.

I let the argument happen in front of me instead of leaning into it.

The desk became useful.

It gave me somewhere to put my hands. Somewhere to look when two adults were shouting about an object shorter than my leg.

Pell's Clerk became funnier too, because I could glance at him only when the contradictions reached a level requiring professional support.

He never gave it.

At one point Hara said, "The fence moved uphill."

Marek said, "Water rises."

Pell looked at him.

I looked at Pell.

Pell looked back at his paper.

Nobody helped Marek.

The company laughed hard enough that Teren let the silence sit.

That was not my joke.

It worked partly because I did nothing.

I was beginning to understand why theatre kept assigning jobs to absence.

By midday, we had the routes.

The fence panel entered with Hara and left with nobody until the end.

The petitions stayed with Pell.

The rope appeared only in the second half, when Marek attempted to demonstrate how the storm had "pulled" the fence.

The demonstration did not help him.

The seal block stayed on its leather square unless I needed it.

Twice.

Nessa made me prove I remembered that.

"First?"

"After both start talking over Pell."

"Second?"

"Before judgment."

"Desk?"

"Never."

"Good."

She took the block and gave it to Marek.

He brightened.

"Justice."

"Take it to the table."

His face fell.

Temporary authority transferred.

Lunch happened in the aisle because the stage was still full of legal property.

Rinna had bread. Hara had two boiled eggs. Pell had something wrapped in leaves that smelled much better than my bread. Marek claimed he had already eaten and then stole half of Davin's apple.

Davin noticed after two bites were gone.

"That's mine."

Marek looked at the apple.

"Evidence unclear."

I held out my hand.

"Bring it before the court."

Davin gave me the apple.

Marek said, "You cannot be impartial. You know the victim."

I took a bite.

"Case dismissed."

Hara laughed into her egg.

Teren, from three rows away, said, "Do not improve the play."

I swallowed.

"Rehearsal never stops."

Rinna passed behind us carrying a small stack of tickets, stopped long enough to steal a piece of Hara's bread, and kept moving before Hara noticed which piece she had taken.

Hara noticed.

"That was the good side."

Rinna bit it.

"Still is."

She kept walking.

After lunch, Jori and Davin replaced the witness rail with a different one because the first had developed a wobble that was not funny enough to justify keeping.

Davin carried it away.

"I said it was crooked."

Jori said, "It was loose."

"Crooked things become loose."

"That is not carpentry."

"It is philosophy."

"Take it outside."

Davin did.

I watched the new rail go down exactly three inches farther left than the first.

No one measured from my crutch.

They measured from the desk.

The result still worked.

That was better.

The afternoon run was cleaner.

My one standing cross worked without thought. Left crutch, right crutch, right foot, up. Around the desk. Two plants to the rail. Stop. The black coat stayed clear. Nessa had been right about the length.

Hara changed one small thing during the run.

When she said the fence had moved uphill, she stopped pointing at Marek and pointed instead at the fence itself, as though the fence had participated in the crime.

Teren let her keep it.

Marek changed nothing.

Pell changed even less.

That was another thing I was learning. Experienced actors did not always decorate a scene when they found something that worked. Sometimes they protected it.

The house filled for the early performance.

Not full.

Enough.

Voices became a low uneven layer beyond the curtain. Someone coughed repeatedly in the third row. A child was told twice not to climb on a bench. Rinna moved through the front with tickets. Backstage, Nessa checked the fence panel for a loose nail that was paint, checked Marek's rope, checked Pell's petitions, then came to me.

"Block?"

"Leather."

"Twice?"

"Twice."

"Desk?"

"Never."

She nodded and moved on.

I was already seated when the curtain opened.

That was strange.

No entrance.

No moment of stepping from backstage into light.

One second I was Greg behind a desk listening to the audience settle.

Then the curtain moved and I was a magistrate who had already been at work before any of them arrived.

Pell came in.

"Morning docket."

"How bad?"

He looked at the petitions.

"Neighbors."

The laugh was better with people.

Not huge.

Warm.

Hara entered carrying the fence.

She dropped it.

"Evidence."

The audience laughed again because apparently bringing an entire fence into a magistrate's room was funny even before anyone explained it.

Good play.

We moved.

The first half went cleanly.

Marek's weather defense got a laugh.

Hara's hammer answer got a larger one.

Pell read three measurements from three years and made each sound more exhausted than the last.

I sat back.

Let them bring the mess.

When both Hara and Marek began talking over Pell, I picked up the seal block and struck the leather square once.

A hard wooden knock.

They stopped.

Correct.

"One at a time."

Written line.

We continued.

Then came the rope.

Marek tied one end around the fence panel and held the other.

"The wind catches here."

Hara said, "Wind has hands now?"

"Enough wind does."

"Then arrest the wind."

A laugh.

Marek pulled the rope.

The fence panel slid six inches across the floor.

He stopped.

Hara looked at it.

The audience understood before she spoke.

"So it can be moved."

That laugh was bigger.

Marek stared at the fence as though betrayed by physical law.

Pell lowered his petitions.

I had a line.

"Your demonstration has become hostile."

I got it out without smiling.

Small laugh.

The play rolled forward.

Then I made the mistake.

It happened because Pell began a line with the same words he used later.

"Before judgment..."

I knew the second strike came before judgment.

My hand moved.

The block hit leather.

Knock.

Pell stopped.

Not because he was supposed to.

Because I had just cut his sentence in half.

For less than a second the stage became very clear.

My hand on the block.

Pell looking at me.

Hara looking at Pell.

Marek still holding the rope.

The audience waiting.

I had ended something early.

Hara turned to me.

Her Widow said, perfectly calm, "If judgment has arrived before the clerk finishes, I would like to know whether I am required to stay for it."

The audience laughed.

Not enormous.

Enough to reopen the room.

Pell looked down at his petition.

"Apparently not."

Another laugh.

Teren would murder us both later.

Marek lifted the rope.

"Can I go too?"

Hara snapped, "You can take your weather."

Bigger.

The scene was alive again.

Pell restarted from the part I had murdered.

"Before judgment, the court has one older survey."

This time I left the block alone.

The Magistrate listened.

The survey described the property line using a pear tree that no longer existed.

Hara said it had died.

Marek said she had cut it down.

Hara said it was her tree.

Marek said that was exactly the question.

The audience liked that.

I did too.

I kept my face.

Then came the strongest beat.

Pell read the final note.

"The disputed strip includes responsibility for the drainage ditch along the north wall."

Silence.

Hara's Widow had spent the entire play fighting for two feet of land.

She looked at Pell.

Then at the fence.

Then at Marek.

"His."

The audience broke.

Marek said, "You cannot surrender it now."

Hara picked up her end of the fence.

"I have spent an hour proving your ownership."

Another wave.

Pell had to wait.

Hara did not smile.

She turned to me.

"Magistrate?"

My written line was, "You are withdrawing the claim?"

She said, "In the interest of justice."

That finished the room.

I waited.

Not because Teren had told me to.

Because I could not speak over them.

When the laughter fell enough, I said, "Remarkable how quickly justice improves drainage."

A decent laugh.

Not Hara's.

Good.

I struck the block a second time.

Correct time.

The leather square did its job.

"Claim withdrawn."

Marek objected.

Pell collected papers.

Hara carried the crooked fence out with the satisfied speed of a woman abandoning property she had spent twenty minutes demanding.

My standing cross came near the end.

I reached the crutches, stood, moved to the rail, and delivered the final exchange without catching coat, desk, stool, rope, Marek, or justice.

The curtain came down.

Backstage noise arrived immediately.

Nessa took the block from me.

"Two."

I looked at her.

"Three."

"Yes."

"Teren?"

"Later."

She went after the fence.

Pell came through behind her still holding the petitions.

"You killed me."

"I heard 'before judgment.'"

"You heard half a sentence."

"Apparently."

Hara passed us.

"Efficient court."

"I apologize."

"No."

She kept walking.

I looked at Pell.

"Was that no to the apology?"

"Probably."

Teren found me after the second short piece.

I had no role in it. I spent the time helping Nessa reset the magistrate room and then watching from the wing while Hara played a woman trying to return a horse she had never purchased.

The horse was represented by a halter and the confidence of the cast.

It worked disturbingly well.

When the audience left, the company became labor again.

Teren waited until I had carried the clerk's stool toward storage.

"Greg."

I stopped.

"Block."

"Early."

"Why?"

"Pell said 'before judgment.'"

"Which was not your cue."

"No."

"Your cue was after the survey."

"Yes."

He nodded.

That was apparently the whole note.

I said, "Hara fixed it."

"Hara continued."

Important distinction.

I accepted it.

"Again tomorrow?" I asked.

"The play?"

"Magistrate."

Teren looked toward Rinna's table.

"Maybe."

Jori had infected everyone.

"Specific."

"If we pair it again."

That was not a promise.

Good.

He moved on to tell Marek that the rope belonged in the rope box, not around the witness rail.

Marek said he was preserving the evidence.

Nobody cared.

Rinna paid me one copper.

Normal theatre money.

I put it away.

The stage was already changing before I left. Jori and Davin took the magistrate desk toward the rear. The blue-trimmed wall stayed because tomorrow's first piece apparently used the same room as a merchant's office.

Davin pointed at the window.

"Versatile."

Jori said, "It's a window."

"Exactly."

The little cream mark I had made two days earlier disappeared into the wing.

Still unrepaired.

Still irrelevant.

I stopped being offended.

Mostly.

Outside, evening had settled over Carrow with the smell of cooking oil, wet stone, and somebody burning something that had probably once been dinner.

My shoulders felt ordinary.

Right hand fine.

The one standing cross had cost less than carrying flowers all day.

The Magistrate had been the easiest physical role I had played in weeks and one of the harder ones to leave alone.

I had hit the block early.

Pell had survived.

Hara had made the room hers.

Theatre.

At home, the brown cloth was still near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

I did not inspect it.

Lyssa was sitting at the table eating bread with something spread on it that smelled sharp enough to improve the room.

She looked at the black coat folded over my arm.

"Role?"

"Magistrate."

She chewed.

"Did they know?"

"Eventually."

"How many people did you punish?"

"None."

"Poor magistrate."

"I did interrupt the clerk."

"On purpose?"

"No."

"Better."

I hung the coat over the chair so I would remember to return it tomorrow.

Lyssa looked at it.

"That yours?"

"Theatre."

"Then don't forget it."

"I was hoping to begin a private legal practice."

"In that?"

She looked at the coat again.

"No."

There was no argument available against the tone.

I sat.

She pushed the bread toward me.

I took some.

After a while she asked, "Good show?"

"Hara won two feet of land."

Lyssa waited.

"Then learned it came with a drainage ditch and gave it back."

She laughed once.

"Smart."

"Her character spent the whole play proving it belonged to her."

"Then smarter late."

I considered explaining the audience timing.

I did not.

The brown cloth stayed folded near the wall, and my cuff still had three loose threads.

Lyssa took the better piece of bread before I could reach it.

I started to object.

She had already bitten it.

I took the other piece.

It had more of the sharp spread on it anyway.

## Chapter 232 — THE COUNTERSIGN

The black coat was still on the chair when I woke.

That made it my first obligation.

Not debt.

Not magic.

Not even breakfast, although breakfast argued.

The coat belonged to the theatre, and I had brought it home because apparently being trusted with clothing meant eventually becoming responsible for remembering clothing.

Lyssa was already gone.

The brown cloth remained near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My cuff had three loose threads.

Same failure.

The room had achieved continuity without me.

I ate bread, drank water, put on my own coat, then folded the theatre coat over my left forearm.

That lasted until I picked up the crutches.

I looked at the coat.

The coat looked expensive enough to resent being dragged through Carrow.

I folded it smaller and tucked it under my right arm instead.

That made the first six steps annoying.

By the bottom of the stairs I had found a better arrangement.

Carrow was cool and damp from night rain. Water sat in the broken places between stones and made every cart wheel choose between mud and argument. A delivery boy ran past me with three covered baskets stacked high enough that he could not see anyone below shoulder level.

I moved.

He did not.

Good system.

The theatre side door was open.

I went in, returned the coat to Nessa, and discovered that my entire theatrical importance for the morning consisted of not losing it.

She checked the hem.

Not me.

The hem.

"Fine."

"I also survived."

"I saw."

"You weren't there when I walked home."

"The coat was."

She hung it.

Behind her, yesterday's magistrate room had already become a merchant's office.

The blue-trimmed window stayed.

Desk turned.

Witness rail gone.

A tall shelf had appeared where Hara had surrendered two feet of drainage responsibility to justice.

Davin was standing on a stool holding the shelf while Jori looked at its feet.

"Left."

Davin moved it left.

"Other left."

Davin looked down.

"You have created too many."

Jori pointed.

Davin moved the shelf.

I watched long enough to see it stop wobbling.

Nobody handed me anything.

That was probably a sign.

Rinna crossed the aisle with a stack of folded notices.

"Working today?"

"Apparently not here."

"Tomorrow maybe."

That was not a call.

It was also not nothing.

I nodded.

She kept moving.

I left before somebody discovered a stool that needed carrying.

Outside, I stood under the theatre awning and considered the day.

I had one copper from yesterday.

I also had a debt that did not become smaller through admiration.

Vale's office was not far.

Outgoing bundles happened most days when needed.

That did not mean there were bundles today.

It did mean I knew where the door was.

Good enough.

I went.

The front room at Antonius Vale's office had acquired two people before I arrived.

One was an older man with a red scarf who was arguing quietly about a charge.

The other was a woman holding a folded receipt between two fingers like it had personally insulted her.

Neither looked happy enough to be staff.

I waited near the wall.

The ink-fingered clerk saw me after finishing with the woman.

"Bundles aren't ready."

"All right."

He looked at me.

I looked at him.

That had been the entire plan.

He glanced toward the rear room.

"Can you read small?"

"Usually."

"That isn't an answer."

"Yes."

"Sit."

Work.

A chair appeared because another clerk pushed one away from a table with his foot.

I moved it myself.

The task was not bundles.

A stack of narrow account slips sat beside a thicker book opened flat under a stone weight. Each slip had a house mark, a name, a date, an amount, and one or more short marks along the lower edge. The book carried the same information in rows, except the rows had more space and worse handwriting.

The ink-fingered clerk put one slip beside the book.

"Returned payment acknowledgments."

I waited.

He tapped the slip.

"Runner brings this back after money is received. We match it to the account line. If name, house, date, and amount agree, you put a small cross here."

He showed me a blank margin beside the row.

"Then?"

"Then I check your cross."

"Efficient."

"It is if you stop talking."

He put another slip down.

"If anything disagrees, no cross. Turn the slip sideways."

"Which disagreement matters?"

"Any."

"Spelling?"

"If you can tell it's the same name, no."

"Date?"

"Yes."

"Amount?"

He looked at me.

"Especially amount."

"House mark?"

"Yes."

"Runner mark?"

"No."

I pointed to one of the lower marks.

"That?"

"Runner."

Another.

"Received by."

Another.

"Late."

"Does late matter?"

"Not for matching."

I nodded.

Four things.

Name.

House.

Date.

Amount.

Everything else could be interesting somewhere else.

I had learned enough recently to distrust interesting.

He gave me six slips.

"Do those."

I started.

The first matched.

Name close enough.

House mark exact.

Date exact.

Amount exact.

Cross.

Second matched.

Third had a date one day later than the book.

I turned it sideways.

Fourth had the right name and date but a different house mark.

Sideways.

Fifth matched.

Sixth had the same amount written two different ways because one number in the book had been corrected over itself.

I stared at it.

The clerk noticed.

"Problem?"

"Maybe."

He came over.

I showed him.

The slip said seven.

The book had once said one thing and now said something that could have been seven if the writer had been attacked during the upper stroke.

The clerk looked at the line above.

Then the line below.

Then the account name.

"Match."

"How?"

"Correction mark."

He pointed to a tiny hook beside the number.

I had thought it was an ink scratch.

"That means the corrected figure is accepted?"

"Here, yes."

"Everywhere?"

"No."

Good.

Of course not.

He took my sideways date slip.

"Right."

Then the house mark.

"Right."

Then my uncertain sixth.

"You should have turned this."

"You just said it matches."

"I know. You didn't."

I looked at him.

He tapped the hook.

"You didn't know the correction mark."

"So uncertainty goes sideways too."

"Yes."

That had not been in the first explanation.

Apparently it had not needed to be until I found some.

He gave me twelve more.

The work was boring in a way I liked.

Not pleasant exactly.

Contained.

The slip either agreed with the line or it did not.

When I knew, cross.

When I did not, sideways.

The difficulty was keeping my eyes from following every mark.

Some accounts had little notes in the book.

Some had lines through old figures.

Some had initials.

One had a dark dot that reminded me of the transferred collection mark from the bundle work.

I did not investigate it.

It was not one of my four things.

Progress.

After twenty slips my right leg wanted a different angle.

I moved my foot.

After thirty, my shoulders wanted me to stop leaning over the book like a man trying to enter it.

I sat back.

The clerk noticed that too.

He noticed everything that cost him time.

"Break if you need one."

"I moved."

"That isn't a break."

"I'm aware."

"Are you?"

I took a break.

I stood with both crutches and walked to the front water jug. The older man in the red scarf was gone. The insulted-receipt woman was also gone. A new man stood at the counter asking whether Antonius was in.

He was told no.

Antonius walked through the rear doorway while the clerk was saying it.

The man at the counter looked at him.

Antonius looked at the clerk.

The clerk did not change expression.

"Not for him," he said.

Antonius kept walking.

The man at the counter reconsidered several things about language.

I drank water.

When I returned, the ink-fingered clerk had added another stack.

"Encouraging."

"You came for work."

"I was hoping for the amount where work becomes decorative."

"Wrong office."

I sat.

The next batch included a slip with the right name, right house, right date, and wrong amount.

Not close.

Not a corrected number.

Wrong.

Sideways.

Another had the right amount and date but the house mark was missing one stroke.

I turned it sideways.

The clerk later checked it and put it back in the match pile.

"Same house."

"Missing stroke."

"Runner drew it badly."

"How do you know?"

He pointed to the name.

Then to the account line.

Then to a second tiny mark beside the house symbol.

"Rear court."

I had seen the tiny mark.

I had not known what it meant.

"That makes the house mark enough?"

"With the name."

"So house marks can be approximate."

"No."

I waited.

He waited.

"That one can."

"Because of the rear court mark."

"Yes."

"Which I don't know."

"Now you do."

I turned the next questionable slip sideways anyway.

He smiled.

Not kindly.

"Learning."

"Slowly."

"Safer."

That sounded like Hessa.

I refused to think about why.

By midday, I had matched enough acknowledgments that the first book closed and a second replaced it.

The second book was older.

The paper had gone soft at the corners. The ink changed color halfway down some pages. House marks were drawn with more confidence and less consistency.

The clerk put his hand on it before I started.

"Older accounts. Don't assume the same mark means the same thing."

I looked at him.

"Why would anyone design that?"

"No one designed it."

There it was.

The explanation for most systems.

He opened to a page.

"This district changed marks after the lane numbers changed."

"When?"

"Before you."

"Useful date."

"It is to me."

He showed me two similar symbols.

"This one is old east court. This one is current east court."

"They're the same."

"No."

He pointed.

One had a short line inside the angle.

I leaned closer.

"That's hostile."

"That's bookkeeping."

"Same field."

He gave me eight slips from the older set.

I went slower.

Two matched.

One had an old mark on the slip and a new mark in the book.

I turned it sideways.

One had a name I could barely read.

Sideways.

One matched everything except the amount was one copper lower.

Sideways.

The clerk checked that one twice.

Then he took it to the experienced clerk at the far table.

They spoke quietly.

The experienced clerk came over, read the slip, read the line, and turned back three pages.

He found an earlier entry.

"Partial."

The ink-fingered clerk frowned.

"Not marked."

"No."

They looked at the returned slip again.

I stayed out of it.

Eventually the experienced clerk took a pencil and made a small notation beside the account line.

"Runner collected the remainder. Earlier payment wasn't carried forward."

The ink-fingered clerk looked at me.

"Sideways was right."

"I enjoy being right through refusal."

"Don't get used to it."

The mistake was theirs.

Not dramatic.

One earlier payment had failed to carry into the current line, so the returned amount looked short when it was actually the remainder.

If I had crossed it, someone would probably have found the problem later.

Probably.

That was the thing about offices.

A great deal of civilization seemed to be one person making a mark so another person could discover whether the first person had made the correct mark.

The experienced clerk fixed the earlier line.

The slip returned to the match pile.

Nobody applauded.

I liked that too.

Lunch was bread with a piece of hard cheese I bought from a woman outside.

I ate on the low stone edge beside the office because the chair had become an enemy through repetition.

A cart rolled past carrying bundled reeds.

Two boys argued over whose turn it was to pull a smaller handcart.

A dog slept under it while they argued.

Neither boy had noticed.

I considered warning them.

The dog opened one eye.

It had made its own decisions.

I ate my cheese.

When I went back inside, Antonius was at the rear table.

He had a stack of papers to his left and nothing to his right.

The nothing was shrinking.

He looked at me once.

"Useful?"

The ink-fingered clerk answered.

"Mostly."

I said, "Cruel."

Antonius looked at the matched stack.

"Mostly is billable."

"To whom?"

"Not you."

Good answer.

I returned to the book.

The afternoon became more complicated because the acknowledgments were not all from the same district.

The clerk separated them before handing them to me.

I learned three marks.

Forgot one.

Asked again.

He told me again without pretending I had not already asked.

That was a kind of mercy.

I made one actual mistake.

A woman's surname on the slip had an extra letter.

The house, date, and amount matched.

I crossed it.

The clerk uncrossed it.

"Wrong account."

"Same house."

"Two sisters."

He turned the book slightly and showed me another line three entries down.

Same house mark.

Almost same name.

Same date.

Different amount.

The returned slip matched the lower line.

I had matched the first familiar-looking name instead of checking the full page.

"Right."

"Don't search until you find something that fits."

"I wasn't."

He looked at my cross.

"I was."

"Yes."

I moved the slip.

The mistake had not gone anywhere.

That was why he checked my crosses.

I appreciated the system more when it was protecting everyone from me.

For the rest of the stack, I read the full name first.

Not the shape of it.

The letters.

Late in the afternoon, Antonius came over.

Not to inspect me.

He wanted the book.

The clerk handed it to him.

Antonius looked at the completed pages.

"How many?"

The clerk gave him a number.

I did not count along.

Antonius looked at the sideways stack.

"Problems?"

"Three real. Two unclear. One ours."

"Resolved?"

"Four. Two waiting."

Antonius nodded.

Then he looked at me.

"You came without being sent."

"Yes."

"Why?"

I considered saying debt.

That was true.

It was also obvious.

"Rinna didn't need me."

"Today."

"Today."

He glanced at my crutches.

"Any trouble with the new tip?"

"No."

"Good."

He took the book.

That was apparently the entire medical examination.

I approved.

"Tomorrow?" I asked.

Antonius looked at the clerk.

The clerk said, "Maybe bundles. Maybe nothing."

Antonius looked back at me.

"Then maybe."

No job.

No schedule.

No promise.
