Also no dismissal.

I was getting very good at employment that existed only when the room happened to contain something I could do.

Antonius recorded the day's credit before I left.

I saw the line added.

He turned the book enough for me to read the balance.

I did.

Then he closed it.

Still there.

Smaller than before.

Not small.

Outside, the light had gone yellow against the upper walls.

I had spent most of the day sitting and still felt worked.

Different work.

Eyes.

Back.

Right leg from holding one position too long.

Hands from paper, not weight.

My shoulders were better than yesterday.

My patience had suffered more.

I stopped at the market and bought onions.

The same woman from before looked at me.

"Faster today?"

"I know how many."

"Growth."

"Two."

She gave me three.

I looked at them.

She looked at me.

"That is three."

"You're improving."

"At what?"

"Counting before you stand here."

I paid for three onions.

Apparently recognition had economic consequences.

On the way home I passed the theatre.

I did not go in.

The side door was open.

Someone inside shouted for a rope.

Someone else shouted that the rope was already there.

Then someone shouted, "The other rope."

Theatre continued successfully without judicial supervision.

At home, Lyssa was there.

The brown cloth was still near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

Lyssa sat at the table with a dark sleeve turned inside out across her lap.

Different work.

She looked at the onions.

"Three?"

"I was given an opportunity."

"You bought too many."

"I was manipulated."

"By onions?"

"Their representative."

She held out a hand.

I gave her one.

She inspected it.

"Fine."

"Thank you."

"Not you."

Of course.

I put the other two down.

My cuff still had three loose threads.

Lyssa saw me look at them.

She did not.

Good.

I sat across from her.

"Vale?" she asked.

"Yes."

"Work?"

"Yes."

"What?"

"Matching returned payment slips to account lines."

She waited.

"I was wrong once."

"Only once?"

"One confirmed time."

"Better."

"That is not supportive."

"It is accurate."

She pulled a needle through the dark sleeve.

I told her about the two sisters with nearly the same name.

She laughed at exactly the part where the clerk showed me my own cross.

Not the bookkeeping.

My humiliation.

Reasonable.

"Did you get paid?"

"Credit."

She nodded.

That was enough.

No balance.

No lecture.

No plan.

I picked up one onion and rolled it beneath my palm.

Lyssa looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You look like you're testing it."

I stopped.

"I am not."

"Good."

I moved the onion to the middle of the table.

Farther from me.

She watched that.

Then went back to the sleeve.

I ate the last of the bread while she worked.

After a while she said, "Tomorrow?"

"Maybe."

"Theatre?"

"Maybe."

"Vale?"

"Maybe."

She looked up.

"Busy."

"Extremely."

Neither maybe belonged to me yet.

That was all right.

The onion stayed exactly where I put it.

So did I.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 233

## THE SEAT

The dark sleeve was gone in the morning.

The brown cloth was not.

Same fold.

Same three pins.

At this point it had become the most stable object in the apartment, which was offensive because my left crutch had required repair and the cloth had apparently achieved immortality through refusing to explain itself.

Lyssa was already out.

No note.

No customer.

No Hessa.

No message from Vale.

My cuff still had three loose threads.

The world was preserving several things I had not asked it to preserve.

I ate one of yesterday's onions with bread because buying three had consequences.

This was not a good breakfast.

It was a principled breakfast.

By the time I finished, I had decided that Rinna's "Tomorrow maybe" still did not count as a call.

It did, however, count as a reason to walk past the theatre before I invented a worse use for the morning.

That distinction felt sound.

Carrow was dry after yesterday's damp, with enough sun on the upper walls to make the lower streets look colder by comparison. A man swept dust out of his doorway and into his neighbor's. The neighbor watched from a chair.

Neither spoke.

Long war.

I respected the discipline.

The theatre side door was open when I reached it.

Nobody greeted me.

Davin told me I was in the road before I had both crutches inside.

Better.

I stepped inside and nearly walked into a painted shelf.

Not a real shelf.

Yesterday it had been a real stage shelf in the merchant's office.

Today it was on its side in the passage with one leg removed.

Davin sat beside it with a wooden peg between his teeth.

He took the peg out.

"You're in the road."

"I just arrived."

"Still."

I moved.

Jori came through carrying the missing leg.

He looked at me, then at the shelf, then at Davin.

"Other side."

Davin pointed at me.

"Road."

Jori pointed the other direction.

I moved again.

No one explained what they were doing.

The shelf leg went back on.

Davin pushed.

Jori watched the joint.

The shelf did not wobble.

"Good," Jori said.

Davin looked at me.

"You witnessed excellence."

"I witnessed furniture."

"History will decide."

Rinna found me before history did.

She had a short list in one hand and a piece of chalk in the other.

"You came."

"Maybe survived."

She looked at the list.

"Can you work?"

"Probably."

"Strong answer."

She pointed toward the stage.

"Strike the office. Keep the blue window. Desk goes rear. Shelf to store. Two benches out. Then Nessa has a table."

"One table?"

"Ask Nessa."

"I was afraid of that."

Rinna handed me the chalk.

I looked at it.

"What is this for?"

"Jori."

Jori, behind me, said, "Mine."

I gave it to him.

Important contribution completed.

The merchant's office was already half gone.

The desk had been turned sideways near the rear passage. The witness rail from the Magistrate had vanished yesterday. The blue-trimmed window remained because apparently painted architecture had better employment security than actors.

Hara was rolling a painted wall section with Pell.

Marek held one end of a long canvas and was contributing mostly opinions.

"Lower."

Pell said, "You lower."

"I am lower."

"You are talking."

"Voice comes from here."

He pointed at his chest.

Hara said, "Then lower that."

I took the loose end before the argument acquired furniture.

Marek looked at me.

"Interference."

"Labor."

"Less interesting."

We rolled the canvas.

Marek actually kept tension correctly once we started, which meant the roll stayed straight.

Hara tied it.

"Store two."

I knew where store two was.

No one gave directions.

That was useful because carrying one end of a rolled canvas while using crutches required enough attention without a lecture.

Marek took the other end.

We moved through the rear passage.

"Door," I said.

He turned his end slightly before we reached it.

The roll cleared.

No flowers.

No lilies.

No education.

Just a door.

We put it on the correct rack.

Marek checked the label before letting go.

I noticed.

I did not tell him.

That seemed kinder.

Back onstage, Nessa had found her table.

Actually three tables.

One was narrow and scarred.

One was square with a repaired corner.

One was a low thing that looked designed to hurt shins.

She stood in front of them.

"Not that one."

I had not spoken.

"Which one?"

She pointed at the low table.

"Why?"

"Because Marek already hit it."

From behind the curtain, Marek said, "Once."

Nessa raised her voice.

"Twice."

"One event."

I looked at the table.

"Strong evidence."

"Take the square one."

Pell laughed.

Marek did not.

The square table needed two people because it was awkward rather than heavy.

I took the near side.

Pell took the far.

My crutches became the problem.

I could carry the table or use both crutches properly, not both at once.

Pell looked at the distance.

"Slide?"

The floor was clear.

"Slide."

We lifted enough to get the repaired corner over a seam, then pushed the table on its feet toward stage left.

Jori watched once, decided the floor would survive, and returned to the shelf.

No speech.

No special method.

Just not doing the stupid version.

The table reached its mark.

Nessa moved it four inches.

Of course she did.

"What is it for?"

"Tonight."

"Play?"

"Cards."

I looked at her.

She was already walking away.

Apparently theatre furniture had private lives too.

My first mistake arrived disguised as familiarity.

Two black benches sat near the wing.

One had been in the funeral room. The other had appeared sometime after I stopped paying attention to bench genealogy.

Rinna pointed.

"That one rear."

I took the nearer bench.

It was lighter than I expected, which should have been information.

I got it halfway to the rear passage before Nessa came around the curtain.

"Why?"

I stopped.

"Rinna."

Nessa looked past me.

Rinna was pointing at the other bench now.

Of course.

I looked down at mine.

"What is this one?"

"Cards."

"Tonight."

"Yes."

"So I have stolen the future."

"You moved a bench."

"Less dramatic."

"Put it back."

I did.

The correct bench had a shallow split under one end and a chalk X on the back rail that I had not seen because I had chosen by position instead of identification.

Jori helped me rotate it through the passage.

"X," he said.

"I know now."

"Good."

That was the entire correction.

I put the wrong bench back exactly where it had been and the correct one in the rear.

Nothing collapsed.

Nobody applauded.

This was probably how most competence improved.

The morning became that kind of work.

Not dramatic.

Not difficult enough to become a story inside the story.

Benches out.

Desk rear.

A box of rolled maps moved from under the stair because somebody needed the stair.

Two cracked practice swords returned to a rack.

A painted jug went to Nessa's table, then off Nessa's table after she discovered it leaked.

Davin repaired one bench foot while Jori worked on the shelf.

Pell carried three folded costumes upstairs.

Hara disappeared for twenty minutes and returned with nails.

Nobody asked where she got them.

Rinna crossed the room often enough that I stopped assuming each crossing involved me.

Once she pointed at a bench.

I moved it.

Once she pointed at Marek.

I did not.

That seemed outside my authority.

By midday the stage no longer looked like a merchant's office.

It did not look like anything.

Which was apparently the first step toward looking like something else.

I sat on the edge of the house aisle and drank water.

My shoulders felt used.

Right hand normal.

Right leg a little tired from repeated short stands and starts.

Residual limb comfortable.

Nothing interesting.

Good.

Hara sat two seats away and began eating bread without asking whether I wanted conversation.

Also good.

Pell came down the aisle carrying a cup.

"Done?"

Hara said, "No."

He looked at me.

"Done?"

"I do not know."

Nessa, from the stage, said, "No."

Pell sat.

"Democracy."

We ate anyway.

Marek arrived with no food.

This was suspicious.

Hara looked at him.

"No."

"I haven't asked."

"No."

"I was going to sit."

"Then sit."

He sat one row behind us.

Thirty seconds later Pell lost half his bread.

"How?"

Marek was chewing.

Pell stared at him.

"You were behind me."

"Angles."

I looked toward the stage.

Jori and Davin were still working.

Davin had the shelf upright now.

Jori pushed the top once.

It held.

Davin opened both hands.

"Furniture."

Jori said, "Shelf."

"Recognition is difficult for you."

Nessa passed them carrying the leaking jug.

Davin pointed.

"Not furniture."

"Excellent," she said.

He looked pleased anyway.

Rinna finally called a stop in the middle of the afternoon.

Not a formal stop.

She looked at the stage, looked at the list, crossed off one thing, and said, "Enough."

Everyone seemed to understand this better than I did.

I stood.

"What now?"

Hara looked at me.

"Food."

"I just ate."

"That was hours ago."

It had not been hours.

It had been enough hours for Hara.

Pell was already collecting his coat.

Marek had vanished.

"Nessa?" I asked.

Hara said, "If she comes."

That was apparently the plan.

There was no plan.

I considered going home.

Not because I needed to.

Because going home after work was what the day usually did.

Rinna came down the aisle with the list folded into her pocket.

"You coming?"

"Where?"

"Food."

Everyone had apparently joined the same conspiracy independently.

"Is this a company requirement?"

"No."

"Paid?"

"No."

"Then your recruitment method is poor."

Rinna walked past me.

"Come or don't."

Strong institution.

I went.

The cookshop was two streets over and half below street level, with six long benches, three narrow tables, and a kitchen window that produced bowls faster than I understood.

I had passed it before.

I had never gone in.

Hara entered first.

Pell behind her.

Rinna behind Pell.

I came through the door and found Marek already seated.

Of course.

"How?"

He lifted a bowl.

"Commitment."

The room smelled like onions, broth, pepper, and something fried in fat.

I approved immediately.

There was one open place on the end bench.

Not one open seat.

One place.

A bowl space.

A person space.

Hara had her coat folded on the bench beside her.

When I reached the table, she moved it to the floor without looking at me.

That was the entire invitation.

I sat.

My crutches fit against the wall behind the bench if I angled them together.

Pell shifted his feet before I asked.

Marek stole nothing during the first minute.

Excellent establishment.

We bought our own bowls.

I did not ask the price aloud.

I paid it.

The debt remained real.

So did soup.

Both could survive.

Rinna chose something with beans.

Hara had stew.

Pell had the same thing as me.

Marek had apparently chosen whatever produced the largest bowl.

Conversation began without a subject.

That was new for me.

At theatre, people talked because a thing needed doing.

At home, Lyssa and I had the entire infrastructure of living together.

At the cookshop, nobody needed anything from me except the space my elbow occupied.

Hara complained that the bread was smaller than last time.

Pell said the bowl was larger.

Hara said that was how they distracted fools.

Marek measured his bread against his thumb.

Rinna ignored all of them.

I ate.

A man at the next table laughed too loudly at something that was not ours.

Nobody looked.

Nessa arrived after we had started.

She had paint on one wrist.

Hara kicked the bench opposite.

"Here."

Nessa sat.

No greeting.

She took one piece of Marek's bread.

He stared at her.

"You said not to touch things."

"This is bread."

"It was mine."

"Was."

Pell almost lost soup through his nose.

Marek looked at me.

"Magistrate."

"No jurisdiction."

"Corruption."

"Established."

The joke survived exactly as long as it needed to.

Then Hara asked Nessa whether the painted jug was dead.

"Cracked under the handle."

"Repair?"

"No."

Marek said, "Stage only."

Nessa looked at him.

He stopped smiling.

"Too soon?"

"Wrong object."

"Important distinction."

She ate the bread.

The conversation moved again.

For several minutes the conversation belonged entirely to shoes.

Hara's left sole had started separating near the toe. She lifted the foot under the table and showed Nessa.

Nessa said, "Not tonight."

"I know."

Pell named a cobbler near the west steps.

Hara said, "Too slow."

Rinna named another near the dye lane.

Pell said, "Too expensive."

Marek said, "I can fix shoes."

Every face at the table turned toward him.

He looked offended.

"I can."

Nessa said, "With what?"

"Leather."

"Whose?"

That slowed him.

Hara lowered her foot.

"I'll go to the west steps."

Pell said, "You just said slow."

"I also enjoy owning shoes."

Decision made.

Nobody asked me.

I knew neither cobbler well enough to have an opinion, which was pleasant. A whole problem existed at the table without becoming mine.

A server came by and collected two empty bowls. She left ours because Marek was still using bread to chase the last of his broth around the bottom.

Rinna watched him for three seconds.

"You're going to wear through it."

"The bowl?"

"The bread."

"Then I have eaten completely."

Hara said, "That is not what completely means."

Marek held up the wet bread.

"Evidence."

I kept eating.

Someone mentioned a performer from another company who had apparently forgotten an entire entrance last week.

Nobody agreed on why.

Hara said drink.

Pell said panic.

Marek said artistic rebellion.

Rinna said, "He was outside."

That ended the theory.

I asked, "Why?"

Rinna ate one bean.

"Wrong door."

There were many ways to fail professionally.

Comforting.

I made one joke about hanging signs on the doors.

Nobody heard it because a tray hit the kitchen floor.

This was good for my character.

By the time bowls were empty, the light outside had changed.

Not dark yet.

Late enough that the street had begun collecting people headed home, elsewhere, or nowhere they intended to admit.

Hara left first.

Pell went with her for half a block, then turned north.

Nessa walked back toward the theatre because apparently paint had not finished with her.

Rinna disappeared into another street after saying, "Tomorrow no."

Clear.

Beautiful.

Marek stood beside me outside the cookshop.

"What now?"

"Home."

He nodded.

"Same."

We walked together for one street.

Then he turned without explanation.

I kept going.

At home, Lyssa was already eating.

Not waiting.

Good.

The dark sleeve was still gone.

The brown cloth remained.

Three pins.

Same fold.

She looked at me.

"You ate."

"Yes."

"Where?"

"With theatre."

She nodded and tore bread.

"Good?"

"Soup."

"That bad?"

"Very good soup."

She pushed the onion bowl toward me.

There were two left.

I had not escaped consequences.

I took one.

"Vale?"

"Not today."

"Magic?"

"No."

"Theatre?"

"Furniture."

She looked at my face.

"And soup."

"Mostly soup."

That satisfied her.

I ate the onion with bread because life was cruel but organized.

My cuff still had three loose threads.

I did not touch them.

The brown cloth did not move.

I took another bite of onion.

It remained a poor reward for good behavior.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 234

## THE CONDITION

Rinna had said no.

Vale had said maybe nothing.

Hessa had said nothing at all.

This produced a morning in which I was technically free and emotionally suspicious.

Lyssa was already gone when I woke. The brown cloth remained near the wall with the same fold and the same three pins. My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with the same three loose threads because I had finally discovered the repair method called leaving it alone.

I ate bread and one of the remaining onions.

The onions were winning the long war.

No note waited under the door.

I checked once.

Then I stopped checking because doing it twice would have become a habit and I already had enough of those.

Outside, Carrow had the clear cold light that made every wet stain on the stone look permanent. A cooper was rolling two empty barrels toward the lower lane. A woman had three chickens tied together by the legs and was losing an argument with all of them.

I went for breakfast that was not an onion.

This was my only plan.

I found a stall selling hot grain with chopped apple and bought a bowl. The woman gave me a wooden spoon with a crack down the handle.

I looked at it.

She said, "It holds."

"Strong standard."

"It holds."

I ate with it.

It held.

When I came home, a folded piece of paper was under the door.

Apparently timing remained a form of mockery.

I put the bowl down on the table and picked up the note.

Hessa's writing.

AFTER MIDDAY.

SAME ROOM.

EAT.

FOUR INTERMEDIATE.

I read the last line again.

Then I turned the paper over.

Nothing.

I looked toward the brown cloth.

"At least you are consistent."

The cloth declined comment.

Four intermediate.

No far.

No new mark.

No new direction written.

If Hessa had decided to invent a secret fifth distance, she had hidden it efficiently.

I did not try to design the session for her.

This was growth and also self-defense.

I spent the rest of the morning doing ordinary things badly enough to remain a person.

I washed the bowl from breakfast.

I swept half the room before discovering the broom was moving dust into the same corner the draft preferred.

I moved it somewhere else.

The draft won again.

I stopped.

I ate more bread before leaving because Hessa had written EAT in capital letters and I had no interest in sitting through the questions if I arrived hungry.

The walk to the Guild stayed ordinary.

Right hand normal.

Wrist normal.

Forearm normal.

Shoulders normal.

Right leg normal.

Residual limb comfortable.

The left crutch tip gripped the dry stone without comment.

My body had nothing new to contribute.

Good.

The same room was waiting.

Hessa had changed one thing.

The order page.

Everything else was where it had been.

Same chair.

Same marks in the floor.

Same board.

Same glass shield.

Same paper-fin target.

Same paper-fin control.

Same intermediate mark.

Same far mark, even though nothing sat there.

I looked at the empty far mark.

"Abandoned."

"No."

"Unused."

"Today."

"Better."

Hessa pointed at the chair.

I put the crutches in their usual place and sat.

My right foot found its mark.

Hips square.

Forearm where she wanted it.

Shoulder down.

She checked every part anyway.

"Food?"

"Grain. Apple. Bread."

"Water?"

"Yes."

"Work?"

"No."

"Theatre?"

"Rinna said no yesterday."

"Vale?"

"No."

"Carrying?"

"Breakfast."

She looked at my hands.

"Anything else?"

"An onion."

"Today?"

"No."

"Why did you say it?"

"I wanted credit for surviving it."

She wrote nothing.

Cruel.

"Hand?"

"Normal."

"Thumb?"

"Normal."

"Wrist?"

"Normal."

"Forearm?"

"Normal."

"Shoulder?"

"Normal."

"Right leg?"

"Normal."

"Residual limb?"

"Comfortable."

"Phantom?"

"Quiet."

She wrote the baseline.

I looked at the page beside her.

INTERMEDIATE.

INTERMEDIATE.

INTERMEDIATE.

INTERMEDIATE.

"That looks lazy."

"It is controlled."

"Same thing four times."

"Yes."

"No far?"

"No."

"No alternate order?"

"No."

"No farther far?"

"No."

"No new direction?"

"No."

"No larger target?"

"No."

"No different paper?"

"No."

"No exciting mistake?"

Hessa looked at me.

"Not planned."

"Good. I was worried."

She moved the page so I could read it properly.

"Last session established two useful things."

"Intermediate moved once."

"And did not move once."

"Far did not move twice."

"Yes."

"So intermediate won."

"No."

"I knew you'd say that."

"Then stop saying it."

I leaned back.

"The current apparatus has produced more clean observed responses at intermediate than far."

"Yes."

"Intermediate response has occurred across more than one session."

"Yes."

"Intermediate also failed cleanly."

"Yes."

"Therefore it is not reliable."

"Yes."

I pointed at the four identical lines.

"So now you want to know whether it behaves when we stop changing distance."

"Approximately."

"That is almost satisfying."

"Do not improve it."

There she was.

Hessa tapped the page.

"Today does not compare distances."

"Because far isn't tested."

"Correct."

"It does not establish range."

"Correct."

"It does not establish that intermediate always works."

"Clearly."

"It does not establish why it works when it works."

"No."

"It asks whether clean response continues to occur when we repeat the same intermediate condition in one session."

"Yes."

I considered the paper fins.

"Four?"

"Predeclared."

"Break?"

"After two external attempts."

"Extra attempt if all four fail?"

"No."

"Extra attempt if all four work?"

"No."

"Repeat one because I dislike it?"

"No."

"Good supervision remains hostile."

"Minimal draw first."

Of course.

Thirty-three successful supervised minimal draws sat behind me.

The number sounded large until Hessa gave the instruction and the actual task became small again.

I settled.

Breathed.

Drew the smallest amount I could manage.

Clean.

Contained.

No thumb spread.

No wrist catch.

No shoulder movement.

No change in the residual limb.

No phantom response.

"Return."

I returned.

Hessa watched the end of it.

"Any lingering sensation?"

"No."

"Count."

Thirty-four successful supervised minimal draws.

She wrote it.

Then shaping.

Same deliberate form as before.

No new shape.

No stronger hold.

No longer duration merely because the count had increased.

I drew under supervision and shaped exactly what she asked.

The sensation held where it should.

My shoulder stayed down.

My wrist remained quiet.

"Return."

I returned.

Hessa checked my hand, wrist, forearm, shoulder.

"Change?"

"No."

"Count."

Thirty supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Then the glass shield came between me and the target.

Hessa moved the paper fin to INTERMEDIATE.

The control remained in its established place.

The far mark stayed empty.

Attempt forty-six.

INTERMEDIATE.

AWAY.

Hessa checked target and control against their marks.

She checked the glass.

She checked the door.

The room was quiet.

"Begin when ready."

I settled.

This should have felt easier than far.

That thought arrived without permission.

I noticed it.

I did not tell the paper.

Draw.

Shape.

Away.

Nothing.

I held the effort where it belonged.

Nothing.

The target remained on its mark.

The control remained on its mark.

My mind started offering suggestions.

More effort.

Different angle.

Longer.

Every suggestion was a way to stop doing the test we had actually planned.

I let them pass.

Hessa called the stop.

I returned.

She checked the target.

Then the control.

"No observed response. Control unchanged."

"Intermediate."

"Yes."

"Again."

"Later."

She wrote.

I looked at the page.

One identical word had already produced a different feeling than I had expected.

Annoying.

Hessa checked my hand.

"Normal."

"I didn't ask yet."

"It is."

"Forearm?"

"Warm. Ordinary effort."

"Wrist?"

"Normal."

"Shoulder?"

"Normal."

"Residual limb?"

"Comfortable."

"Phantom?"

"Quiet."

Attempt forty-seven.

Same target position.

Same control.

Same glass.

Same body geometry.

Same direction.

Same stupid paper.

Hessa reset the target even though it had not moved.

She checked the mark anyway.

I watched.

"Do you expect it to move?" she asked.

That was new.

I looked at her.

"You did not ask that last time."

"I am asking now."

"Is that another condition?"

"No. It is a note."

I looked at the target.

"Less than before."

"Why?"

"The first one didn't."

She wrote.

I disliked being preserved.

"Begin when ready."

I settled.

Draw.

Shape.

Away.

For several seconds, nothing.

Then the target shifted.

Small.

Enough to be obvious because I had spent too much of my life staring at paper.

It moved away from its mark and turned slightly at the end.

The control did not move.

I returned when Hessa told me.

She crossed the room.

Measured.

Checked target.

Checked control.

Checked glass.

Then checked all three again.

"Observed target response. Small net displacement away. Minor rotation. Control unchanged."

I smiled.

Hessa looked at me.

"I am allowed to have a face."

"Yes."

"Good."

She wrote.

Attempt forty-six, no response.

Attempt forty-seven, response.

Same intermediate condition.

That was already enough to make the room feel less interested in my preferences.

We took the planned break.

I stood with both crutches and walked the room twice.

Right leg stiff from sitting.

Normal.

It loosened.

Forearm warm.

Normal.

Shoulders worked, not painful.

Residual limb comfortable.

No weakness.

No tingling.

No reason to stop.

Hessa made me drink water.

I did.

"Any change from before the external attempts?"

"Forearm warmer."

"Expected?"

"Feels like ordinary effort."

She wrote it.

I sat again.

The order page still had two identical words left.

INTERMEDIATE.

INTERMEDIATE.

"Do you expect the third one to move?" Hessa asked.

I looked at her.

"You've made this worse."

"Answer."

"Yes."

"More or less than attempt forty-seven?"

"More."

"Because forty-seven moved."

"Yes."

She wrote.

I pointed at the page.

"That is going to become embarrassing later."

"It is already data."

"Hostile profession."

Attempt forty-eight.

Target at intermediate.

Control unchanged.

Glass unchanged.

Door shut.

Same chair marks.

Same body position.

AWAY.

I began.

Draw.

Shape.

Hold.

Nothing.

I waited.

The urge to help arrived faster because I expected a response.

A little more would probably do it.

That was the thought.

Not knowledge.

Not evidence.

Not permission.

I kept the effort where it had been.

The target remained still.

The control remained still.

Hessa called the stop.

I returned.

She checked.

"No observed response. Control unchanged."

I laughed once.

Not because it was funny.

Because the paper had excellent timing.

Hessa looked at me.

"You expected response."

"Yes."

"And?"

"It did not care."

She wrote that too.

"Please don't write 'did not care.'"

"I didn't."

"Good."

She checked my hand and wrist.

No change.

Forearm warm.

Shoulder normal.

Right leg normal.

Residual limb comfortable.

One external attempt remained.

Attempt forty-nine.

Same intermediate mark.

Same target.

Same control.

Same glass.

Same AWAY direction.

Hessa reset everything.

Then she looked at me.

"Expectation?"

I considered lying for variety.

"Less."

"Why?"

"Because forty-eight didn't move."

She wrote.

"I am very predictable."

"Not the target."

That landed.

I looked at the paper.

"Rude."

"Begin when ready."

I settled.

The room became small.

Not exciting.

Not mystical.

Chair.

Glass.

Paper.

My own hand.

The sensation I could produce under supervision and still did not understand well enough to trust.

Draw.

Shape.

Away.

Nothing.

I held.

Nothing.

My forearm warmed another degree.

The target stayed where it was.

The control stayed where it was.

Hessa called the stop.

I returned.

She checked both fins.

No movement.

"No observed response. Control unchanged."

I nodded.

That one did not sting much.

Maybe expectation mattered to disappointment even when it did not matter to paper.

Hessa finished the line.

Forty-six: intermediate, no observed response, control unchanged.

Forty-seven: intermediate, small observed response away, minor rotation, control unchanged.

Forty-eight: intermediate, no observed response, control unchanged.

Forty-nine: intermediate, no observed response, control unchanged.

One clean response.

Three clean non-responses.

No control movement.

No apparatus disturbance.

Same condition repeated four times.

I read the list.

"Ugly."

"Useful."

"You need another word."

"No."

I leaned back.

"Intermediate can still respond."

"Yes."

"It did today."

"Yes."

"Under the same apparatus."

"Yes."

"Without far between attempts."

"Yes."

"So far wasn't causing the intermediate response."

Hessa did not answer.

I closed my eyes.

"Too large."

"Yes."

I tried again.

"Today shows an intermediate response can occur in a block where far is not tested between attempts."

"Yes."

"Better."

"Accurate."

"Intermediate also failed three times in the same block."

"Yes."

"So unreliable remains."

"Yes."

"More unreliable?"

"No."

I opened my eyes.

"Because we do not have a defined rate."

"Among other reasons."

"Does this weaken the distance difference?"

"Not by itself."

"Because we did not test far today."

"Correct."

"Does it strengthen intermediate existence?"

Hessa considered.

That meant the wording mattered.

"It adds another clean observed intermediate response under the current apparatus."

"Across another session."

"Yes."

"So the response has repeated across sessions and within a same-condition block."

"Observed response has occurred across sessions. Today contains one response within a repeated intermediate block."

I stared at her.

"You built that sentence to hurt me."

"I built it to be true."

Fair.

I looked at attempts forty-six through forty-nine.

One movement.

Three nothing.

"Could fatigue explain the three failures?"

"No."

"Could expectation explain them?"

"No."

"Could anything?"

"Many things could."

"Useful."

"We did not test those things."

There it was.

Hessa stacked the pages.

I looked at her hand.

"Next question?"

"Not chosen."

"Different again?"

"Yes."

"More different?"

She did not answer.

I accepted defeat.

"Restrictions?"

"Unchanged."

"Independent draw?"

"No."

"Independent shaping?"

"No."

"Paper?"

"No."

"Coins?"

"No."

"Thread?"

"No."

"Larger objects?"

"No."

"External testing?"

"No."

"Practice?"

"No."

"Barrier?"

"No."

"Theatre?"

"No."

"Loopholes?"

"No."

I nodded.

"Thirty-four, thirty, forty-nine."

"Yes."

The counts had grown again.

Nothing else had.

This no longer surprised me.

Hessa checked my body one final time.

Right hand normal.

Thumb normal.

Wrist normal.

Forearm warm from effort.

Shoulder normal.

Right leg a little stiff from sitting.

Residual limb comfortable.

Phantom quiet.

No concerning change.

At the door, I looked back at the empty far mark.

"Do we still think distance matters?"

Hessa did not look at the board.

"Under the current apparatus, the accumulated record still supports a difference associated with distance."

"Associated."

"Yes."

"Not range."

"No."

"Not reliable intermediate."

"No."

"Not generalized."

"No."

"Good."

Hessa looked at me.

I smiled.

"Still hate the word."

"Leave."

I left.

Carrow had reached late afternoon while we were arguing with one piece of paper.

The streets were busy enough that I had to wait at two crossings. A cart loaded with clay jars blocked half the lower lane. Someone above me shook a rug out a window and created weather from dust.

I bought a small piece of cheese and ate it walking slowly home.

No debt calculation.

No reward calculation.

Cheese.

At the apartment, Lyssa was still out.

The brown cloth remained.

Three pins.

Same fold.

I looked at it.

"One of us is reliable."

I regretted the sentence immediately.

I ate the rest of the cheese.

By dark, Lyssa had not returned.

That happened.

I put beans in the pot, cut one onion, and used less salt than before.

The room became warmer.

Someone downstairs laughed hard enough to cough.

A cart rattled past.

No note came under the door.

When Lyssa finally returned, she looked tired in the ordinary way, not injured. She had no bundle.

She looked at the pot.

"Beans?"

"Improved beans."

She tasted them.

"Beans."

Cruel but fair.

We ate.

She did not ask about Hessa.

I did not volunteer.

Halfway through the bowl she noticed the folded note beside the basin.

"Paper?"

"One."

She looked at me.

"Out of four?"

"Yes."

"Same distance?"

"All intermediate."

She nodded and kept eating.

That was the entire analysis.

After supper she moved the empty bowls aside and put both elbows on the table.

I did the same.

The brown cloth stayed by the wall.

Three pins.

Still nothing I understood.

I looked at Lyssa.

She looked back.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

For once, the most reliable thing in the room was not the paper.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 235

## THE TAGALONG

Lyssa was still home when I woke.

That was the first surprise.

The second was that she was not working.

The brown cloth remained near the wall with its three pins and its refusal to become my business. My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with three loose threads and the good sense to stay there. The table held bread, a small knife, two empty bowls, and Lyssa's forearms.

Nothing else.

She was sitting with both elbows on the table exactly as she had been the night before.

I looked at her.

She looked at me.

"You're still here."

"Yes."

"Is something wrong?"

"No."

I waited.

She waited longer.

"Good morning," I said.

"Better."

I got up.

Right leg normal after sleep. Residual limb comfortable. Shoulders fine. Left crutch tip boring. The Guild had left me with nothing more serious than the memory of paper refusing to cooperate, which was where I preferred it.

No note sat under the door.

I did not check twice.

Lyssa tore the loaf.

"Working?"

"Nobody has claimed me."

"Theatre?"

"No."

"Vale?"

"No."

"Hessa?"

I looked at the door.

"No."

Lyssa nodded.

Then she said, "Come with me."

I stopped halfway through reaching for bread.

"Where?"

"Market."

"What kind?"

"The kind with food."

"There are several."

"The west one."

"Why?"

She ate.

I waited.

Finally she said, "Because I am going."

That was apparently the complete structure.

I took bread.

"Am I carrying something?"

"Maybe."

"Ah."

"You don't have to come."

That changed it.

Not much.

Enough.

I looked around the room as though a competing obligation might rise from the basin.

Nothing did.

"I'll come."

Lyssa nodded once and kept eating.

I had apparently passed the interview.

We left after breakfast.

She locked the door. I took the stairs first because it was easier than trying to negotiate two crutches around her on the landing. By the bottom, she had the cloth bag over one shoulder and I had nothing except my coat and the strange feeling that I had joined an errand without being assigned a function.

Outside, Carrow was bright and cold.

Yesterday's dust had settled. The lower stones still held dark seams of damp where the sun had not reached. Someone across the street was beating a rug over a rail. A child below it was trying to catch the dust in a cup.

Useful education.

Lyssa started west.

I fell beside her.

Not quite beside.

The street narrowed around a cart wheel, so she went ahead and I followed. Then it widened and we came even again.

"What are we buying?"

"Food."

"You've said."

"Oil."

"That is not food."

"Beans."

"Better."

"Bread."

"We have bread."

"Not enough."

"Salt?"

She looked at me.

"Probably."

"I used less."

"Yes."

"Successfully."

"Yes."

That was all I got.

We crossed South Lane where two women were arguing about a basket of apples. Neither seemed to own the basket. Both seemed committed to the argument.

Lyssa slowed near a fruit stall.

I expected her to stop.

She did not.

A woman behind the stall called, "Lyssa."

Lyssa lifted one hand.

"Morning."

The woman pointed at a stack of pears.

"Better today."

Lyssa changed direction immediately.

I followed.

Apparently we were buying pears.

The woman picked one up and handed it to Lyssa.

Lyssa turned it once, pressed near the stem, and put it back.

"Still hard."

"Less hard."

"That is not ripe."

"Tomorrow."

"Then sell them tomorrow."

The woman looked at me.

"She always like this?"

I considered the available loyalties.

"About pears?"

Lyssa looked at me.

I said, "I have no evidence outside pears."

The woman laughed.

Lyssa did not.

We did not buy pears.

Ten steps later, Lyssa said, "Coward."

"I protected the relationship."

"Yours."

"Exactly."

She bumped her shoulder lightly against mine.

I nearly planted the left crutch too far out because I was watching her instead of the street.

"Violence," I said.

"You survived."

"Strong standard."

She gave me a look.

I regretted borrowing the breakfast woman's line before the thought had fully formed.

Good.

Some jokes deserved to die young.

The west market sat in a broad square with three lanes feeding into it and enough people to make every route temporary. Stalls crowded the edges. Carts claimed the middle until someone louder needed the space. Smoke from two cooking braziers moved sideways under the awnings.

I knew the square.

I did not know it the way Lyssa did.

She turned left before the bread sellers.

I would have gone right.

I followed.

A narrow stall sold dried beans, grain, salt, and things in sacks that all looked like different shades of dust until someone named them.

Lyssa greeted the man behind it with no name.

He greeted her the same way.

"What beans?"

"Dark."

"Old or new?"

"Old."

He scooped from a sack.

I looked at Lyssa.

She saw it.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Ask."

"Why old?"

The seller answered before she did.

"Cheaper."

Lyssa said, "And they cook."

He held up a scoop.

"Eventually."

"See?"

I looked at the beans.

They looked exactly like a future argument with water.

"How much eventually?"

The seller poured them into Lyssa's bag.

"Long enough."

This city had a hostile relationship with units.

Lyssa paid.

I watched because money remained money.

Not to inspect her.

Not to calculate household income.

Just because coins leaving a hand were real.

The seller added a small handful after the measure.

Lyssa noticed.

She did not comment.

Neither did he.

I wondered whether that was habit, favor, measurement correction, or an attempt to remove the worst beans from his sack.

I did not ask.

Progress.

We bought salt next.

Lyssa let me choose the amount.

This was a trap.

I knew it was a trap.

"Small."

The seller waited.

Lyssa waited.

I held two fingers apart.

He filled a paper twist.

Lyssa looked at it.

"Enough?"

"Yes."

"For how long?"

"Until I improve."

She took the salt from me.

"Then more."

The seller added another pinch.

Betrayal from both sides.

We moved on.

A boy ran between us carrying a basket and almost clipped my right crutch. I stopped. Lyssa did not grab me. She had already stepped aside because she knew I would stop.

The boy shouted an apology over his shoulder without slowing.

"Excellent," I said.

Lyssa said, "You were in his way."

"He was in mine."

"He was faster."

"Law by velocity."

"Useful law."

I could not completely disagree.

At the bread stall, Lyssa rejected two loaves and bought the third.

I asked why.

"The bottom."

She turned it over.

One was burned.

The second had a pale soft patch where it had rested too close to another loaf.

The third was ordinary bread.

I had bought all three kinds before without knowing I was making choices.

"Your standards are exhausting."

"You eat them."

"That is different."

"No."

She paid for one loaf.

I bought another.

Lyssa looked at me.

"Why?"

"Two people."

"We had one."

"Not enough, according to an authority."

She considered that.

Then nodded.

My bread survived review.

We carried one loaf each for half a street before I had to change the arrangement. A crutch, a loaf, and a crowd did not produce enough hands. I tucked mine under my coat arm.

Lyssa watched me fight with it.

"Bag."

"I have it."

"Bag."

"I am proving something."

"What?"

I moved the loaf again because it was slipping.

"Unknown."

She held the bag open.

I put the loaf in.

"Thank you."

"Useful."

There were words she could weaponize across years.

We bought lamp oil from Olin.

That had not been my idea.

Lyssa turned toward his shop and I nearly asked whether she knew him. Then I remembered that knowing where an oil merchant worked did not constitute a secret professional network.

I was learning.

Olin was behind the counter with a tin open in front of him and a rag in one hand. His boy was not there.

He saw me.

"Theatre."

Better than oil man.

"Home," I said.

He looked at Lyssa.

She put the small household tin on the counter.

"Fill."

Olin did.

No warning.

No folded message.

No brown coat.

No question about Rinna.

He filled the tin, wiped the neck, checked the stopper, named the price, and took Lyssa's coin.

Ordinary commerce had never seemed so aggressively respectable.

I almost liked him for it.

Olin looked at my crutches.

"Tip holding?"

I looked down.

"Yes."

He nodded.

That was apparently the entire subject.

Outside, Lyssa said, "You know him."

"Theatre oil."

"Of course."

"I carried one tin once and suffered a reputation."

"What reputation?"

"Oil man."

She laughed.

I pointed at her.

"Do not."

"Oil man."

"Relationship damaged."

"Carry the oil."

"No."

She handed me the tin.

I stared at it.

She kept walking.

This was how empires collapsed.

The tin was small enough to carry by its loop in my right hand for short stretches, but that hand also belonged to the right crutch. I tried the loop over my wrist.

Bad.

It swung.

I stopped.

Lyssa turned around.

I held up the tin.

"Engineering failure."

She came back, took it, and put it into the bag.

No commentary.

Worse.

"Say it."

"What?"

"Whatever your face is doing."

"My face is walking."

"Your face is very talented."

She started again.

I followed.

We left the market with beans, salt, two loaves, oil, and no pears.

I had expected the trip to feel like labor by then.

It did not.

Not exactly.

My shoulders were working because streets were streets. My right hand had the ordinary warmth of a morning on crutches. The bag stayed with Lyssa because pretending equality required identical loads was stupid and both of us knew it.

I carried one loaf again once the crowd thinned.

That was enough.

Near the edge of the square, Lyssa stopped at a stall selling cooked onions, flat cakes, and small strips of browned meat.

I looked at the onions.

"No."

She ordered two flat cakes.

"Thank you."

"One is mine."

"Still."

We ate standing near a wall because the nearest bench was occupied by a woman with three baskets and no visible intention of surrendering territory.

Lyssa tore a piece from her cake and held it out.

I took it.

Mine had more onion.

Hers had more meat.

We traded another piece without discussing the economics.

For several minutes we did not talk.

People moved around us.

A man in a green cap tried to carry six clay cups in two hands and lost one. It broke. He looked at the five surviving cups, then at the pieces, then kept walking.

A dog sat under the meat stall with the concentration of a saint.

Two girls shared a red scarf while their mother negotiated over carrots.

Nobody needed anything from me.

Lyssa finished first.

She wiped her fingers on a cloth.

"Afternoon," she said.

"What about it?"

"I have work."

There it was.

Not a problem.

Not a betrayal.

Just the edge of the morning.

"Where?"

"North."

I nodded.

"Home first?"

"No."

She shifted the bag on her shoulder and took out one loaf.

She handed it to me.

Then the salt.

Then the oil tin.

"Ah."

"Home."

"I have become transport."

"You asked what you were carrying."

"Hours ago."

"Now you know."

I looked at the collection.

The oil tin could go in the cloth bag if I had the cloth bag.

Lyssa handed me that too.

"Are you leaving me with everything?"

"Beans come with me."

"Why?"

"Because I bought them."

This was not an explanation.

It was enough.

I arranged the bag across my shoulder so it rested against my left side and did not swing into the crutch. The oil tin sat low. Bread above it. Salt tucked near the top.

Lyssa watched the arrangement.

"Good?"

"Probably."

"Strong standard."

I looked at her.

She smiled.

Fine.

That one had lived.

We started toward the split where north road left the square.

At the corner, Lyssa stopped.

I expected a work instruction.

Instead she put one hand on the front of my coat and kissed me.

Not long.

Not one of the quick polite touches people gave in doorways either.

Enough that I forgot the bag for a second and had to correct my balance when we separated.

"You attack around crutches," I said.

"You complain around everything."

"Consistency."

"Home."

"North."

She turned.

I watched her go for three steps.

Then she looked back.

"What?"

I had not said anything.

"Nothing."

"Good."

Cruel woman.

I went home.

The bag arrangement worked until the stairs.

Then it did not.

The oil tin shifted. The bread compressed against my ribs. The salt tried to migrate into a corner that did not exist.

I stopped on the first landing and reorganized.

A woman from the floor below came down carrying a bucket.

She waited.

I moved the bag.

She waited more.

"Go," I said.

"You sure?"

"Yes."

She passed.

No speech about courage.

No attempt to carry me.

Just a bucket needing the stairs.

I appreciated her immediately.

At the apartment I put the oil by the lamp, salt near the cooking things, and bread on the table.

The brown cloth remained near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

I did not speak to it.

Growth.

The damaged shirt stayed on the shelf.

Three loose threads.

Also growth.

I had the room to myself.

For the first time in several days, that did not feel like a gap waiting to be filled by a note.

I washed the morning bowls.

I checked the lamp wick because we had bought oil, not because I was conducting a study.

It needed trimming.

I trimmed it badly.

The flame leaned.

I adjusted it.

Better.

Not data.

I sat.

Then I did something dangerous.

Nothing.

No theatre.

No Vale.

No Hessa.

No errands left that belonged to me.

The debt remained.

The theatre would exist tomorrow or not.

Hessa had questions she had not chosen.

Lyssa was somewhere north doing work that did not require my witness.

I had bread.

I ate some.

At some point I slept.

Not a planned nap.

A chair, a warm room, and a full stomach negotiated without consulting me.

When I woke, the light had moved across the floor.

My neck hurt slightly from the angle.

Good.

Human.

I stood, stretched, and went downstairs for water.

The woman with the bucket was coming back up.

Empty bucket now.

She looked at me.

"Still here?"

I almost laughed.

"Apparently."

She kept going.

That was the entire relationship.

By late afternoon I had started the old beans.

Not Lyssa's new beans.

Those had gone north for reasons that remained outside my authority.

The old ones softened slowly.

I cut an onion.

One left.

Victory approached.

I considered making the food before Lyssa returned.

Then I remembered she had said work.

No promise about supper.

So I made enough for both of us and ate my portion when it was ready.

This was a skill I had acquired very slowly.

Not waiting was different from not caring.

I left the rest covered.

Lyssa returned after dark.

No bundle.

Again.

She opened the door, looked at the table, then at me.

"You ate."

"Yes."

"Good."

She set the bean bag down.

Still beans.

Apparently the north had not consumed them.

"What did the beans do?"

"Waited."

"For?"

"Tomorrow."

I nodded as if that explained an entire day.

It probably did to her.

She washed her hands.

I uncovered the pot.

"Old beans."

She looked inside.

"Soft?"

"Eventually."

She tasted one.

"Soft."

I took the victory.

She sat and ate.

I sat across from her even though I had already finished.

No report waited in my mouth.

No experiment.

No show.

No office problem.

After several bites she said, "You slept."

I stared at her.

"How do you know?"

"Face."

"What is wrong with my face?"

"Chair."

That did not answer anything.

"Did the chair tell you?"

"You have the line."

I touched my cheek.

There was, in fact, a shallow mark where my sleeve seam must have pressed into it.

Betrayed by upholstery.

"I was resting."

"You were sleeping."

"Unsupervised."

She looked at me.

I regretted that immediately.

"No magic joke," I said.

"I didn't."

"Good."

She ate another bean.

I looked at the brown cloth.

Still there.

I looked back at Lyssa.

"Good morning."

She frowned.

"What?"

"This morning. It was good."

Her face changed very little.

Enough.

"Yes."

Then she reached across the table and took the last piece of my bread from beside my hand.

I stared at the empty space.

"That was mine."

"You ate."

"Earlier."

"You survived."

"Relationship damaged again."

She ate the bread.

I stayed anyway.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 236

## THE DISTRIBUTOR

The new beans were gone when I woke.

I noticed because they had spent the previous day traveling farther than I had without becoming any more informative.

The brown cloth was still near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with three loose threads, which made it the most stable project in the apartment.

Lyssa was gone.

No note under the door.

No theatre coat on the chair.

No paper from Hessa.

No Vale clerk waiting in the room with a book large enough to ruin breakfast.

I ate bread.

The last onion remained untouched.

It had survived through discipline and cowardice.

Someone knocked before I finished.

I looked at the door.

The door had not been part of my plan.

The knock came again.

I got the crutches, crossed the room, and opened it.

A boy stood on the landing with a stack of folded handbills under one arm.

Not Olin's boy.

Younger than Davin, older than a child who should have been trusted with that much paper.

He looked at me, then at my crutches.

"Greg?"

"Unfortunately."

"Rinna says if you're free, come before midday."

I waited.

He waited.

"That's all?"

He looked down at the top handbill as though more instructions might have been printed there.

"She said if you're free."

"Not dying?"

"No."

"Building on fire?"

"No."

"Someone missing?"

"No."

"Excellent message."

He frowned.

"She said you'd ask things."

That sounded like Rinna.

I took one of the handbills from the stack.

He pulled it back.

"Those aren't yours."

"Good boundary."

He left.

I closed the door.

The morning had acquired a shape.

Not an emergency.

Not a mystery.

Work, probably.

I finished breakfast, drank water, and left the onion alive.

Outside, Carrow had the washed-blue sky that made every roofline look sharper than it was. A wagon full of split wood occupied most of the lower lane. Two women were already arguing with the driver about whether most of the lane meant all of it.

Nobody needed me.

I went around.

My shoulders felt normal after yesterday's market. Right hand normal. Neck fine. Residual limb comfortable. Left crutch tip held.

The theatre side door was open when I arrived.

Inside, Rinna had turned one table into paper.

Handbills in stacks.

Handbills folded.

Handbills not folded.

A bowl of paste that nobody seemed to be using.

Three short lengths of string.

One pencil.

Marek sat on the edge of the stage folding paper badly enough that the corners never met.

Nessa was doing something with a dark green coat near the rear passage.

Jori and Davin were carrying a narrow door frame across the stage.

Teren was nowhere visible.

Rinna looked up.

"Free?"

"Until somebody improves my life."

"Good."

"I hate that word."

"Five places."

She pointed at five stacks.

"Cookshop near South Steps. Cobbler on Red Lane. Lamp-glass woman. The little tea room by the old fountain. Bread stall at West Gate."

"Handbills."

"Remarkable."

"How many?"

"Five each."

Marek held up a folded bill.

"Unless they love theatre."

Rinna said, "Five."

Marek lowered it.

I looked at the stacks.

"The boy brought these?"

"He brought some. You're taking the rest."

"Why me?"

"Because Davin and Jori have the door. Nessa has coats. Hara and Pell are with Teren. Marek has north."

Marek said, "I have the better route."

"You have the shorter route," Rinna said.

"Better."

Rinna ignored him.

"Ask before you leave them. If they say no, bring them back."

"Do I explain the plays?"

"If they ask."

"Do I promise anything?"

"No."

"Do I argue?"

"No."

"Do I perform in the shop?"

Rinna looked at me.

Marek said, "Yes."

Rinna said, "No."

I took the stacks.

Twenty-five sheets weighed almost nothing.

Twenty-five sheets plus two crutches still required somewhere to put them.

Rinna slid a narrow strap bag across the table.

"Use that."

I looked at her.

"You own a bag."

"We own many things."

"Somebody should tell Nessa."

Nessa, from the rear passage, said, "I know every bag."

Of course she did.

The strap sat high enough across my chest that the paper rested against my right side without catching the crutch. I adjusted it once.

Rinna watched.

"Works?"

"Yes."

"Bring the bag back."

There it was.

The real responsibility.

The first cookshop took five.

The woman behind the counter read the top line, looked at me, and said, "Last one brought people who ordered water."

"I apologize for the arts."

"They bought soup after."

"Then we saved the economy."

She put the handbills near the door.

I left before the claim could be examined.

The cobbler on Red Lane took three.

I had counted five onto the counter.

He pushed two back.

"Three."

"Rinna said five."

"My wall says three."

I looked at the wall.

The wall already held a wrestling notice, two room advertisements, a lost-dog sketch, a church supper announcement, and something written in letters so faded I could no longer tell what had once been urgent.

"Strong authority."

"Three."

I put two back in the bag.

The route had changed already.

Good.

Not everything became more convenient because I had done it once.

At the tea room, I made my mistake.

The owner said yes while carrying a tray.

I reached into the bag, counted five against my thumb, set them on the side table, and moved away so she could pass.

A girl sweeping near the wall looked at the stack.

"Seven."

I stopped.

"What?"

"Seven."

I counted.

Seven.

Apparently my thumb had become generous.

The owner did not stop moving.

The girl handed me two.

"Rinna will be devastated."

"Who?"

"Correct."

I put the extras away.

The girl resumed sweeping.

Useful correction.

No ceremony.

By the time I reached West Gate, the bread stall had no room.

Not no room metaphorically.

The seller had hung strings of small notices from two poles, and every available section fluttered with rooms, work, performances, sales, missing things, found things, lessons, debts, and one very aggressive drawing of a goat.

He looked at my handbills.

"No."

"Five?"

"No."

"Three?"

"No."

"One heroic handbill?"

He pointed at the goat.

"What am I supposed to cover?"

The goat did have presence.

I put the handbills back in the bag.

"Fair."

I had one stop left.

Lamp glass.

The shop was narrow, bright in the dangerous way of rooms where most surfaces could cut you, and warmer than the street. Small panes leaned in racks along one wall. Chimneys, globes, and shaped pieces sat behind the counter.

The woman behind it looked up when I entered.

Her eyes went to the bag.

"Theatre?"

"Handbills."

"How many?"

"Five unless your wall has a goat."

She looked toward the front window.

"No goat."

"Excellent."

She came around the counter and pointed at a board beside the door.

"Bottom."

I put five there.

I was straightening the stack when she said, "Wait."

I stopped.

Not fear.

Not yet anything.

Just a word.

She looked past me through the front glass, then back.

"For Rinna."

I took my hand off the handbills.

"What?"

"A man came yesterday."

Yesterday.

After Lyssa and I had bought oil from Olin, maybe before, maybe while I was sleeping in a chair.

The ordinary day remained ordinary.

This was new.

"What man?"

"Brown coat. Dark hair. Narrow face."

My attention tightened.

"Quiet voice?"

"Yes."

"Did you know him?"

"No."

"Did he give a name?"

"No."

She folded her arms.

"He asked about the theatre."

I did not ask what I wanted to ask first.

Bren.

Mason's Cut.

Cart.

Money.

Instead I heard Rinna asking a boy for exact words.

"What did he ask?"

The woman thought.

"First if I supplied the hall."

"What did you say?"

"That I sell glass."

Good answer.

"Then?"

"He asked, 'Do they take deliveries through the front or the back?'"

I repeated it.

"Do they take deliveries through the front or the back?"

"Yes."

"Exact?"

"As exact as I remember."

"Anything else?"

"He asked who opens for deliveries."

That was more.

My hands tightened slightly on the grips.

"What did you say?"

"That if he needed glass, I could sell him glass."

I almost smiled.

"Did he buy any?"

"No."

"Did he threaten you?"

"No."

"Offer money for an answer?"

"No."

"Ask when the theatre is empty?"

"No."

"Ask about Rinna's money?"

"No."

"Ask about the cart?"

"No."

"Say Bren?"

"No."

She watched me.

"Should he have?"

"No."

The answer came faster than I intended.

I corrected it.

"I don't know."

Better.

She nodded once.

"Tell Rinna."

"I will."

I looked at the board of handbills.

One corner of the top sheet had curled.

I pressed it flat.

The woman said, "Five is fine."

It took me a moment to understand.

"Right."

Theatre.

Handbills.

The job still existed.

I left.

Outside, the street had not changed because one man had asked a better question.

A porter was unloading two crates of clay lamp bases.

A woman was trying to persuade a child to wear both shoes.

Someone farther down the lane shouted about fish.

I stood against the wall for a moment and considered going directly back.

Then I looked at the bag.

Two extra from the cobbler.

Five refused by the bread stall.

The route was not finished merely because something more interesting had happened.

That was an irritatingly useful fact.

I went back to the theatre after finishing the loop I had already finished, which was to say I walked there carrying seven handbills nobody wanted.

My right palm was warm. Shoulders worked. Nothing unusual.

Marek arrived from the north at nearly the same time.

His bag was empty.

I looked at it.

"Nobody refused?"

"One place took eight."

"Rinna said five."

"They asked."

"Did you invent demand?"

"They wanted more."

I could not prove otherwise.

Inside, Jori and Davin had the narrow door frame upright.

It was not attached to anything.

Marek looked at it.

"Door."

Jori said, "Frame."

"Door soon."

"Maybe."

Marek nodded as if the distinction had been settled in his favor.

Rinna was at the paper table.

I put the bag down.

"Seven back."

She looked at me.

"Seven?"

"Red Lane took three. West Gate said no."

"Why?"

"Goat."

Rinna waited.

"Wall full."

"Better."

I slid the unused bills onto the return stack.

Then I said, "Lamp glass had a message."

Her hand stopped.

Not dramatically.

Enough.

She took the pencil.

"Tell me."

I did.

Brown coat.

Dark hair.

Narrow face.

Quiet voice.

Unknown man.

No name.

Asked whether she supplied the hall.

Asked, exact as remembered: "Do they take deliveries through the front or the back?"

Then asked who opens for deliveries.

No purchase.

No threat.

No offered money.

No question about empty hours.

No cart question.

No money question.

No Bren.

Rinna wrote the wording down.

Marek had stopped pretending not to listen.

Nessa came closer from the rear passage, still holding the green coat.

Jori did not. He was checking the frame.

Davin held it steady.

The theatre did not become a meeting because information had entered the building.

Rinna read what she had written.

"Description consistent with Olin's."

I said, "Not confirmed."

"No."

"Question is new."

"Yes."

Marek said, "Front or back."

Rinna looked at him.

"Yes."

"That's not money."

"No."

"That's doors."

"Excellent work."

Marek smiled.

Then stopped when he realized she had not meant it as praise.

I said, "It adds access."

Rinna looked at me.

I tried again.

"It adds a question about delivery access."

"Better."

Annoying.

Accurate.

Nessa set the green coat on the table edge.

"Did she answer?"

"No."

"Good."

Rinna wrote one more line.

NO USEFUL ANSWER GIVEN.

Nessa said, "We already tell deliveries where to come."

Rinna nodded.

"We keep doing that."

Marek frowned.

"Nothing changes?"

Rinna looked around the theatre.

"Something already changed. We know another question."

"That's it?"

"For now."

I understood the disappointment.

A pattern had moved.

The body wanted an action to match it.

Lock something.

Move something.

Follow someone.

Invent a guard.

Go find Mason's Cut and stare at every brown coat until the city became evidence.

Rinna capped the pencil.

Marek frowned.

"So nothing changes?"

"Not because he asked a question."

Nessa set the green coat on the table edge.

"Back latch sticks."

Rinna looked at her.

"Still?"

"Still."

"Then fix the latch."

Jori said from the stage, "After frame."

That was the right size of reaction. A stranger had asked about doors. The theatre still had one door that actually stuck.

The theatre had acquired one more fact about an unknown man and still had a bad latch.

Both could be true.

I helped with the frame.

Not because the pressure demanded labor.

Because the frame needed holding while Davin changed the lower brace.

Jori had one side. I took the other from a seated position near the stage edge, keeping the weight where my shoulders could manage it without turning the crutches into furniture.

Davin loosened two screws, shifted the brace, and said, "Now."

Jori moved.

I held.

Marek offered advice.

Nobody accepted it.

The frame settled square.

Davin checked the lower corner.

Jori checked the top.

They disagreed by less than a finger.

They adjusted it anyway.

Nessa carried the green coat past us.

"Tomorrow."

I looked at her.

"What?"

She stopped.

"You're wearing this tomorrow."

I looked at the coat.

Dark green.

Short enough not to reach my knees.

"Why?"

"Teren."

That explained nothing.

Rinna, from the table, said, "Pages."

She held up a folded set.

I released the frame when Jori told me to.

Then I crossed to her.

The top page had a role marked in the margin.

MESSENGER.

I looked at Rinna.

"That's insulting."

"You brought a message."

"Once."

"Today."

"That is how names start."

Marek said, "Message man."

I pointed at him.

"No."

Rinna handed me the pages.

"Tomorrow morning. Rehearsal first. Performance if Teren keeps it paired."

"How many lines?"

"Eight."

"Entrances?"

"Three."

"Running?"

"No."

"Good."

Rinna looked at me.

I sighed.

"Still hate it."

The piece was called The Missing Key.

I did not read farther while standing.

That was how mistakes began.

I put the pages in the now-empty handbill bag.

Rinna took the bag back out.

"Mine."

I held the pages.

Of course.

At the end of the afternoon she paid me the normal copper.

Handbills and frame work had apparently become a day.

I put the coin away.

No debt calculation followed.

The debt remained smaller than it had once been and larger than I wanted it.

Outside, Marek walked with me for half a street.

"Back door."

"Question about back or front."

"Same thing."

"No."

He thought.

"Mostly same."

"No."

"Annoying."

"Yes."

He turned north.

I went home.

The apartment was empty.

The new beans were still gone.

The brown cloth remained.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf.

Three loose threads.

No one had repaired my life while I was distributing paper.

I set the pages from The Missing Key on the table.

Eight lines.

Three entrances.

Messenger.

I read them once while bread warmed near the pan.

Then again because the second entrance came sooner than I expected.

No magic.

No Vale.

No answer about the man.

Lyssa returned after I had eaten half my bread.

She had no beans.

No bundle either.

She looked at the pages.

"Theatre?"

"Tomorrow."

"Today?"

"Paper."

She looked at the handbills I was not carrying.

"Successful?"

"Seven survived."

"Poor things."

I told her I had a role tomorrow.

"Messenger."

She looked at me.

I waited.

She did not say oil man.

I respected her restraint.

Then she said, "Fits."

"Relationship damaged."

She took bread.

I looked at the brown cloth.

Still there.

Then at the pages.

Lyssa took another piece of bread and leaned over the first page.

"Eight?"

"Eight."

She handed it back.

The beans stayed wherever tomorrow had put them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 237

## THE BEARER

The pages were still on the table when I woke.

That was useful because I had put them there for exactly that reason.

The brown cloth was also still near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with three loose threads.

Lyssa was gone.

No beans.

Apparently tomorrow had kept them.

I did not investigate.

I read The Missing Key again while eating bread.

Eight lines.

Three entrances.

Messenger.

The second entrance still came sooner than my body wanted it to. The first was simple. Deliver a note. Leave.

The second came after barely half a page.

The third had enough room before it that I could forget I existed.

Dangerous structure.

I read the second cue twice, folded the pages, and left before I could turn eight lines into a military campaign.

The morning was cool and dry. Carrow had already filled the lower streets with carts, baskets, shouting, and one man carrying a chair on his head because civilization was flexible.

My neck was fine.

Shoulders normal.

Right hand normal.

Residual limb comfortable.

Left crutch tip boring.

Good.

The theatre side door opened cleanly when I pushed it.

I stopped.

Closed it.

Opened it again.

No catch.

Jori, somewhere behind the stage, said, "Yes."

I looked into the room.

"Was that for me?"

"The latch."

"Fixed?"

Davin appeared in the rear passage with a small file in one hand.

"Mostly me."

Jori said, "Mostly the file."

Davin looked at the file.

"Then pay it."

I went inside.

The narrow door frame from yesterday now stood onstage with an actual door hanging in it. The door had been painted a tired brown that looked respectable from ten feet away and diseased from three.

Nessa was at the property table with three folded notes, a brass-colored key, and the short dark-green coat.

She pointed at the coat.

"On."

"Good morning."

"Coat."

"Warmer."

She looked at me until I put my pages down.

The coat fit across my shoulders better than the black Magistrate coat had. Short hem. Clear of the crutches. Deep inside pocket on the right.

I put one hand into it.

Nessa slapped the outside of the pocket.

"Not yours."

"I was checking."

"You found it."

She handed me the first folded note.

"One."

Then the second.

"Two."

Then the third.

"Three."

They were not identical.

The first was folded once.

The second twice.

The third had one corner tucked under.

I looked at her.

"Useful."

"Yes."

"Did you do that for me?"

"No. I did it for the play."

Fair.

I put them into the inside pocket in order.

Marek came through the stage door wearing a pale vest and carrying the brass-colored key.

Nessa held out her hand.

He stopped.

"I just got here."

"Key."

"I need it."

"Later."

"It is called The Missing Key."

"And this one is not missing yet."

He gave it to her.

Healthy system.

Hara sat at the edge of the stage tying the repaired shoe tighter. The front no longer opened when she flexed it.

"Comfortable?" I asked.

"No."

"Still attached?"

"Unfortunately."

Pell was reading near the first row.

Teren came in from the house aisle with his own pages.

"Places."

No speech.

No encouragement.

The profession remained efficient.

The Missing Key was worse than I had understood at home.

This was praise.

Hara played the Mistress of the house.

Marek played her younger brother, who had borrowed the key to a locked writing cabinet and then denied borrowing anything.

Pell played a family clerk who kept an inventory of objects nobody else respected.

My Messenger worked for someone who was not in the play and had apparently spent the entire day carrying increasingly unhelpful notes to the same address.

The missing key mattered because the Mistress needed a paper from the cabinet before an aunt arrived.

The aunt never appeared.

The paper might not have mattered.

Nobody knew.

The cabinet was represented by a narrow painted box on the side table.

The first note said the absent master had taken the key with him.

The second said he had sent it back yesterday.

The third said it was under the blue vase.

There was no blue vase onstage.

There had been.

Marek's character had broken it before the play began.

Excellent construction.

We started with entrances.

I waited outside the brown door frame with the first note in my pocket.

Hara and Marek argued about the cabinet.

Pell read from the inventory.

Hara said, "Then where is the key?"

I entered.

Teren said, "No."

I stopped.

"I have a message."

"You have a door."

I looked at the door.

"Yes."

"Use it."

"I did."

"You entered like the wall had failed."

I looked back at the frame.

The door was still swinging.

Apparently I had pushed harder than necessary.

Again.

Hara: "Then where is the key?"

I opened the door.

Too slowly.

Teren said, "No."

I looked at him.

"Strong range."

"You're deciding the entrance matters."

"I am entering."

"Correct."

That was not helpful.

Hara said, "He means stop presenting the entrance."

Teren looked at her.

She shrugged.

"Did I improve it?"

"Unfortunately."

Again.

This time I opened the door and came through it because I needed to be on the other side.

Better.

I crossed toward Hara.

The easiest route took me in front of Pell.

Jori said, "Back."

I backed up.

He pointed at the space behind Pell's chair.

"Through there."

The lane was wide enough if I kept the right crutch close.

I tried it.

Clear.

No chair.

No coat hem.

No foot.

"Keep," Teren said.

Nessa put a chalk nick near the door side of the route.

Not a speech.

A place.

Again.

I entered, used the lane, stopped beside Hara, and held out the first note.

"Message for this house."

Hara took it.

I waited.

She opened it.

Read.

Looked at Marek.

I waited more.

Teren said, "Why are you still there?"

"I want to know what it says."

"Greg does."

"Messenger also might."

"Messenger has work."

I looked at the door.

"Exit."

"Yes."

I left.

That was the correction.

Not mysterious.

Deliver.

Leave.

The second entrance was worse because the scene had barely recovered from the first note.

Marek insisted the absent master had the key.

Pell found a receipt showing the key had been sent.

Hara asked who had brought the receipt.

Pell said, "A messenger."

I entered.

Teren said, "No."

I stopped in the doorway.

"That is literally me."

"That is not your cue."

I looked at the page.

My cue came two lines later.

Marek had to say, "Then find the fool who carried it."

I closed the door.

From the stage Hara said, "Convenient."

"Hostile workplace."

Again.

This time I waited through "A messenger."

Waited through Hara asking which messenger.

Waited through Marek saying he did not care.

Then:

"Then find the fool who carried it."

I opened the door.

"Again?"

Small laugh from Hara.

Not audience.

Just Hara.

Teren let it stand.

I handed the second note to Pell.

Then I stayed to see him open it.

Teren pointed at the door.

Right.

I left.

Third entrance.

By then the brother had admitted he might have touched the key.

The Clerk had established that touching and borrowing were different entries in the household accounts.

Hara was considering murder.

My third note came after a longer exchange.

I almost relaxed too much.

Nessa caught me reading over Marek's shoulder from offstage.

"Ready."

"I am."

"You're not."

She tapped my pocket.

I had put the third note in the wrong inside fold after the second pass.

I checked.

First note gone.

Second note gone.

Third note had slid flat under my pages.

I fixed it.

"Thank you."

"Pocket."

There were relationships built entirely from nouns.

We ran it again.

Then again.

The door stopped being an event.

The notes stayed in order.

I left after delivering them.

My second entrance waited for the actual cue instead of the word messenger.

By the fourth pass, Teren stopped stopping me.

This felt suspicious.

At midday, Rinna came in with bread, two apples, and no new information.

I knew that because nobody asked.

She set the food down.

Marek reached for an apple.

Rinna slapped his hand with a folded handbill.

"Paid performers first."

"I am a performer."

"Not paid yet."

"Technical distinction."

Hara took the better apple.

Of course.

I sat on the stage edge to rest my right leg.

Ordinary stiffness.

Shoulders worked.

Right palm warm from the crutches.

Nothing concerning.

Pell sat one seat below me.

"Messenger."

"Clerk."

He nodded.

We had communicated fully.

Rinna looked at Teren.

"Keep it?"

"Maybe."

I looked at the pages.

"Performance?"

Teren looked at me.

"Eat."

Clear.

We ate.

Nobody said brown coat.

Nobody said lamp glass.

Nobody said front door or back door except Davin, who came through the repaired rear passage and told Jori the back door now shut properly.

Jori went to test it.

It did.

They moved on to the next problem.

By early afternoon, Teren had decided.

"The Missing Key stays."

Marek raised both hands.

"Justice."

Teren ignored him.

Rinna looked at me.

"Messenger."

"I remain."

"Today."

"Yes."

Nessa took the dark-green coat off me, brushed chalk from one sleeve, and handed it back.

Apparently that had been a reset.

The first piece was one Greg was not in.

Good.

I spent it backstage with the coat on a peg and the three message props on Nessa's table.

Marek was in the first piece too.

He came off after one scene sweating under the pale vest.

"Audience good."

"How many?"

"Audience."

"Useful."

"They laughed."

"At you?"

"Near me."

More honest than expected.

Hara came through behind him.

"Not at him."

There it was.

When The Missing Key came up, the set changed quickly.

Brown door frame.

Two chairs.

Small table.

Painted cabinet.

No blue vase.

The missing vase was represented by its absence, which was economical.

Nessa placed the three notes in my coat pocket herself.

"One. Two. Three."

"I know."

"I know you know."

This was somehow worse.

The house quieted.

Hara and Marek began.

From offstage, I could hear the play find its shape.

Marek was better with an audience.

Not because he became smarter.

Because his denial grew more confident every time the room doubted him.

Pell entered with the inventory book.

Hara asked where the key was.

My first cue.

I opened the door.

Not important.

Just a door.

Cross behind Pell.

Stop.

"Message for this house."

Hara took the note.

I left.

The audience barely noticed me.

Good.

Behind the flat, Nessa held up two fingers.

Second note.

I put my hand into the pocket and found the double fold.

The scene moved faster than rehearsal.

That was the first problem.

Pell said, "A messenger."

My body prepared.

Not cue.

Hara asked which messenger.

Marek said he did not care.

"Then find the fool who carried it."

I opened the door.

"Again?"

The audience laughed.

More than Hara had.

Not a lot.

Enough to make the next beat feel longer.

I crossed.

Handed Pell the note.

Then made my mistake.

I stayed.

One beat.

Two.

I wanted to hear the laugh settle.

I wanted to see Pell open the note.

I had spent the whole morning being told not to do exactly this.

Teren was not visible.

He did not need to be.

Hara looked at me.

Not Greg.

Messenger.

She held out one hand.

"Unless you've brought the key too?"

Written line.

My exit was supposed to happen before it.

Because I was still there, the question landed directly on me.

I said my next written line too early.

"No key."

That line belonged to the third entrance.

Pell looked at me.

Marek looked at me.

I knew immediately.

The audience did not.

Hara did.

She looked at my empty hand.

Then at Pell's note.

Then said, "Wonderful. We have acquired a messenger who spoils tomorrow."

The room laughed.

Not a giant explosion.

A good one.

She turned away from me.

That was my exit.

I took it.

Backstage, my face was hot.

Nessa held out one hand.

I stared at her.

"Third note."

Right.

I took it from my pocket and gave it to her.

"No."

She put it back into my hand.

"Keep it."

"I just used the line."

"Not the note."

Correct.
