The scene continued.

I had created a problem.

Hara had continued.

Important distinction.

I stood by the door and listened.

Pell read the second note.

The absent master claimed he had sent the key yesterday.

Marek's brother said that proved nothing.

Hara asked what exactly would prove something.

The audience laughed before the next line because they had learned him.

Good.

My third cue approached.

I had already spoken "No key."

The third entrance still existed.

The note still existed.

The remaining lines still existed.

I did not invent a replacement.

Marek admitted that there had once been a blue vase.

Hara became very still.

Pell checked the inventory.

"Blue vase. Hall table."

Hara said, "Where is it?"

Marek said, "Define is."

Big laugh.

Mine came after.

I opened the door.

Third entrance.

The audience recognized me.

A smaller laugh started before I spoke.

I did not wait for it.

"Last message."

Hara looked at me.

"Does it contain the key?"

That was supposed to set up the line I had already used.

No key.

I could not say it again without making the mistake visible.

For half a second, I had nothing.

Then Pell took the note from my hand.

Not a rescue flourish.

He simply took it because the Clerk had taken the previous one.

"Perhaps we should read it."

His line was not written there.

It worked.

Hara turned to him.

The scene moved.

I left.

Pell opened the third note and read the actual message.

"The key is under the blue vase."

Silence.

Hara looked toward the empty table.

Then at Marek.

Marek looked at the empty table too.

"Define under."

The audience broke.

Hara did not hurry.

She walked to him.

Slow.

Held out one hand.

Marek reached into his vest and produced nothing.

Other pocket.

Nothing.

Then he looked toward Nessa's property table offstage as though the missing vase might be hiding there.

Hara said, "Which piece?"

That was written.

It owned the room.

Marek's answer disappeared under the laugh.

He waited.

Good.

Then tried again.

The scene finished with Pell discovering the cabinet had never been locked.

The brass-colored key had belonged to the hall cupboard.

Hara opened the painted cabinet with one finger.

Looked inside.

Looked at Marek.

Closed it.

Curtain.

The audience gave us the kind of applause a short stupid play deserved.

Warm.

Not immortal.

Enough.

Backstage, I took off the green coat.

Nessa checked the pocket before taking it.

All three notes accounted for.

"Good," she said.

I looked at her.

"Don't."

She almost smiled.

Teren found me while the others were resetting.

"You stayed."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"The laugh."

"Yours?"

"Partly."

"Then leave with it."

I nodded.

That was specific enough to hurt.

"I also used the third line."

"Yes."

"Pell continued."

"Yes."

"Hara too."

"Yes."

I waited.

Teren looked at me.

"Again tomorrow if it stays paired."

Not praise.

Not punishment.

A work condition.

"Same role?"

"Unless I change it."

"Useful."

"Don't improve it."

There he was.

Rinna paid me one copper.

I put it away.

No Vale calculation.

No threat calculation.

Money.

The back latch closed cleanly when people began leaving.

I noticed because yesterday it had not.

That was all.

Hara sat on the stage edge retightening the repaired shoe.

I stopped beside her.

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"Continuing."

She looked at me.

Then at Teren across the room.

"Did he make you say that?"

"No."

"Then you're getting strange."

"Already happened."

She nodded.

"Fair."

Marek appeared with the brass-colored key.

Nessa appeared behind him.

He put it down without being asked.

Growth.

Possibly fear.

I left before anyone found more work.

At home, Lyssa was already there.

The brown cloth was still near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt still had three loose threads.

Lyssa had a bowl in front of her and something wrapped in paper near her elbow.

Not beans.

I looked at it.

She looked at me looking.

"No."

"I didn't ask."

"You were going to."

"Maybe."

She ate.

I put The Missing Key pages on the table.

"Show?"

"Yes."

"Good?"

I took bread.

"Hara was."

Lyssa nodded as if this confirmed an existing law.

"I was useful."

"Less good."

"Relationship damaged."

She ate another spoonful.

I sat across from her.

No report about lamp glass.

No analysis of doors.

No magic.

No Vale.

After a minute she pointed at the pages.

"Tomorrow?"

"Maybe."

"Then don't lose them."

I looked at the title.

The Missing Key.

I looked back at her.

She had already gone back to eating.

I kept the pages where I could see them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 238

## THE SEALER

The pages for The Missing Key were still on the table in the morning.

That did not make them a schedule.

I knew this because Teren had said, "Again tomorrow if it stays paired," which contained both tomorrow and if, and only one of those words was dangerous.

Lyssa was already gone.

The small paper-wrapped thing from last night was gone too. I noticed because it had been beside her elbow, then stopped thinking about it because objects were allowed to leave our apartment without giving testimony.

The brown cloth had not exercised that right.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with three loose threads.

At least somebody respected continuity.

I ate bread, drank water, and read the Messenger pages once.

No knock came.

I waited until the bread was gone.

Still no knock.

Theatre had taught me many things, most of them about waiting in the correct place until somebody wanted me. Debt had taught me the opposite.

I folded the pages and left them on the table.

If the play stayed paired, Rinna knew where I lived.

If it did not, I had saved myself a walk.

Either way, Antonius Vale still existed.

The morning was colder than yesterday and brighter. Carrow had the hard clean light that made chipped plaster and old paint look newly accused. A cart of cabbages blocked half the lower lane. The driver was asleep on the seat while three people moved around him with the patient hatred of people who had decided waking him was somehow more trouble.

I went east.

My body had recovered normally from the theatre day. Right hand fine. Shoulders fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb comfortable. Left crutch tip dull and trustworthy.

The Vale office was already open.

The ink-fingered clerk looked up when I came in.

"Bundles?" I asked.

"Later."

"Acknowledgments?"

"Done."

"Excellent. I have successfully arrived for nothing."

He pointed to the far table.

"Seals."

I looked.

A shallow tray held folded outer wrappers, a squat wax pot near a little lamp, two brass stamps, a stack of account copies, and enough string to hang a very small criminal.

"What am I sealing?"

"Outgoing account copies."

"Why?"

He stared at me.

"Because open paper is less private than closed paper."

"Strong system."

"Sit."

I sat.

The chair was the same one I had used before, which meant I already knew which rear leg complained and how far my crutches could lean without falling into the passage.

The clerk put six packets in front of me.

"Not all of them."

"Good."

"Practice row."

"Less good."

He showed me the work.

Each packet already had the account copy inside its outer wrapper. My job was not to decide the account, correct the amount, or interpret any mark I did not know. I checked the outer name and house mark against the top line visible before the final fold. If they matched, I folded the wrapper closed along an existing crease, tied it once around with string, then waited.

The waiting mattered.

The clerk checked the face of the packet and put a short ink stroke beside the house mark.

Only then did I seal the string knot with wax and press the plain office stamp.

"Not the other stamp," he said.

I looked at the second brass stamp.

It had a deeper cut and a small edge mark.

"What does that one do?"

"Not your work."

"Efficient training."

"Good."

I looked at him.

He did not care.

The first packet went badly.

Not catastrophically.

That would have been interesting.

I used too much wax.

The drop spread under the stamp, squeezed past the knot, and made a red-brown lump with one recognizable edge and the general dignity of stepped-on fruit.

The clerk looked at it.

I looked at it.

"Private," I said.

"Ugly."

"Still private."

He took a narrow knife, lifted the wax before it fully hardened, and handed the packet back.

"Less."

"Technical language remains strong here."

"Less."

I used less.

The second seal looked like a seal.

The third looked almost competent.

On the fourth packet I got ahead of myself.

Name matched.

House mark matched.

Fold.

String.

Wax.

The clerk caught my wrist before the stamp came down.

Not hard.

Enough.

"No stroke."

I looked at the packet.

He had not checked it yet.

"Right."

"Why?"

"Because your check and your authority are different things."

He took his hand away.

I disliked how cleanly that sentence fit the office.

"I matched it."

"You did."

"And I still wait."

"Yes."

He checked the face, added the ink stroke, and pushed it back.

I stamped.

No lesson music played.

The packet joined the others.

By the end of six, the seals were all recognizable and none of them had become attached to the table.

The clerk gave me twelve more.

Apparently I had been promoted from dangerous to useful enough.

The office filled around the work.

A woman came in with two account slips and argued about a date. Not loudly. She had the controlled anger of somebody who had already explained herself somewhere else and resented having to own the story again.

The ink-fingered clerk listened, compared her slips to a ledger, then called another clerk over.

Neither asked me.

Good.

A man carrying a narrow crate wanted someone named Sel.

Nobody named Sel was there.

He left the crate anyway.

A boy came for three sealed packets and was told two.

He took two.

Another man stood near Antonius's door for almost ten minutes before being admitted and spent the whole time pretending not to look at anyone else.

Commerce.

I kept tying string.

The work had a rhythm once my hands stopped trying to improve it.

Check name.

Check house mark.

Fold.

Tie.

Wait.

Ink stroke.

Wax.

Stamp.

Set aside.

The clerk checked faster than I worked. That meant I never had to wait long enough to become philosophical.

Excellent design.

I was on the second stack when I found a problem.

The outer wrapper said MARRIS HOUSE, SOUTH WALL.

The visible top line inside said MARRIS HOUSE, SOUTH WALK.

One letter.

Different mark below it too.

I stopped.

The names matched.

The amount was none of my business.

The house did not.

I turned the packet sideways.

The clerk came over.

"What?"

I pointed.

He read it.

Then pulled the account copy free.

"Wrong wrapper."

"Do I win?"

"No."

"Do I at least avoid losing?"

"Continue."

He found the correct wrapper in the stack below.

No hidden conspiracy.

No meaningful connection.

Somebody had put one paper inside another paper.

The world survived.

I tied the correct packet.

Near midday, a boy arrived asking for me.

This one I knew.

Not his name.

His function.

Rinna's handbill boy from yesterday.

He stood in the office doorway looking uncomfortable with the amount of paper surrounding him.

The ink-fingered clerk looked at him.

"Business?"

"Theatre."

The clerk looked at me.

I closed my eyes briefly.

Of course.

The boy said, "Rinna says Teren kept the piece. If you're coming, come now."

There it was.

The if had changed.

Not completely.

Enough.

I looked at the stack in front of me.

Seven packets left in the row.

Another stack behind it.

The wax pot warm.

My hands already in the work.

"Performance?"

The boy shrugged.

"Rehearsal now. Show later."

"Messenger?"

"She said same."

The ink-fingered clerk had gone back to his ledger.

I said, "Can I leave this and come back?"

He looked at the wax.

Then at the packets.

"Today?"

"Yes."

"No."

Not cruel.

Not threatening.

The answer of a man with paper that had to leave today.

"If I go?"

"Someone else finishes."

"Credit?"

He looked at me.

I regretted asking it that way.

Not because money was shameful.

Because I had accidentally asked him to invent a rule for my feelings.

"Antonius credits work completed," he said.

There it was.

No speech.

No punishment.

No promise that my partial stack was worthless either.

The theatre boy shifted in the doorway.

I looked at him.

"Tell Rinna I'm working."

"You aren't coming?"

I looked at the seven packets.

Then at the wax.

Then at the boy.

"No."

He nodded.

No disappointment.

No argument.

He left.

The door closed.

I sat still for one breath longer than necessary.

The clerk said, "Wax."

I looked down.

The drop on my knife was cooling.

"Right."

I reheated it.

That was the choice.

Not dramatic enough for a play.

Debt credit instead of eight lines and three entrances.

I expected to feel more certain after making it.

I did not.

Good.

People who felt certain every time they chose between two useful things were probably lying or rich.

I continued.


The next packet had a house mark I recognized from an earlier acknowledgment stack.

That recognition was almost useful.

My hand started toward the string before I had checked the name.

I stopped it.

Different family.

Same house mark.

I read the line again.

The clerk saw me pause.

"Problem?"

"No."

He waited.

"I knew the mark and almost let that do the rest."

He nodded once.

Not praise.

Not correction either.

I finished the comparison properly and folded the packet.

A few minutes later the boy who had come for two sealed packets returned with one of them.

He held it by the edge.

"Cracked."

The wax had split across the center.

My seal.

I knew it because the stamp sat slightly off level.

The clerk took it, bent the wrapper gently, and the wax opened along the crack.

"Bad?"

I asked.

"Broken."

"Cause?"

He looked at the thin seal.

"Too little."

I stared at him.

"This morning you said less."

"Less than too much."

The office had found a philosophical position after all.

He scraped the old wax away, handed me the packet, and watched while I resealed it with a slightly larger drop.

"That?"

"Yes."

The boy took it.

No one recorded my journey from too much wax to not enough wax and back toward mediocrity.

Civilization would have to survive without the chart.


The woman with the date problem left with one corrected slip and the same expression she had entered with.

The crate for Sel disappeared while I was looking at wax.

Antonius came out once, saw me, saw the sealed packets, and went back into his room.

I received no medal.

By early afternoon my right hand had begun to feel the fine repetitive work differently from crutch use. Thumb and forefinger warm from string. A small wax smear dried near one nail. Shoulders fine because I had been seated. Right leg stiff enough that I stood during a natural break and walked the length of the room twice.

The clerk did not interpret this.

Neither did I.

I drank water.

Sat again.

Finished the row.

Then the stack.

The last packet had a thick fold and fought the string.

I pulled harder.

The knot shifted sideways.

The clerk looked over.

"Again."

"It is tied."

"Badly."

"It has commitment."

"Again."

I untied it.

The second knot sat flat.

Wax.

Stamp.

Done.

The clerk counted the finished packets without asking me to count with him.

Then carried them to Antonius.

I cleaned the knife and put the string ends into the scrap bowl because leaving them everywhere was apparently how offices became theatres.

Antonius came out with the account book.

He opened it to my line.

I saw the current figure before he wrote the new credit.

Still not small.

Smaller after.

He wrote.

Closed the book.

"Useful?"

I asked.

He looked at the sealed packets.

"They are leaving."

This family of answers had infected the city.

"Credit recorded?"

"Yes."

"Good."

Antonius's eyebrow moved.

I regretted nothing.

Outside, afternoon had already started bending toward evening.

I could have gone home.

Instead I went to the theatre.

Not because I thought they needed me now.

That possibility had already been answered by time.

I wanted to know.

The front doors were open and people were coming out.

So the performance had happened.

That answered one question before I entered.

Inside, the house was becoming a room again.

Audience voices thinning.

Benches visible.

Rinna at the side with coins and a small ledger.

Nessa carrying two costume pieces toward the rear passage.

Jori lifting the brown door frame with Davin.

The Missing Key had survived.

I had not been required.

For one stupid second that hurt.

Then Marek came offstage with the brass-colored key in one hand.

He saw me.

"Dead."

"What?"

"You died."

"I was at Vale."

"Debt death."

"Was the play good?"

He considered.

"Hara was."

Accurate.

"Messenger?"

Marek pointed with the key.

"Venn."

Good.

Venn existed.

The world had not waited for my body to become available.

Nessa reached Marek and held out her hand.

He put the key into it immediately.

She looked at me.

"You missed coat."

"I noticed."

"Venn fit."

I looked at the green coat over her arm.

"Better?"

"Different."

That was probably the kindest answer available.

Teren came down the house aisle.

He saw me.

"Vale?"

"Yes."

"Fine."

I waited.

He kept walking.

I turned.

"That's it?"

He stopped.

"What do you want?"

"I don't know."

"Then yes."

Fair.

"Did Venn do Messenger?"

"Yes."

"Good?"

"He left."

That landed exactly where he intended it to.

I smiled despite myself.

"Excellent."

"Tomorrow, different pair."

"So The Missing Key is done?"

"For now."

No punishment.

No reclaimed role.

No schedule.

It had run because it was useful today.

I had not been there.

Somebody else had done the work.

That was theatre too.

Rinna finished with the ledger and came over.

"The boy found you."

"Yes."

"You stayed."

"Yes."

"Vale?"

"Credit."

She nodded.

"Good."

I pointed at her.

"No."

She almost smiled.

No theatre pay waited for me because I had not done theatre work.

This also seemed offensively fair.

I helped nobody with strike.

Not because I was angry.

Because the workday I had actually chosen had already used my hands, and Jori and Davin had the frame.

I said goodbye to nobody formally.

Marek was arguing with Pell about whether a key could be considered missing if the wrong key had been found.

Hara had taken off the repaired shoe and was rubbing one heel through her stocking.

Nessa had the green coat.

Teren had another set of pages.

The theatre continued.

I left.

On the way home I bought a small hot pastry filled with mashed roots.

I paid for it.

No debt arithmetic.

I had just spent the day reducing the debt and was still allowed to be hungry.

The pastry burned my tongue.

Justice.

At home, Lyssa was there before me.

The brown cloth remained near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf.

Three loose threads.

The paper-wrapped item was not on the table.

The beans were still wherever beans went when they acquired plans.

Lyssa looked at the empty space in my hands.

"Theatre?"

"Yes."

"Show?"

"Yes."

She waited.

"Without me."

That got her attention.

"Why?"

"Vale had work."

"Good?"

I sat down.

"Depends who you ask."

"Who?"

"Vale credited me."

She nodded.

"Theatre replaced me."

Another nod.

Neither answer seemed to trouble her.

I took bread.

"Venn did it."

"Did what?"

"Messenger."

She had already lost interest in the administrative structure of my disappointment.

Probably healthy.

I ate.

After a while she said, "You chose."

"Yes."

"Want different?"

I thought about the green coat.

The warm wax.

Teren saying fine.

The account figure getting smaller.

Hara probably being good without me.

"No."

Lyssa nodded.

Then reached for my pastry.

I moved it.

Her hand followed.

"You ate," I said.

"So did you."

"Earlier."

She looked at me.

I had made a tactical error.

I tore the pastry in half.

She took the larger piece.

Of course.

I ate mine before the office could send anyone to seal it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 239

## THE WAITER

Lyssa was still home when I woke, which meant I had misunderstood the sound of the door.

She was standing beside the table with her hair half tied back and one shoe on, looking through the small jar where we kept salt.

This was not promising.

"How bad?"

She tipped the jar toward me.

Enough white crystals slid down the side to insult us.

"Technical answer?"

"No."

"Low."

"Good."

"That was not good."

"I know."

The brown cloth remained near the wall with the same narrow fold and the same three pins. My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with three loose threads. The beans were still absent. The paper-wrapped thing from two nights ago was still absent. Nothing had returned merely because I was awake enough to notice it.

Lyssa put the salt jar down.

"I'm going north."

"Work?"

She looked at me.

"Right. Stupid question."

"Yes."

I tore yesterday's bread in half. It resisted enough that I had to brace it against the table.

Lyssa watched.

"Buy bread."

"I had identified that."

"Salt."

"I had not identified that."

"Now you have."

She finished tying her hair.

"Anything else?"

"No."

That should have been manageable.

Bread.

Salt.

Two objects.

Neither magical.

Neither theatrical.

Neither attached to Antonius Vale.

I had recently completed work involving names, house marks, string, wax, authorization, and enough procedure to make two household purchases feel offensively easy.

Lyssa took the smaller half of the bread.

I stared.

"You assigned me an errand and taxed the starting provisions."

"You'll buy bread."

"With what strength?"

She bit into it.

"Old bread."

Then she left.

No Hessa note appeared under the door.

No theatre boy knocked.

Nobody from Vale arrived carrying a warm pot of wax and a threat about incomplete packets.

The morning remained mine.

This felt suspicious for almost five minutes.

Then I ate the other half of the bread, washed, checked my left crutch tip because it had become boring enough to deserve respect, and went west.

The air was colder than the day before, but the sky had lost the hard brightness. Clouds flattened the light over Carrow and made the painted signs look older. The stones near the drain channels were damp without being wet enough to justify caution, which was the worst kind of damp.

My shoulders felt normal after yesterday's seated work. Right hand normal. Thumb and forefinger no longer warm from string. Residual limb comfortable. Right leg fine. The left crutch tip held.

I bought bread first.

This was important because bread had witnesses.

The baker gave me a loaf with a split along the top and named the price. I paid it. He handed it across.

One task completed.

I put the loaf into a narrow cloth bag and hooked the bag high against my right side where it would not swing into the crutch.

Salt next.

I did not buy salt next.

This was Hara's fault.

I saw her outside a cobbler near the west steps with one shoe on and the other in her hand.

Technically, I could have continued walking.

Socially, she saw me.

"Greg."

I stopped.

"That sounded accusatory."

"It is."

She held up the shoe.

I recognized it.

Left shoe. The sole had separated near the toe a few days ago. She had complained about it over soup while everyone else offered competing cobblers and Marek offered a crime against leather.

The sole was attached now.

The heel apparently had declared independence.

"What happened?"

"The repair worked."

"That sounds terrible."

"It is."

She turned the shoe and pressed one thumb inside near the heel.

"I wore it yesterday."

"I saw."

"You saw my shoe?"

"I saw you take it off after the show."

"Strange."

"I was in the room."

"Still strange."

Fair.

The cobbler appeared in the doorway behind her. He was narrow, gray-haired, and had a leather apron with enough cut marks to count as writing.

"It is not the sole," he said.

Hara turned.

"I know."

"You brought it back like the sole failed."

"I brought it back because the shoe hurts."

"That is a different complaint."

"I have one foot in it. I know."

The cobbler looked at me.

I raised one hand.

"Not involved."

"Good."

Hara said, "Coward."

"I learned from professionals."

The cobbler took the shoe back from her and pressed the heel between both thumbs.

"The new stitch pulled this side tighter."

"You stitched it."

"Yes."

"So fix it."

"I am."

"Excellent."

He disappeared inside.

Hara looked down at her stockinged left foot.

Then at me.

Then at the street.

"How long?"

The cobbler called from inside, "Half an hour."

Hara closed her eyes.

I should have left.

I still needed salt.

Half an hour was not an obligation.

Then Hara said, "Sit."

I looked at the bench beside the cobbler's door.

"Was that to me?"

"You're the only person here with two crutches."

"That does not establish authority."

"Sit."

I sat.

Hara sat beside me and stretched her left foot out so the stocking did not touch the damp stone.

For several seconds neither of us spoke.

This was new.

At theatre, silence usually meant somebody had forgotten a cue or Teren was about to make the silence our fault.

Here it meant a cobbler had Hara's shoe.

A cart rolled down the west steps too fast and received three separate insults from people who had to move. A woman carrying bundled reeds stopped at the corner to argue with a man selling onions. Someone above us shook a rug from a window and immediately apologized to nobody.

Hara said, "You missed yesterday."

There it was.

Not accusation.

Fact.

"Vale had work."

"I know."

"How?"

"Rinna said."

"Of course she did."

"Venn survived."

Hara looked at me.

"Did you think he wouldn't?"

"No."

I paused.

"Not exactly."

She nodded.

No rescue.

No reassurance.

Good.

I looked toward the cobbler's open door.

"Did the play survive?"

"Yes."

"Was Marek still innocent?"

"No."

"He wasn't innocent when I was there."

"He disagreed."

"Of course."

Hara watched a man carry two baskets down the steps.

"Venn left after his lines."

I looked at her.

She did not smile.

"Everyone is becoming hostile."

"Maybe you should learn."

"I was told not to improve it."

"Then don't."

That was all the theatre talk we managed.

The cobbler remained inside.

I remembered salt.

"I have an errand."

Hara looked at my bread bag.

"You bought bread."

"One of two."

"Salt?"

I stared at her.

She smiled.

"Lyssa?"

"Yes."

"Go."

"You ordered me to sit."

"I changed my mind."

"Strong leadership."

I stood.

Hara stood too, then looked down at her stockinged foot.

"No."

I looked at her.

She sat again.

"Correct."

The salt stall was visible from the top of the next lane if I took the shorter way around the dye carts. I could have gone, bought salt, returned, and still spent most of the cobbler's half hour listening to Hara insult leather.

Instead I said, "I'll get yours if you need anything."

She looked at me.

I regretted the sentence because it sounded more useful than intended.

"Salt?"

"No."

"Bread?"

"No."

"Then I have successfully offered nothing."

"Wait."

I waited.

She dug into the small purse at her belt and held out a copper.

"Roasted peas. Stall by the red awning."

I looked down the lane.

"Why?"

"Because I'm hungry."

"Excellent reason."

"Small bag."

"How small?"

She pointed at the coin.

"This small."

I took it.

Now I had three tasks.

Dangerous.

The salt seller was where I remembered. I bought a small paper twist of coarse salt and put it carefully beside the loaf where bread could not become seasoned through structural failure.

Two tasks completed.

The roasted-pea stall had a red awning and a woman with one arm elbow-deep in a basket of dried pods.

"Small bag," I said.

She looked at the copper.

"For Hara?"

I stopped.

"That was fast."

She pointed past me.

Hara was visible at the cobbler's bench.

"Less impressive."

The woman scooped roasted peas into a folded paper cone.

"She usually buys two."

"She gave me one copper."

"Then she gets one."

"No loyalty discount?"

"No."

"Healthy business."

She handed me the cone.

I brought it back.

Hara took it and immediately ate three peas.

"You got salt."

"Yes."

"Good."

"Stop saying that."

She held out the cone.

I took one pea.

This was apparently my courier fee.

The cobbler came out ten minutes later with Hara's shoe and a strip of dark leather folded over one finger.

He handed her the shoe.

"Try."

Hara put it on.

Her face changed.

Not much.

Enough.

"Different."

"Better?"

"Different."

I looked at her.

She noticed.

"Don't."

I said nothing.

The cobbler crouched in front of her and pressed the heel while she stood.

"Walk."

Hara took six steps along the flat section beside the shops, turned, and came back.

"Less."

"Good."

She looked at me.

I pointed at the cobbler.

"His word."

"Still hate it."

"Now you understand."

The cobbler ignored us.

"Walk farther. Come back if it bites."

"Bites?"

"You know."

"I know."

Hara paid him.

Then she looked down the street.

I had bread.

I had salt.

My errands were complete.

I could go home.

Hara said, "Walk."

I stared.

"You have both shoes now."

"Yes."

"So why am I involved?"

"If it starts hurting again, I need a witness."

"To what?"

"My murder."

"Of the cobbler?"

"He'll know."

The cobbler, still in the doorway, said, "Go away."

We went away.

Hara set the pace without asking whether I could match it. She already knew how I moved from months of stages, passages, streets after work, and one cookshop where everyone had paid for their own bowl. She did not slow dramatically or take my bag. She simply did not choose the broken edge of the lane when the middle was clear.

We walked south from the west steps, then turned toward the lower market.

"Still?"

I asked after one street.

"Fine."

"That sounded disappointed."

"I paid for a complaint."

"You paid for less pain."

"Less interesting."

A child ran between us chasing a hoop.

Hara moved left.

I moved right.

The hoop survived.

Nobody learned anything.

At the lower market, Hara stopped at a vegetable stall.

I stopped because she did.

The seller was an older man with a nose like a badly carved handle and hands blackened with soil.

He looked at Hara.

"Late."

"I was buying my own foot back."

He looked down.

"Again?"

"Different problem."

"Same shoe."

Hara pointed at him.

"Don't."

He grinned and started gathering greens without asking what she wanted.

I watched.

"Regular?"

Hara looked at me.

"No. Hostage."

The seller put two bundles on the cloth.

"One."

Hara pushed one back.

"Two."

"One."

"You always take two."

"Not today."

He looked at me.

"She always difficult?"

"About vegetables?"

"Everything."

Hara stepped on my right crutch tip.

Not hard.

Enough.

I leaned away.

"Violence."

"Accuracy."

The seller laughed and took her coin.

He did not ask who I was.

Healthy.

Hara tucked the greens under one arm.

"Still fine?"

I asked.

She took two steps.

"Yes."

We kept walking.

The roasted peas did not survive to the next corner.

Hara folded the empty paper cone into a small square and put it in her pocket.

"You keep trash?"

"Until I see a rubbish barrel."

"Responsible."

"You sound surprised."

"I have seen Marek."

"Low standard."

At a cookshop near the lower lane, steam rolled through the open front and smelled like onions, beans, and something peppered enough to make my nose hurt pleasantly.

Hara stopped.

"Food."

"I have bread."

"That is an object."

"It is food."

"Later."

I could have gone home.

Again.

I did not.

Inside, the room was narrow and already half full. Hara took a table near the wall after a man lifted his coat from the second stool without being asked.

She sat.

I put my crutches against the wall where they would not trip the server.

No one moved a chair for me.

Also good.

A woman came over.

Hara said, "Bean."

The woman looked at me.

"Same."

Hara looked at me.

"You don't know what it costs."

"I have money."

"Vale ruined you."

"Rinna said that first."

"Then listen."

The bowls came with beans, chopped greens, and a piece of dark bread soaked at one edge.

I paid for mine.

Hara paid for hers.

The day remained financially complicated enough without merging lunch.

For a while we ate.

Hara was different when nobody was waiting for her to speak.

Less still than onstage, somehow.

At theatre, she could hold a room by doing almost nothing because everyone was watching. Here nobody watched. She bent over the bowl and ate like somebody who had spent the morning arguing with a shoe.

A man at the next table recognized her.

Not me.

"Hara?"

She looked up.

He frowned as if checking his own memory.

"The widow."

"The one with the ditch?"

He smiled.

Hara closed her eyes.

"Yes."

"Good show."

"Thank you."

He went back to his bowl.

I waited.

Hara looked at me.

I smiled.

"No."

"I said nothing."

"You were about to."

"I was going to ask whether justice improved drainage."

She pointed her spoon at me.

"Don't."

I ate beans.

Her face slowly betrayed her.

She laughed once.

Quiet.

Then went back to eating.

That was enough.

He did not ask her to repeat the line or perform anything for him. He went back to lunch.

Outside, we walked another two streets because Hara wanted to test the heel before going wherever she was going next.

I did not ask where.

This showed significant growth.

The shoe stayed on.

The heel did not bite.

At the crossing near South Steps, Hara stopped.

"This is me."

I looked down both streets.

"Which?"

"Not your business."

"Excellent."

She adjusted the greens under her arm.

"Salt."

I looked at my bread bag.

The paper twist was still there.

"Yes."

"Good."

I pointed at her.

She walked away before I could improve the argument.

By the time I reached home, my shoulders felt used and my right palm was warm from the longer walk. Right leg ordinarily tired. Residual limb comfortable. Nothing injured. Nothing new.

The room was empty.

Brown cloth.

Three pins.

Same fold.

Damaged shirt.

Three threads.

Same shelf.

I put the bread on the table.

Then the salt beside it.

Two tasks completed despite social interference.

I considered this an excellent record and did not write it down.

Lyssa came back late enough that I had already cut the loaf.

She carried one small apple and a wedge of cheese wrapped in cloth.

She looked at the table.

"Bread."

"Yes."

"Salt."

I put one hand over my heart.

"Both."

"Good."

I stared at her.

She bit the apple.

"You've had a difficult day."

"You have no idea."

She looked at my face, then at the bread.

"Theatre?"

"No."

"Vale?"

"No."

"Magic?"

"No."

That exhausted the usual categories.

Lyssa waited.

"Hara's shoe."

She chewed.

"What?"

"Exactly."

I told her the sole repair had tightened the heel, the cobbler had adjusted it, and Hara had made me walk until the shoe failed to murder her.

Lyssa listened to maybe half.

"Did it?"

"Did what?"

"Murder her."

"No."

"Good."

I pointed at her again.

She took another bite of apple.

I gave up.

We ate bread with the cheese and split the apple badly enough that Lyssa got more apple.

The brown cloth remained near the wall.

The shirt remained on the shelf.

No one asked anything of me for the rest of the night.

It was almost enough to make waiting feel like a job.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 240

## THE SAMPLE

Hessa's note was under the door.

This improved the morning and made it more expensive.

Not in money.

In attention.

I picked it up before I put weight on the left crutch and read it standing.

AFTER MIDDAY.
SAME ROOM.
FAR ONLY.
EAT FIRST.

I read the third line again.

FAR ONLY.

The last session had been INTERMEDIATE four times in a row. One response. Three non-responses. Clean control every time.

Apparently Hessa had chosen what came next.

Lyssa was already gone.

The brown cloth remained near the wall.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf.

Three loose threads.

The beans remained absent. The small paper-wrapped thing remained absent. Hara's shoe was somewhere in Carrow attached to Hara, which was the correct place for it and no longer my concern.

I put Hessa's note beside the salt jar.

Then moved it away from the salt jar because yesterday had taught me that salt was capable of acquiring obligations.

I ate bread and the last of the cheese.

EAT FIRST had become a recurring insult only because Hessa knew me.

Fair.

There was no theatre call.

No Vale runner.

No reason to invent work before midday because a note had already given the day a shape.

I washed the bowl, checked the crutch tip, and spent part of the morning doing almost nothing.

That was harder than it sounded.

I sharpened the kitchen knife a little better than last time. I stopped before improvement became damage. I sat by the window. A man across the street tried to lower a rolled rug from an upper window with a rope, discovered the knot was not attached to the rug, and had to come downstairs anyway.

Carrow provided education freely.

By late morning I was hungry again.

I ate another piece of bread.

Hessa would have been unbearable if I arrived hungry after being told twice in four lines not to.

The walk to her room felt familiar enough that I stopped thinking about each turn.

That was useful.

The room still did not feel familiar.

Hessa had the board set where it belonged. The glass shield was in place. The target and control fins were on their marks. The chair stood on the same floor lines. INTERMEDIATE and FAR remained marked where they had been.

Nothing new had appeared because I was curious.

Hessa was seated at the table reading her own notes.

She looked up.

"Eat?"

"Twice."

"Good."

"I dislike that word now."

"Sit."

That was worse.

I put my crutches where they usually went and sat.

My body baseline was ordinary. Shoulders fine. Right hand fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb comfortable. Left crutch tip still boring.

Hessa looked at me for several seconds.

"What is the question?"

I looked at FAR.

"You tell me."

"I wrote it down."

"You wrote FAR ONLY."

"Yes."

"That is a condition, not a question."

One corner of her mouth moved.

Possibly approval.

Possibly gas.

"Then answer."

I looked at the marks again.

Last time, four INTERMEDIATE attempts. Same direction. Same apparatus. One target response.

Before that, the alternating sessions had shown INTERMEDIATE responding more often than FAR under the current setup, though not reliably. FAR had responded cleanly before. It had also failed plenty.

I said, "You held intermediate fixed because alternating might have been hiding something about sequence."

"Close enough."

"Now you hold far fixed."

"Why?"

"To see whether clean FAR response still occurs when we stop alternating it with INTERMEDIATE."

"Better."

I waited.

"That is the question?"

"Yes."

It felt offensively small.

Which usually meant Hessa liked it.

"So not range."

"No."

"Not finding the farthest point."

"No."

"Not changing distance."

"No."

"Not changing direction."

"No."

"Not increasing effort."

"No."

"Not testing whether I can make FAR behave like INTERMEDIATE."

Hessa looked at me.

"Especially not that."

"Good. I wanted the full collection."

She slid the record page toward herself.

"Same room. Same board. Same shield. Same target and control. Same body geometry. FAR. AWAY."

"Four?"

"Four."

"Break after two?"

"Yes."

The shape mirrored the last session.

That was the point.

Hessa checked the floor marks anyway.

I knew better than to be offended by this now.

Memory was not measurement.

Neither was familiarity.

She checked the glass, then the target and control. I watched her confirm what I thought I already knew.

Nothing had shifted.

"Minimal first," she said.

I placed my right forearm where she wanted it.

No shortcuts.

No independent draw because I had done this thirty-four times under supervision and could imagine the shape of the next ten.

That did not make the thirty-fifth mine.

Hessa watched.

I drew.

Clean.

Small.

Controlled.

No strange symptom. No pain. No movement outside the expected body work.

Hessa marked it.

Thirty-five supervised minimal draws.

Then deliberate shaping.

I held the form she had allowed, narrow and familiar, with no expansion and no experiment inside the experiment.

The first few seconds felt too easy.

That made me suspicious.

I corrected nothing because nothing had actually gone wrong.

The old urge was still there, to improve a success while it was happening.

I let it be what it was.

Hessa marked the completion.

Thirty-one supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Then she reset the page.

"External."

FAR.

AWAY.

Attempt fifty.

I settled into the same position.

The far target looked small enough that my eyes wanted to make it important.

I did not.

Hessa gave the start.

I worked.

Nothing moved.

Target still.

Control still.

No twitch I could defend.

Hessa waited the usual amount of time before checking.

"No observed response," she said.

"Control unchanged."

She marked both.

Attempt fifty-one.

Same condition.

Same direction.

Same everything we could reasonably keep the same.

I expected less this time.

That was information about me, not the apparatus.

I did not tell the target.

Hessa gave the start.

I worked.

Nothing.

Again.

Target still.

Control unchanged.

Two FAR attempts.

Two clean non-responses.

Hessa marked them and closed the record page.

"Break."

"I feel fine."

"Good."

I stared at her.

She stared back.

I stood.

My right leg had begun to stiffen from sitting, not enough to matter and enough to exist. I took the crutches and walked the short permitted circuit inside the room.

Hessa poured water.

For herself.

I looked at the cup.

She drank.

"This profession lacks hospitality."

"You ate twice."

"That was at home."

"Successful planning."

I sat again after the stiffness eased.

She was already looking at the page.

I tried not to.

Failed.

"Two nothing."

"Yes."

"Which matches a great deal of FAR."

"Yes."

"But not all of it."

"No."

I looked at the far mark.

"What would four nothing mean?"

"Four nothing."

"You enjoy this too much."

"No."

"You answer too quickly for someone suffering."

Hessa set the cup down.

"If all four are clean non-responses, that adds four clean non-responses at FAR under this fixed condition."

"And if one moves?"

"Then one moves."

"Profound."

"You keep asking before the record exists."

That was fair.

Annoying.

We waited the rest of the break.

Hessa rechecked my hand and forearm.

Normal warmth from work, no pain, no weakness, no tingling.

Residual limb comfortable.

Right leg better after walking.

"Continue?"

"Yes."

She reopened the page.

Attempt fifty-two.

FAR.

AWAY.

I knew exactly how little I was supposed to change.

That knowledge did not make sameness easy.

The body always wanted to help.

Shoulder slightly higher.

Breath held a little longer.

Hand tightening because the last two had done nothing.

I noticed the hand first.

I loosened it before the start.

Hessa saw.

"Ready?"

"Now."

She gave the start.

I worked.

For a moment, nothing.

Then the far paper fin moved.

Small.

Clean enough that I did not need to argue with my eyes.

The target shifted AWAY and settled.

No obvious rotation that I could see.

The control remained still.

I stopped because the attempt had ended, not because I wanted to stare at it until it became a theory.

Hessa was already checking.

She looked at the target mark.

Then the control.

Then the glass.

Then me.

"Small response," she said.

"Net away."

"Control unchanged."

I exhaled.

Hessa marked it.

I smiled.

She noticed.

"One clean FAR response," she said.

"FAR moved."

"Under the current apparatus, yes."

"Again."

"One attempt remains."

"I meant the fact."

"I know."

I looked at the page.

Attempt fifty-two.

A clean FAR response.

Not the first.

Not reliable.

Still real.

"One out of three."

Hessa said nothing.

Right.

There was still another attempt.

Attempt fifty-three.

This was where my mind became unhelpful.

The target had moved once.

Now I expected it to move again.

Or I expected the expectation to ruin it.

Or I expected myself to think about expecting it, which was worse.

Hessa watched me.

"You're doing something."

"Thinking."

"Stop doing it with your face."

"That seems outside the experimental restrictions."

"Ready?"

I looked at my hand.

Loose.

Shoulder down.

Breathing normal enough.

"Yes."

Start.

I worked.

Nothing.

The target remained still.

The control remained still.

No second response arrived to make the first easier to explain.

Hessa checked.

"No observed response."

"Control unchanged."

She marked attempt fifty-three.

Then she put the pencil down.

I looked at the page.

Four FAR attempts.

One response.

Three non-responses.

I laughed once.

Hessa looked at me.

"What?"

"That's rude."

"What is?"

"Last session."

She waited.

"Four INTERMEDIATE. One response."

"Yes."

"Today. Four FAR. One response."

"Yes."

I pointed between the two pages.

"Same."

"No."

The answer came so fast I nearly laughed again.

"One out of four."

"Yes."

"One out of four."

"Yes."

"Those are extremely similar fractions."

"They are the same fraction."

"Thank you."

"They are not the same record."

I leaned back.

"Explain the insult."

Hessa pulled the older sheets closer.

"Because these four attempts do not erase the attempts before them."

"I know that."

"You are trying to make them."

"I am trying to admire symmetry."

"Admire it quietly."

She ran one finger down the earlier marks.

INTERMEDIATE responses across more than one session.

FAR responses too, but fewer in the accumulated current-apparatus record.

Clean non-responses in both.

A contaminated attempt where target and control had both moved, still counted as an attempt and not counted as clean target-specific evidence.

Different orders.

Now one fixed INTERMEDIATE block.

One fixed FAR block.

Hessa said, "If I take only the last eight attempts because they make a neat pair, I have selected the part of the record I like."

"One and one."

"Inside two groups of four."

"Exactly."

"Inside a longer record."

I sighed.

"Fractions do not get to be beautiful here."

"They can be beautiful. They cannot outrank the rest of the page."

That was probably the nicest thing Hessa had ever said about fractions.

I looked again at attempt fifty-two.

"So what changed?"

"FAR produced another clean observed response."

"Which establishes?"

"That FAR response can recur under the current apparatus."

I waited.

"Reliably?"

"No."

"Range?"

"No."

"Distance stops mattering?"

"No."

"INTERMEDIATE and FAR are equivalent?"

"No."

"One in four?"

"In this block."

"Not a rate."

"Correct."

I hated being trained this well.

"The apparent distance difference?"

"Still supported by the accumulated record."

"Even though the two fixed blocks match."

"Yes."

"Because the fixed blocks are part of the accumulated record, not replacements for it."

Hessa looked at me.

"Yes."

I had stolen her line before she could use it.

Small victory.

She wrote for a while.

I flexed my fingers.

Ordinary warmth in the forearm.

No pain.

No tingling.

No weakness.

No symptom worth promoting into plot.

"What next?" I asked.

Hessa did not answer immediately.

Good sign.

Or bad.

With Hessa those were often identical.

She looked at the records again.

"Nothing selected."

"You had five chapters."

She looked up.

"I had a life."

Right.

That landed without needing improvement.

I nodded.

She went back to the page.

I waited.

Eventually she said, "There are questions."

"There are always questions."

"Yes."

"But no next experiment."

"Not yet."

No reward.

No expanded permission.

No new object.

No direction change.

No closer or farther mark.

The room remained exactly as restrictive as when I entered.

Only the record had grown.

That should have been less satisfying than it was.

It wasn't.

I collected my crutches.

Hessa handed me no practice assignment because practice remained prohibited.

She handed me no target because targets remained hers.

She handed me no theory because the record did not owe me one.

At the door I looked back at FAR.

"One out of four."

Hessa did not look up.

"Leave."

I left.

Outside, Carrow had warmed by perhaps one degree and become windier out of spite.

I bought nothing.

This felt financially responsible until I remembered I was simply not hungry yet.

By the time I reached home, my shoulders felt used from the walk and my right forearm still carried mild warmth from the session. Right hand worked normally on the crutch. Right leg fine after moving. Residual limb comfortable. Left tip normal.

The room was empty.

Brown cloth.

Three pins.

Same fold.

Shirt.

Three threads.

Same shelf.

No beans.

No paper-wrapped return.

The universe resisted bookkeeping.

I put Hessa's note on the table and sat.

For several minutes I did nothing useful.

Then I made the mistake of drawing eight small marks on a scrap of ordinary paper.

Not magic.

Just ink.

Four marks on one side.

Four on the other.

One mark in each group darker.

I looked at them.

Same.

Hessa's voice existed in my head without permission.

Not the same record.

I turned the paper over.

Problem solved.

Lyssa came home after dark carrying nothing I could identify as my business.

She saw Hessa's note.

"Magic?"

"Yes."

She took off her outer layer and hung it.

"Good?"

I considered several answers.

"One moved."

She looked at me.

"Far?"

"Yes."

That was enough to make her pause.

"Good?"

"There it is again."

"What?"

"The word."

Lyssa sat down.

I told her the short version because she had not asked for the long one.

Four FAR attempts.

One response.

Three nothing.

Control unchanged every time.

Same as the last INTERMEDIATE block if all you looked at was one out of four.

Not the same as the whole record.

Lyssa listened while unwrapping bread she had apparently acquired somewhere without requiring my assistance.

When I finished, she tore a piece off.

"Moved once."

"Yes."

She handed me bread.

I took it.

"Still don't know."

"Correct."

She nodded.

That was the entire analysis she intended to provide.

Healthy.

I ate.

After a while I said, "Hessa says the fractions can be beautiful."

Lyssa looked at me.

"Did she?"

"Approximately."

"No."

"Emotionally."

"No."

I ate more bread.

The brown cloth remained folded.

The shirt remained damaged.

The note remained on the table.

Fifty-three external attempts now existed whether I liked their shape or not.

One far movement had made the page more interesting.

It had not made it simpler.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 241

## THE SCRAPER

There was blue paint on the boy's sleeve.

That was how I knew the theatre wanted labor before he said anything.

He stood outside our door with one hand on the frame and the expression of someone who had already climbed too many stairs for other people's employment.

"Rinna," he said.

"Of course."

"Before midday if you're free."

I looked at his sleeve.

"Blue?"

He looked too.

"Davin."

That explained less than he thought.

"What happened?"

"Wall."

"Better."

He shrugged.

"Bring clothes you don't care about."

Then he left.

I closed the door.

Lyssa had already gone. No note. No customer. No explanation.

The brown cloth remained where it had been.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf with three loose threads.

That created a problem.

I had just been told to wear clothes I did not care about, and the shirt I cared about least was also the shirt most likely to become a pile if I gave it additional work.

I put on the other one.

The Hessa note from yesterday still sat on the table. FAR ONLY. EAT FIRST.

Done.

The counts in my head were thirty-five, thirty-one, fifty-three.

They could stay there.

One clean far response out of four had not changed any rule. It had not created practice. It had not created range. It had not created a reason to spend the morning staring at paper.

Theatre had created a reason to leave.

I ate.

Outside, Carrow was gray without committing to rain. The stones still held yesterday's dust, but the air had the wet smell that meant somebody, somewhere, was about to blame the sky for something.

My body was ordinary after the Hessa session. Right forearm normal again. Shoulders fine. Right leg fine. Residual limb comfortable. Left crutch tip still boring.

I took the lower route because the upper lane had two wagons trying to occupy the same width of street.

They were discussing geometry loudly.

I let them solve it without me.

The theatre's front doors were open, but the stage was dark.

I heard scraping before I saw anybody.

Not rehearsal scraping.

Real scraping.

A dry, ugly rhythm came from the rear yard.

Shhk.

Shhk.

Pause.

Shhk.

I went around.

Two wall flats stood on trestles in the courtyard with their painted faces turned toward the light. One had been part of the blue-trimmed merchant room. The other had a pale cream surface with a brown rectangle painted where a door had once pretended to exist.

Both looked diseased.

Paint had blistered in thin scales across the lower halves. One blue strip had lifted enough that I could see another color beneath it.

Green.

Davin sat on an upturned bucket with a broad dull scraper in one hand.

Jori stood at the far end marking short chalk lines around sections of paint.

Rinna was at the rear door with a ledger under one arm.

She looked at me.

"Free?"

"Currently."

"Good."

I hated the word now.

She pointed at the flats.

"Those need to be usable tomorrow."

"As walls?"

"That is the ambition."

"What are they tomorrow?"

"Kitchen."

I looked at the blue trim.

"Blue kitchen."

"Not after Davin."

Davin raised the scraper.

"I improve."

Jori said, "He removes."

"Improvement by subtraction."

Rinna looked at me.

"You know how to scrape paint?"

"Yes."

Jori said, "No."

I looked at him.

"I know the concept."

"That's different."

Fair.

Rinna went back inside before the argument could become billable.

Jori handed me a second scraper.

It had a wooden handle polished dark by hands and a blade with one corner slightly rounder than the other.

"Loose only."

"I understand loose."

"No, you understand attacking."

"I have never attacked a wall."

Davin looked at the blue flat.

"Give him time."

Jori tapped one of his chalk lines.

"Anything outside the marks comes off if it's lifting. Inside stays unless I say."

"Why?"

"Because we can use some of the old color under the new coat."

I crouched enough to look at the edge.

The blue trim was not one layer.

Blue sat over cream.

Cream sat over something dark red.

At one chipped corner, a thin black line curved under all three.

"How old is this?"

Jori shrugged.

"Wall."

"That's not an age."

"It was here before you."

Davin said, "Older than Greg."

"Most furniture is."

"Not Marek."

"Marek is not furniture."

Jori looked toward the building.

"Debatable."

I sat on a low stool so I could work the lower half without leaning over my crutches. They rested against the courtyard wall where nobody needed the lane.

Jori showed me the angle.

Flatter than I expected.

Not digging.

Slide under what had already lifted and let the bad layer choose to leave.

My first pass produced nothing.

"Good," Jori said.

"I did nothing."

"Exactly."

Hostile trade.

I tried again.

The blade caught a loose edge.

A strip of blue paint lifted, curled, and came away in a piece as long as my thumb.

Green showed underneath.

Davin pointed.

"Wall."

"I had begun to suspect."

We worked.

The sound settled into rhythm.

Shhk.

Tap the blade against the bucket.

Shhk.

Brush flakes aside with a rag.

Jori moved between the two flats, testing edges with his thumb before scraping. Davin worked faster but stopped every few minutes to run his palm over the surface and check whether the lifted area actually ended where it looked like it ended.

I was slower than both.

That was fine.

The lower section in front of me had enough bad paint to make progress visible without requiring skill I did not have yet.

Blue came away in islands.

Cream appeared.

Then green.

At one point a little gold star emerged under the cream.

I stopped.

"Star."

Nobody answered.

I scraped around it carefully.

The whole shape appeared.

Five points.

Badly painted.

Davin looked over.

"Oh."

"What was that?"

"Star."

"Strong historical record."

Jori came around.

He looked at it.

"Old nursery piece."

"You remember?"

"No."

I looked at him.

"Then how do you know?"

He pointed to two more tiny stars hidden farther up the flat.

"Pattern."

Davin said, "Could've been a bedroom."

Jori shrugged.

"Could've."

That was all the theatre archaeology I received.

Nobody named the play.

Nobody told me who had stood in front of the stars.

The wall had been a wall more times than any of us needed to count.

Jori scraped straight through one of the stars.

I stared at him.

"You destroyed history."

"It was loose."

"Monster."

"Scrape."

I scraped.

A little later Venn came into the yard carrying a bucket of water and two rags.

I had seen him yesterday only in other people's sentences.

Venn fit the green coat.

Venn played Messenger.

Venn left.

Today he was a narrow man with dark curls pressed flat on one side of his head and a shirt that had already lost an argument with white paint.

He put the bucket down.

Jori said, "Edges."

Venn nodded.

No introduction.

Apparently we had both worked here enough to skip one.

He started wiping dust from the sections Davin had finished.

I watched for a few seconds.

"Messenger."

Venn looked at me.

"Yesterday."

"Good exit."

He stared.

Behind me, Davin made a noise that might have been a cough.

Venn said, "I walked off."

"Exactly."

He looked at Jori.

"Is he like this all day?"

Jori said, "Sometimes worse."

Excellent.

Venn went back to wiping the wall.

That settled our relationship.

By late morning, my right palm had started to warm where the scraper handle pressed into it.

Not pain.

Different work.

I changed grip and used the rounder corner on a small patch near the bottom.

The problem with simple work was that it became easier exactly when it became dangerous.

At first I had thought about every stroke.

Angle.

Pressure.

Loose edge.

Chalk.

Then my body learned enough of the motion that my mind wandered.

Not far.

Just far enough.

I found a long lifted edge and followed it.

Blue curled away.

Cream beneath.

The strip came beautifully.

Six inches.

Eight.

Ten.

Then Jori said, "Stop."

I stopped.

The blade was two inches inside his chalk line.

I looked down.

The peeled strip crossed cleanly into the section he had told me to preserve.

"Ah."

Davin leaned over from the other flat.

"Future."

I looked at him.

"What?"

"You're scraping tomorrow now."

Jori crouched beside me.

He rubbed the exposed cream with one finger.

It was solid.

Not loose.

I had simply gotten under it because I had been enjoying myself.

"That stays," he said.

"Apparently not all of it."

"No."

I waited for the lecture.

None came.

Jori stood.

"Davin."

Davin looked over.

"Blue."

"Later."

"Mostly him."

"Yes."

I frowned.

"You're not supposed to agree that quickly."

Davin grinned.

Jori handed me a piece of chalk.

"New line."

I looked at the flat.

"Where?"

"Here."

He showed me the edge of the area again.

I redrew the line around the damage I had made.

"Now?"

"Don't cross it."

"I understood that the first time."

"Evidence mixed."

Venn laughed into his rag.

I went back to work.

The mistake cost us exactly what it had cost.

A little more paint later.

No shame ceremony.

No story about learning boundaries.

I just had a chalk line I had personally made and stronger reasons to notice it.

Around midday, the gray sky finally produced rain.

Not much.

Enough to send all four of us into motion.

Jori and Davin lifted the blue flat.

Venn grabbed the rear trestle.

I took my crutches and got out of the lane.

That was my contribution.

The flat went under the rear overhang.

The second followed.

The rain lasted three minutes.

Davin stood under the overhang staring at it.

"Done."

Jori said, "Weather?"

"Yes."

"Good repair."

"Mostly me."

I ate bread against the wall.

Venn had an onion pie that smelled better.

I looked at it.

He looked at me.

"No."

"I said nothing."

"You looked."

Apparently Lyssa had spread.

Rinna came through carrying a stack of folded cloths.

"How much?"

Jori pointed at the flats.

"Enough."

Rinna inspected the blue one.

Her eyes found my pale scrape because of course they did.

"That?"

"Greg," Jori said.

I raised my bread.

"Present."

Rinna looked at the patch.

"Problem?"

"Paint."

"Tomorrow?"

"Fine."

She nodded.

Then she handed the cloths to Venn.

"Front room."

Venn took them.

No argument.

Rinna disappeared again.

I looked at Jori.

"That's it?"

"What?"

"I damaged company property."

Davin said, "You improved by subtraction."

"Do not help."

Jori picked up his scraper.

"Paint isn't company property."

I looked at the wall.

"The wall is."

"Then don't scrape through the wood."

Clear standard.

After bread, we turned the cream flat around.

The back was black.

Not painted black for a scene.

Black in the practical theatre sense, dull and uneven, with old nail holes and two patches where canvas had been repaired.

Nessa appeared in the doorway.

She had a shallow wooden box against one hip.

"Keep that side."

Jori said, "We are."

She pointed at the bottom corner.

"Not that."

I looked.

A little square of canvas had begun separating from the frame.

Davin put his scraper down.

"Glue?"

"Stitch first," Nessa said.

Davin pressed the canvas gently.

"Still good."

"Yes."

She handed him the box.

Inside were heavy thread, needles, two small wood pieces, and things I did not recognize.

Then she left.

Davin changed jobs immediately.

No protest about being the paint man.

No speech about authority.

He sat where I had been, pulled the loose canvas edge into place, and began working the repair with the kind of concentration that made conversation feel rude.

I moved to the other flat.

Jori said, "Top half."

I looked up.

Standing work.

"How long?"

"Until you're tired."

Specific enough.

I planted both crutches, leaned them against the trestle one at a time, and worked a section I could reach without twisting.

The scraper needed both hands only sometimes.

Most of the time one hand did the work while the other steadied me against the trestle or took the crutch again when I changed position.

It was slower.

Jori did not offer to make it fast.

He moved to the opposite side and kept scraping his section.

After ten minutes my right leg began to feel the standing.

After fifteen, my shoulder wanted a different angle.

I sat.

Nobody congratulated me for recognizing fatigue.

Davin had repaired the canvas corner before I noticed he was done.

He handed the box back to Nessa when she returned.

She checked the patch.

Pulled once.

"Good."

Davin looked at me.

I pointed at him.

"Don't."

He smiled.

Nessa took the box inside.

The afternoon became paint.

Old paint.

Bad paint.

Dust in my hair.

Dust on my sleeves.

Dust inside the fold of my collar.

The cream flat surrendered a patch of dark red wide enough to look like a stripe from an older room. Venn returned and wiped the cleaned sections. Jori used a small brush to clear the frame edges. Davin mixed a thin wash in a bucket for the scraped patch I had created.

I watched him.

"Blue?"

"Blue."

"Same blue?"

He looked into the bucket.

"Blue enough."

Healthy artistic standard.

He painted over my mistake.

The wet patch was visibly newer than the rest.

Jori looked at it.

"Dry darker."

Davin said, "Mostly."

"How much mostly?"

"Tomorrow."

There was no answer to that.

By late afternoon, the two flats were not beautiful.

They were usable.

Loose paint gone.

Edges cleaned.

Canvas corner repaired.

My pale mistake blue again.

The old gold stars mostly erased except one high enough that nobody had needed to touch it.

I looked at it.

Jori followed my eyes.

"Loose?"

"No."

"Then it stays."

History survived through structural integrity.

I liked that more than I should have.

Rinna came out with a coin.

One copper.

Normal theatre work.

I took it.

"No rehearsal?"

"No."

"Tomorrow?"

"Not for you yet."

Clear.

"No wall role?"

Rinna looked at the flats.

"You've had enough."

Davin said, "He could stand very still."

"Better than Marek," Venn said.

I looked at him.

"You've been here six hours and already betrayed him."

"I've been here longer than six hours."

Right.

Other people existed before I noticed them.

Annoying feature of the world.

We carried the tools in.

I carried only the bucket of rags because it could hang from two fingers while I used the crutches carefully through the rear passage. Venn took the scraper box. Jori and Davin took the flats once the paint was dry enough to move.

Nobody gave me the awkward wall to prove anything.

Good workplace.

The repaired back latch shut cleanly behind us when Jori tested the door after the last flat came through.

It shut because it had been repaired.

Then he opened it again because Davin was still outside.

Ordinary technology remained complicated.

No one mentioned brown coats.

No one mentioned deliveries.

No one mentioned who opened the door for them.

The latest fact stayed where it was.

Rinna was arguing with a paper at the front table when I left.

Not a person.

The paper appeared to be winning.

I did not volunteer.

Outside, the rain had passed and left the streets darker without making them cleaner.

Blue paint remained under two fingernails despite washing.

My right palm was warm from the scraper. Shoulders used. Right leg mildly tired from the standing section. Residual limb comfortable. No pain. No weakness. No new problem.

I bought nothing on the walk home.

This was less financially noble than it sounded. I had bread waiting.

Lyssa was there before me.

That happened often enough now that neither of us treated it as information.

She was at the table with a dark piece of cloth that was not the brown cloth.

I stopped.

She looked at me.

"Don't."

"I have learned."

"Have you?"

"No."

She went back to the dark cloth.

I put my crutches against the wall.

The brown cloth remained in its old place.

Three pins.

Same fold.

The damaged shirt remained on the shelf.

Three threads.

Same failure.

I washed my hands again.

Blue came off one finger and stayed under another nail.

Lyssa looked over.

"Paint."

"Wall."

"Blue."

"Mostly."

She looked at me.

I pointed.

"Davin."

That explained exactly as much to her as the boy's answer had explained to me.

"Work?" she asked.

"Yes."

"Show?"

"No."

"Role?"

"Scraper."

She nodded.

Apparently valid.

I cut bread.

Lyssa worked for another minute, then said, "You missed."

I looked at the loaf.

"No."

She pointed at my sleeve.

A small blue streak crossed the outside of my forearm.

"That is theatre."

"On your shirt."

"Still theatre."

"Your shirt."

I looked at it.

Not the damaged one.

The better one.

Of course.

I rubbed the streak with my thumb.

It spread.

Lyssa watched.

"Improved."

I stopped touching it.

"Everyone has been saying that today."

She almost smiled.

I ate bread.

After a while she moved the dark cloth farther from my painted sleeve without comment.

That was fair.

"What was the wall before?" she asked.

I thought about the green layer.

The cream.

The dark red.

The little gold star.

"Several things."

"What now?"

"Kitchen."

She accepted that.

No questions about magic.

No questions about Vale.

No questions about the theatre's strangers.

I did not offer any.

The new dark cloth remained whatever it was.

The old brown cloth remained whatever it was.

My shirt had acquired blue paint without solving the three loose threads on the other one.

This felt like progress in the most honest available sense.

Before bed, I washed my hands a third time.

The last blue mark under my nail stayed.

I left it there.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 242

## THE SPENDER

The right crutch grip had turned.

Not much.

Enough.

I noticed it because the seam that normally sat along the underside had moved against the base of my thumb sometime between yesterday's wall and this morning's bread.

I turned the crutch in my hand.

The grip did not move.

Only the wrapping had.

This was better than the crutch breaking and worse than the crutch being free.

I pressed the edge with my thumb.

No tear.

No exposed wood.

No sharp tack.

The wrap had simply shifted around the handle and tightened unevenly.

Ordinary wear.

I hated ordinary wear.

It had no villain.

Lyssa was already gone.

The dark cloth from last night was not on the table. The brown cloth was.

Three pins.

Same fold.

My damaged shirt remained on the shelf.

Three loose threads.

My better shirt had a blue paint streak on the sleeve because I had spent yesterday improving theatre property by damaging my own.

I wore it anyway.

A blue streak was not structural.

I had learned that word.

I ate bread, drank water, and checked the grip again as though a second inspection might produce a different economy.

It did not.

The right handle felt slightly thicker on one side and slightly thinner on the other.

No pain.

No weakness.

Right palm normal after sleep.

Shoulders normal.

Right leg normal.

Residual limb comfortable.

Left tip boring.

The crutch worked.

I could ignore it.

That was how maintenance became repair.

I took both crutches and left.

The repairer's shop was open.

He was working on somebody else's walking stick when I arrived, which offended me in a small private way.

I had become accustomed to shops existing specifically at the moment I needed them.

The man behind the counter sat with the stick across his knees. A brass-colored ferrule lay beside him. He was shaving a thin curl from the end of the wood with a small knife.

He looked up.

Then at my crutches.

"Tip?"

"Grip."

He put the knife down.

"Which?"

"Right."

He pointed at the bench.

"Sit."

This relationship had not grown warmer.

It had grown shorter.

I sat.

The other customer was an older man in a dark cap who stood near the door with his hands folded over his stomach. He looked at the walking stick, not at me.

The repairer finished the shaving, fitted the ferrule, twisted it once, removed it, shaved another sliver, then fitted it again.

The older man said, "Too tight?"

"Was."

"Now?"

The repairer knocked the ferrule once against the heel of his hand.

"Now not."

Strong sales language.

He fixed it in place, handed the stick over, and made the man test it on the floor.

The man leaned on it.

Turned.

Tapped it twice.

"Good."

"Pay."

I liked this shop.

The older man paid and left.

The repairer looked at me.

"Right."

I handed him the right crutch.

He turned it over once.

Then twice.

His thumb found the shifted seam immediately.

"You twist."

"I walk."

"You twist too."

"Accusation."

"Grip."

He held the crutch horizontally and showed me where the wrap had crept.

The material around the handle was dark and smooth from my palm. One edge had shifted far enough that the overlap no longer sat evenly beneath the wood.

"Replace?" I asked.

"No."

That improved my mood.

"Why not?"

"Still good."

That improved it further.

He picked at the end of the wrap with a blunt tool.

The material lifted.

"Loose here. Tight here."

He pointed to opposite sides.

"Take it off?"

"Part."

"How much is part?"

He looked at me.

"Enough."

Apparently Jori had relatives.

He loosened the outer turns without unwrapping the entire handle, pulled the material flat, then worked it back around with even tension.

I watched for maybe thirty seconds before deciding I understood the process.

This was false.

"Could I do that next time?"

"Yes."

I waited.

He kept working.

"That sounded too easy."

"It is easy."

"Then why am I paying you?"

"Because you brought it here."

Fair.

He pressed the seam down with his thumb and reached for a small tack.

I looked at the tack.

"That was there before?"

"No."

"Why now?"

"Because it moved."

"Is the tack going into my hand?"

"No."

"Useful standard."

He set it where the underside overlap met the wood, well away from where my palm closed, then drove it flush with two light taps.

He ran his thumb over it.

Then mine.

"Feel?"

I rubbed the underside.

The tack was there if I searched for it.

Not if I gripped normally.

"No."

"Good."

He handed the crutch back.

I closed my right hand around it.

The handle felt narrower than it had this morning.

Not actually narrower.

Even.

My palm noticed the change because it had spent too many hours learning the wrong one.

"Stand."

I stood.

Both tips on the floor.

Weight through the grips.

No slip.

No edge under the thumb.

I took two steps.

Turned.

Took two back.

The repairer watched my right hand rather than my leg.

I appreciated the accuracy.

"Turn again."

"Which way?"

"Both."

I turned left.

Then right.

The wrap stayed where it belonged.

"Fine," he said.

"I enjoy how moved you are."

"Other one."

I looked at the left grip.

"What about it?"

"Give."

I handed him the left crutch.

He checked the wrap.

Pressed the seam.

Twisted the handle in both directions.

Then handed it back.

"Fine."

"Should we do that one too?"

"No."

"For balance?"

"No."

"Matching?"

"No."

He looked almost offended.

"If good, leave."

That was a cruel policy for a man who took money for repairs.

I looked at the right grip.

"How long will it last?"

He shrugged.

"Until it doesn't."

Hessa and this man should never meet.

Or perhaps they had and the universe had wisely kept it from me.

I paid him.

The amount was ordinary.

The loss felt personal.

Not because it was large.

Because it had been money before I woke and was now grip.

Necessary grip.

Still grip.

I put the remaining coins away.

I had bought no new ability. The crutch did not become faster. I did not become taller. I had paid to make one irritating seam return to where it used to be.

Maintenance had terrible marketing.

The repairer had already picked up another piece of work from behind the counter.

No farewell.

I left.

Outside, the right grip felt too new for perhaps half a street.

Then my hand stopped noticing.

That was what I had paid for.

Carrow was brighter than yesterday.

The rain had cleaned nothing important.

Mud remained in the joints between stones. Wagon wheels had redistributed it. The air smelled of damp wood, cooking fat, and something sharp from a dyer's lane I did not take.

I had no theatre call.

Rinna had said not for me yet.

No Hessa note.

No reason to invent one.

Vale existed.

The debt also existed.

I had just spent money maintaining the thing that allowed me to move around the city and earn more money.

This was probably defensible.

Antonius would still prefer the money.

I stood at the next corner longer than necessary.

Home was one direction.

Vale's office was another.

I had not been promised work.

That mattered.

I went to Vale anyway.

Not because the repair had ruined me.

It had not.

Because debt did not become less real on days when nobody summoned me.

The office door was open.

The ink-fingered clerk was at the front desk with three stacks of paper arranged around him.

He looked up when I entered.

Then looked past me.

"No bundle."

"I did not bring one."

"No, ours."

"Ah."

He went back to the papers.

I waited.

He looked up again.

"What?"

"Work?"

"No."

That had been fast.

"None?"

"None for you."

Important distinction.

I looked at the three stacks.

"Those appear extremely work-shaped."

"They are."

"And yet."

"And yet."

I was beginning to suspect every profession in Carrow shared one teacher.

"What are those?"

"Accounts."

"I have handled accounts."

"These need decisions."

"I can make decisions."

"That is the problem."

I leaned on the repaired right grip.

It did not move.

"What is suitable?"

"Nothing today."

No apology.

No promise about tomorrow.

No attempt to create work because I had arrived with debt.

Correct.

Still annoying.

"What about outgoing packets?"

"Done."

"Returned acknowledgments?"

"Done."

"Sealing?"

"Tomorrow, maybe. Not today."

There it was.

Maybe.

The most expensive word in Carrow.

I looked toward the rear.

Antonius was not visible.

"Is he here?"

"Yes."

"Does he have work?"

The clerk looked at me.

"For you?"

"That is usually the relevant category."

"No."

I nodded.

Then stayed where I was.

The clerk finished a line.

Dipped his pen.

Wrote another.

Eventually he said, "Standing there doesn't create it."

"I was testing."

"Result?"

"Negative."

"Good."

I hated that word.

I turned to leave.

"Greg."

I looked back.

The clerk pointed at my right crutch.

"New?"

"Adjusted."

"Tip?"

"Grip."

He nodded.

That was all.

Apparently the office kept its interest in my equipment at the level of whether I could continue being useful.

Consistent.

Outside again, I had accomplished something important.

I had confirmed I could not earn debt credit today.

This felt like paying for information.

I had not paid for the information.

Small victory.

My stomach interrupted before I could develop a philosophy around unemployment.

I walked toward the cookshop district.

Not the theatre cookshop.

Another one.

I had eaten there once before, far enough back that I could not remember what I had ordered and the woman behind the counter did not remember me at all.

Healthy relationship.

The board listed stew, beans, and a meat pie that cost more than I wanted it to.

I looked at the pie.

Then at the stew.

Then at my money.

The grip repair had already happened.

The debt still existed.

Hunger also existed.

Three systems.

Only one could be solved with stew.

I bought stew.

The woman put it in a heavy bowl and pointed to an open place near the wall.

I sat.

A laborer across from me had sawdust on both sleeves and one red mark across his forehead where something had rested there.

He ate without speaking.

I respected him.

For almost five minutes, nothing happened.

Nobody asked me to perform.

Nobody asked me to test magic.

Nobody asked me to compare account lines.

Nobody asked whether the theatre used its front or back door.

I ate stew.

It was too salty.

I finished it anyway.

The laborer left before me.

A woman took his place, put a basket under the table, and began eating beans.

Carrow replaced people quickly when seats were useful.

I paid attention to the right grip when I stood.

Still flat.

Still even.

The tack did not touch my hand.

The repair was becoming invisible.

Good repair.

I left the cookshop with less money and more body.

That was the entire exchange.

On the way home I passed the lane toward the theatre.

I did not take it.

No call.

No maybe transformed by proximity.

Not for me yet had been clear.

I kept walking.

A handcart blocked half the street near a cooper's yard while two men rolled a barrel toward it.
